paragraphs.text: VARIOUS SOUL-PROFITING TEACHINGS OF OUR HOLY FATHER. PROLOGUE BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR. It should be known that there have been two men named Dorotheus and two named Barsanuphius. One pair was sick with the errors of Severus. The other embraced orthodoxy and perfect asceticism, and it is these who appear in this book. For this reason we hold the book to be acceptable, virtuous and highly profitable to the soul, since it is truly the work of the blessed Dorotheus, who proved to be orthodox and distinguished among the Fathers, and not of the other one, who held different opinions and was [?]. Our father and confessor of Christ, Theodore, the all-wise abbot of the Studium, taught this very well in the testament he left to his disciples. After setting out the content of his own faith and anathematizing all the godless heretics together, he spoke as follows: "And I accept every divinely inspired book of the Old and New Testament, and also the lives and divine writings of all the holy and inspired Fathers, both teachers and ascetics. I have said this because of [?] Pamphilus, who came from the East and slandered these holy men, I mean Mark, Isaiah, Barsanuphius, Dorotheus and Hesychius. I do not mean the Barsanuphius, Isaiah and Dorotheus who were 'headless' along with the Acephali, and 'horned' along with the so-called Decacerati [?], and who are anathematized by Sophronius, now among the saints, in his book. Those men are clearly different from the ones mentioned above,

whom I accept as handed down by the fathers. I did so after inquiring of the most holy patriarch Tarasius, who formerly held the high priesthood, and of other trustworthy persons, both natives and easterners. Another reason is that the image of Barsanuphius stands with the holy Fathers Antony, Ephraim and others on the sacred altar-covering of the Great Church. And I have found nothing impious in their teachings, but on the contrary much benefit for the soul." See, then: our great father Theodore has clearly distinguished the reputations of the two men named Dorotheus, and has declared the teaching of the one presented here to be most beneficial. And it truly is very profitable to the soul. Whoever orders his life carefully according to it will advance to the perfect measure of virtue in Christ. Having attained this, he will be adorned with the crown of dispassion, and will be counted worthy [?] of eternal life with the saints.

A letter to the brother who asked that the discourses spoken by our holy father Dorotheus be sent to him. 1. I praise your resolve. I call blessed your zeal for the good, and your blessed soul, which is truly a lover of the beautiful, most beloved brother. To search so diligently into the life of our truly blessed and God-worthy father, who bears the name of God's gift, and to praise it so sincerely, is to praise virtue, [?] to love God, and to care for the true life. For as the blessed Gregory says, praise begets zeal, zeal begets virtue, and virtue begets blessedness. So it is right to rejoice, and truly to rejoice with you, at such progress of yours. You seem to be following in the footsteps of the man who imitated the One who is meek and lowly of heart. He contemplated the spiritual renunciation of Peter and those with him, and so stripped himself of attachment to visible things, and so gave himself over to the things that were his according to God, that he too, I know well, could say to the Savior with boldness: "Behold, we have left everything and followed you." So, made perfect in a short time with God's help, he fulfilled long years. He did not live in physical deserts and mountains, nor did he set great store by ruling over the wild beasts of the body. Instead he embraced the desert of the soul, longed to draw near to the eternal mountains, knew wonderfully how to give light, and knew how to tread on the heads of soul-killing serpents and scorpions. With the help of Christ he was soon counted worthy to attain these things, through the athletic slaying of his own will. This won for him the unerring path of the fathers. This showed him that the blessed burden is light, and revealed that the saving and kindly yoke is truly kindly. [?] 27.

2. He learned humility, the best road to the heights. He received the saying "Be merciful and meek" both in deed and in keeping with the words of the holy elders, and through these he was adorned with all the virtues. So the blessed man always had on his lips that saying of the elders: "He who has succeeded in cutting off his own will has reached the place of rest." He sought rightly and found that self-love is the root of all the passions, and that self-love is made up of our bittersweet will. So he used this powerful remedy and withered the evil shoots together with the root. He became a pure cultivator of immortal things and bore the fruit of true life. He acquired the treasure hidden in the field, which he had sought well and found, and he became truly rich in things that are never emptied. I wished that my tongue and mind were capable enough for me to be counted worthy to set out his holy life in detail, for the common benefit and as a most exact pattern of virtue. I wished to show how that blessed man ran along the road that is narrow, yet spacious and paradoxical. It is narrow because it is unerring and does not spread out, and because it guards against straying over the cliff on either side. This is how the friend of God, the truly great Basil, defines the narrowness of the hard and saving road. It is spacious because of his freedom from attachment and his openness toward those who led him to God, and above all because of the height of humility, which alone, according to the great Antony, rises above all the snares of the devil. So in him was truly fulfilled the verse: "Your commandment is exceedingly broad." 3. But since this is beyond my power, I will pass over it. For I know that among all the good qualities of the blessed man was this as well: like a truly wise bee, he gathered from the sayings of the so-called outside philosophers whatever he found useful, and readily put it forward for instruction at the right time, such as "Nothing in excess," "Know yourself," and the like. As I have said, I am driven to pass over these things, if not by willing choice, then at least by the necessity of my own inability. But what your zealous soul, which loves the beautiful, commanded me, I have confidently done, since I was wary of the weight of disobedience and afraid of the penalty for sloth. With this present letter I have sent to you, prudent bankers under God, the talent that lay idle with me. I mean the teachings of the blessed man that have been found, both those he himself was counted worthy to receive from his own fathers and those he handed on to his own disciples. In this he followed our first and true Guide and [?], both doing and teaching. We have not been able to find all of his holy discourses, only very few, and these were gathered here and there by certain zealous people through God's providence. Still, it will be enough

1617 DOCTRINE [?] I. 1618 to set even this little before your dexterity, according to the saying: "Give an occasion to a wise man, and he will become wiser." [Proverbs 9:9 (?)] But first, more briefly, the story of the blessed Dositheus, who became the first disciple of the blessed Abba Dorotheus while Dorotheus was still in the monastery of Abba Seridos, completing the struggle of submission in Christ.

INSTRUCTION 1 OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS ABBA DOROTHEUS. On Renunciation. 1. In the beginning, when God made man, he placed him in paradise, as the divine and holy Scripture says. He adorned him with every virtue and gave him a commandment not to eat from the tree in the middle of paradise. And man lived in the delight of paradise, in prayer, in contemplation, in the midst of glory and honor. His senses were sound, and he was [?] in his natural state, just as he had been created. For God made man according to the image of God, that is, immortal, free to choose, and adorned with every virtue. But when he transgressed the commandment and ate from the tree that God had commanded him not to eat from, he was cast out of paradise. He fell from the natural state and came to be in a state contrary to [Genesis (?) 2:15.]

nature, that is, in sin, in love of glory, in love of the pleasures of this life, and in the other passions. He was dominated by them, for he had enslaved himself to them through the transgression. From then on evil gradually increased and death reigned. There was no godliness anywhere, and everywhere there was ignorance of God. Only a few, as I said, knew God: the Fathers who were moved by the natural law, such as Abraham and the other patriarchs, Noah, Jacob, and, in short, just a few. Those who knew God were very rare. For then the enemy spread out all his wickedness, since sin reigned. Then idolatry began, and polytheism, sorcery, murders and the rest of the devil's wickedness. Then the good God had pity on his creature and gave the written law through Moses. In it he forbade some things and prescribed others, as if saying: "Do this; do not do that." He gave a commandment and immediately said: "The Lord your God is one Lord," so as to draw their minds away from polytheism for the time being. And: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your mind." Everywhere he proclaims that God is one and that there is no other. For by saying "You shall love the Lord your God," he showed that God is one and that there is one Lord. And again in the Ten Commandments: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone, and cleave to him, and swear by his name." Then he adds: "You shall have no other gods, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above or on the earth below." For they used to worship every created thing. 2. So the good God gave the law as a help, for turning back and for correcting evil, and yet evil was not corrected. He sent prophets, and they could not do it either. For evil prevailed, as Isaiah says: "Neither wound nor bruise nor festering sore: there is no ointment to apply, nor oil, nor bandages." It is as if he said: The evil is not partial, nor in one place, but in the whole body. It encompasses the whole soul and holds all its powers in its grip. "There is no ointment to apply," and so on. That is to say, everything has been enslaved to sin, everything is held fast by it. And Jeremiah also says: "We treated Babylon, and she was not healed [?]." That is: "We made your name known, we proclaimed your commandments, your benefits, your promises, we warned beforehand of uprisings of enemies, and still she was not healed." That is, she did not repent, she was not afraid, and she did not turn back from her wickedness. As he also says elsewhere: "They did not accept discipline," that is, admonition and teaching. And in the psalm it says: "Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death." [?] ibid. 14 [?] Deuteronomy. Variant: "we announced beforehand." Variant: "elsewhere."

3. Then the good God, who loves mankind, sends his only-begotten Son. For only God could heal and overcome such a disease, and the prophets knew this. So David said plainly: "You who sit upon the cherubim, appear; stir up your power and come to save us." And: "Lord, bow the heavens and come down," and other things like these. The other prophets, too, each cried out a great deal in various ways. Sometimes they entreated him to come down, and sometimes they were fully assured that he would certainly come. So our Lord came, becoming man for our sake, so that, as Saint Gregory says, he might heal like by like: the soul by a soul and the flesh by flesh. For he becomes man in every respect, without sin. He took our very substance, the firstfruits of our lump of dough, and he becomes a new Adam, according to the image of the one who fashioned him. For he renews the natural state and makes the senses sound again, as they were in the beginning. By becoming man he renewed fallen man. He set free the man who had been enslaved to sin and was held by it by force. For man was led by force and tyranny by the enemy. Even when we did not want to sin, we sinned almost by force, as the Apostle says, speaking in our person: "For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do." 4. So God, having become man for our sake, freed man from the tyranny of the enemy. He destroyed all the enemy's power, shattered his very strength, and rescued us from being under his hand and enslaved to him, unless we ourselves willingly choose to sin. For, as he said, he gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and on all the power of the enemy, having cleansed us of every sin through holy baptism. For holy baptism forgives every sin and wipes it away. But the good God also knew our weakness and foresaw that we would sin again even after holy baptism, as it is written: "For the heart of man is [?] intent on evil from his youth." So in his goodness he gave us holy commandments that cleanse us, so that if we wish, we may be cleansed again by keeping them, not only from our sins but also from the passions themselves. For the passions are one thing and sins are another. The passions are anger, vainglory, love of pleasure, hatred, evil desire and the like. Sins are the activities of the passions, when someone actually puts them into practice and carries out through the body the deeds that the passions suggest to him. Indeed, someone can have the passions without acting on them. Variant: "Gregory." Variant: "to heal."

5. So, as I said, he gave us commandments that cleanse us even from our passions themselves, from the very evil dispositions of our inner man. For he passes on to the inner man the discernment of good and evil, wakes it up, and shows it the causes by which it comes to sin. And he says: "The law said, 'Do not commit adultery,' but I say, 'Do not even desire.' The law said, 'Do not murder,' but I say, 'Do not even be angry.'" For if you desire, then even if you do not commit adultery today, the desire will not stop troubling you inside until it throws you into the act as well. If you become angry and stir yourself up against your brother, sooner or later you fall into slandering him as well, then into plotting against him. Advancing like this little by little, you finally come even to murder. Again, the law says: "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth," and so on. But he urges us not only to accept patiently the blow of the one who strikes us, but also to turn the other cheek to him with humility. Back then the aim of the law was to teach us not to do what we do not want to suffer. So it held us back from doing evil through the fear of suffering it. Now, as I said, what is required is to drive out hatred itself, love of pleasure itself, love of glory itself, and the rest.

6. Simply put, the aim of our Master Christ now is to teach us how we came into all these sins and how we fell into all these evil days. First, as I have already said, he set us free through holy baptism, giving us the forgiveness of sins. He gave us the power to do good if we wish, and no longer to be dragged into evil by force, so to speak. For whoever is enslaved to sins is weighed down and dragged along by them, as it says: "Each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins." Then he teaches us through the holy commandments how to be cleansed from the passions themselves as well, so that we do not fall into the same sins again through them. Further, he shows us the cause by which one comes to despise and disobey even the commandments of God themselves. So he provides us with the cure for this as well, so that we may be able to obey and be saved. What, then, is this cure,

[?] obedience and the salvation of souls. By this I mean true humility. I do not mean humility in words alone or in outward bearing, but a humble disposition formed within the heart itself. 7. So whoever wishes to find true humility and rest for his soul, let him learn humility. Let him see that in it lies all joy, all glory and all rest, just as in pride lies everything opposite. For how did we come into all these afflictions? Was it not because of our pride? Was it not because of our folly? Was it not because we clung to our evil choice? Was it not because we held fast to the bitterness of our own will? How else? Was man not created in every delight, in every joy, in every rest, in every glory? Was he not in paradise? He was commanded, "Do not do this," and he did it. Do you see the pride? Do you see the stiff neck? Do you see the insubordination? Then God, seeing that shamelessness, says: "This one is a fool. He does not know how to rejoice. If he does not go through bad days, he will go off and perish completely. For if he does not learn what affliction is, he will not learn what rest is." Then he gave him what he deserved and cast him out of paradise. He was handed over to his own self-love and his own wills, so that it might break his bones. This was so that he might learn not to follow himself but the commandment of God, and so that the very misery of disobedience might teach him the rest that comes from obedience. As he says in the prophet: "Your apostasy will discipline you." Even so, as I have often said, God's goodness did not neglect his own creature. Again he urges, again he calls: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest." It is as if he said: "See, you have labored. See, you have suffered misery. See, you have experienced the evil of your insubordination. Come now, turn back. Come, recognize your own powerlessness, so that you may come into your rest and your glory. Come, live through humility, you who were put to death by haughtiness. 'Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.'" 8. Ah, my brothers, what pride does! Ah, what humility can do! What need was there for all these roundabout ways? If from the beginning he had humbled himself, obeyed God and kept the commandment, he would not have fallen. Then again, after he had disgraced himself, God gave him an opportunity to repent and receive mercy, and still his neck stayed stiff. For God came and said to him: "Adam, where are you?" This means: "From what glory have you come to what shame?" And then he asks him: "Why did you sin? Why did you transgress?" Variant: "shamelessness."

In this way he was urging him in particular to say: "Forgive me." But there is no humility anywhere. And where is the "Forgive me"? There is no repentance anywhere, but the opposite. Adam contradicts and answers back: "The woman whom you gave me." He does not say, "My wife deceived me," but "The woman whom you gave me," as if to say, "The calamity you brought down on my head." For this is how it is, brothers: when a man does not hold fast to blaming himself, he does not shrink even from accusing God himself. Then God comes to her and says to her: "Why did you too not keep the commandment?" It is as if he were saying in particular: "At least say 'Forgive me,' so that your soul may be humbled and you may receive mercy." And again, there is no "Forgive me" anywhere. For she too answers: "The serpent deceived me," as if to say: "If he sinned, what has that to do with me?" What are you doing, you wretches? Make a prostration, acknowledge your fault, take pity on your nakedness! But not one of them deigned to blame himself, and not one [?] was found to have even a little humility. And now, see plainly where our condition has come to. See how many and what kinds of evils it has brought on us: justifying ourselves, holding fast to our own will, and following ourselves. These are the offspring of pride, the enemy of God. In the same way, the offspring of humility are blaming oneself, not trusting one's own understanding, and hating one's own will. Through these one is counted worthy to recover oneself and return to the natural state, through the [?] of the holy commandments of Christ. For without humility one cannot submit to the commandments or arrive at anything at all. As Abba Mark said: "Without contrition of heart it is impossible to be rid of evil and acquire virtue." For through contrition of heart one accepts [?] the commandments [?], is freed from evil, acquires the virtues, and so returns to one's own rest. All the saints knew this, and they hastened by every humble way of life to [?] themselves to God. For there were some lovers of God who, after holy baptism, wished not only to cut off [?] the activities of the passions but also to conquer the passions themselves and become dispassionate. Such were Saint Antony, Pachomius [?], and the other God-bearing Fathers. 9. Their aim, then, was to cleanse themselves, as the Apostle says, from every defilement of flesh and spirit. They knew that by keeping the commandments, as we have already said, the soul [?] is cleansed. That is, the mind too is cleansed, recovers its sight and comes into its natural state, for "the commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes." They realized that while they were in the world they could not easily achieve virtue. So they devised for themselves a strange life, a strange way of living, I mean the solitary

…life, and they began to flee the world and to live in the deserts, in fasting and sleeping on the ground, in vigils and every other hardship, renouncing all homeland and kin, money and possessions; in short, they crucified themselves to the world. And they not only kept the commandments but also offered gifts to God. Let me tell you how. The commandments were given to all Christians, and every Christian is bound to keep them; they are, as one might say, the taxes owed to the king. Who says, “I will not pay taxes to the king,” and escapes punishment? But there are great and illustrious men in the world who not only pay their taxes to the king but also bring him gifts, and these are counted worthy of great honor, great rewards and high rank. So too the Fathers not only kept the commandments but also offered gifts to God. And the gifts are virginity and poverty. These are not commandments; they are gifts. For nowhere is it written, “Do not take a wife, do not have children.” Nor again did Christ give a commandment saying, “Sell your possessions.” Indeed, when the lawyer came to him and said, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” he answered, “You know the commandments: You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,” and so on. And when the man said, “All these I have kept from my youth,” he added, “If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor,” and so on. See, he did not say “Sell your possessions” as one giving a command, but as one giving advice. For to say “If you wish” is not the language of one commanding but of one advising.
11. So, as we said, the Fathers offered to God, besides the other virtues, the gifts of virginity and poverty; and, as we said before, they crucified the world to themselves, and then they strove to crucify themselves to the world as well, as the Apostle says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” What, then, is the difference? The world is crucified to a man when the man renounces the world and becomes a monk, leaving parents, money, possessions, business and trade; then the world is crucified to him, for he has left it. And this is what the Apostle means by “The world has been crucified to me.” Then he adds, “and I to the world.” How, then, is a man crucified to the world? When, after being freed from external things, he struggles also against the pleasures themselves, against the very desires for things, and against his own wills, and puts his passions to death; then he himself is crucified to the world and is counted worthy to say with the Apostle, “The world has been crucified to me,

and I to the world.” Our Fathers, as we said, having crucified the world to themselves, strove through their struggles and crucified themselves to the world as well. We, for our part, think we have crucified the world to ourselves because we left it and came to the monastery, but we are not willing to crucify ourselves to the world; for we still have its pleasures, we still have its attachments, we are attached to its glory, we are attached to food and clothing. If a tool is a good one, we become attached to it, and we let that little tool work its effect in us, as Abba Zosimas said. We think we have gone out of the world and left [?] it, and we come to the monastery, and then we satisfy our attachment to it through cheap things. This happens to us out of great folly: having left great and precious things, we indulge our passions over trifles. For each of us left what he had: the one who had great things left great things, and the one who had anything at all, he too left what he had, each according to his means; and we come to the monastery and, as I said, satisfy our attachment through cheap and worthless things. We ought not to act like this. Rather, just as we renounced the world and its things, so we ought also to renounce our very attachment to material things, and to know what this renunciation is, why we came to the monastery, and what the habit is that we receive, and to fashion ourselves according to it, and to struggle as our fathers did.
12. The habit we wear is a colobium without sleeves, a leather belt, an analabos, and a cowl. These are symbols, and we ought to learn what the symbols of our habit signify for us. Why do we wear a colobium without sleeves? Everyone else has sleeves; why do we not? The sleeves are symbols of the hands, and the hands stand for action. So when a thought comes to do something with our hands that belongs to the old man, say, to steal or to [?], or simply to commit any sin at all with the hands, we ought to pay attention to our habit and learn that we have no sleeves; that is, we have no hands for doing anything that belongs to the old man. Our colobium also has [?]

[?] robe. First, as a king, for he is the King of those who reign and the Lord of those who rule; and then also as one mocked by those impious men. So we too, having the purple mark, promise, as I said, to bear all his sufferings. And just as a soldier does not leave his service and go off to become a farmer or a merchant, since he would then lose his rank, as the Apostle says, “No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him,” so we too ought to keep up the contest and be free from care about all the things of this world, and give our time to God alone, as it says, so that one may be a virgin, devoted and undistracted.
13. We also have a belt. Why do we wear it? The belt we wear is a symbol, first, that we are ready for work. For everyone who wants to work first girds himself and then begins the work, as it says, “Let your loins be girded.” And again, it means that just as the belt is made from a dead body, so we too should put our desire to death. For the belt is worn around our loins, and there are the kidneys, in which the desiring part of the soul is said to be. This is what the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are on earth: fornication, impurity,” and so on. We also have the analabos. The analabos is placed crosswise over our shoulders; that is, we carry the symbol of the cross on our shoulders, as it says, “Take up your cross and follow me.” And what is the cross but complete mortification, which is accomplished in us through faith in Christ? For faith, as it says again in the Gerontikon, always clears away what hinders us and makes our labor unimpeded, the labor that brings us to such complete mortification. That is, a person should mortify himself to all the things of this world: if he has left his parents, he should struggle against his attachment to them as well; likewise with money or possessions; and whatever thing he renounces, he should be willing to renounce his very attachment to it too, as we have already said. This is perfect renunciation. We also receive the cowl, and this is the symbol of humility. For little, innocent children wear cowls, but a grown man does not wear a cowl. We wear it, then, so that we may be infants in malice, as the Apostle says: “Do not be children in your thinking, but be infants in malice.” What does it mean to be an infant in malice? An infant, having no malice, is not angry if it is dishonored, and is not vain if it is honored; if someone takes its things, it is not upset; for it is an infant in malice: it does not avenge a wrong, it does not lay claim to glory. Again, the cowl is a symbol of the grace of God. For just as the cowl covers and warms a child's head, so too the grace

of God covers our mind, as it says [?] mortification of irrational desire; and the cowl [?] a sign of innocence and of infancy in Christ.
14. Let us therefore live in keeping with our habit, as the Fathers said, so that we do not wear a habit that is not ours. But just as we have left the great things, let us leave the small ones too; we have left the world, let us leave its attachments too. For attachments, as I said, bind us to the world again even through small things of no account, and we do not notice it. If, then, we want to be completely set free and liberated, let us learn to cut off our wills, and in this way, little by little, with God's help, we make progress and arrive at freedom from attachment. For nothing benefits people as much as cutting off their own will; truly, a person advances by this practice almost more than by any other virtue. A man traveling along a road who finds a shortcut and takes it gets far ahead on that road by means of the shortcut. So it is with one who travels this road of cutting off the will. For by cutting off his own will a person acquires freedom from attachment, and from freedom from attachment he comes, with God, to perfect dispassion. One can cut off ten wills in a short space of time. And how? [?] A person is walking for a little while and sees something, and his thought says to him, “Look over there,” and he says to the thought, “No, I will not look,” and he cuts off his will and does not look. Again, he comes upon some people who are slandering, and his thought says to him, “You say such-and-such too,” and he cuts off his will and does not say it. Again his thought says to him, “Go and ask the cook what he is cooking,” and he does not go, and cuts off his will. He sees something, and his thought says to him, “Ask who brought it,” and he cuts off his will and does not ask. And by cutting off in this way he gets into the habit of cutting off; beginning with the small things, he begins to cut off the great ones too with ease, and so in the end he comes to have no will of his own at all, but whatever happens contents him as though it were his own. And though he does not want to do his own will, he is always found doing it. For the one who has nothing of his own finds that everything that happens is his own. And so he is found, as we said, to be without attachment, and from freedom from attachment, as I said, he comes to dispassion.
15. See to what progress [?], little by little, cutting off one's own will leads. Such was that blessed Dositheus. From what a life, from what luxury, from what dullness he came, a man who had never heard the word of God! And yet you have heard to what heights, in a short time, holding fast to obedience and cutting off his own will brought him; and how God glorified him and did not allow

such virtue of his to be forgotten, but revealed it to the holy elder, who saw him among all those saints, enjoying their blessedness. I will tell you something else as well that happened in my own time, so that you may learn that obedience, and having no will of one's own, delivers a person even from death. Once, when I was at Abba Seridos's monastery, a disciple of a great elder from the region of Ascalon came there, sent by his abba on an errand to someone. He had an order from the elder to return to his own cell by evening. Meanwhile a very violent storm broke, with heavy rains, and the nearby torrent was in full flood. Yet he wanted to leave because of the elder's word. We begged him to stay, knowing that it was impossible for him to get across the river safely. But he would not be persuaded to stay. In the end we said, “Let us go with him as far as the river; when he sees it, he will turn back of his own accord.” So we went with him, and when we reached the river, he took off his clothes, tied them on his head, girded himself with his maphorion, and threw himself into the river, into all that fearsome current. We stood there astonished and trembling for fear he would die. But he kept on swimming and was at once on the other side; he put on his clothes, made a prostration to us from there, took his leave, and went off running. We stayed there marveling and amazed [?] at the power of the virtue: we were afraid even to look, while he crossed without danger because of his obedience. And that brother whom his abba sent on account of their needs to their agent in the village: when he saw himself being drawn by the agent's daughter into shameful intercourse, he had only to say, “God of my Father, deliver me,” and at once he found himself on the road to Scetis, going to his Father.
16. See the power of virtue, see the efficacy of a word, how much help there is in calling on God through the prayers of one's Father! He had only to say, “God, through the prayers of my Father, deliver me,” and at once he found himself on the road. Consider the humility and reverence of both of them. They were in straits, and the elder wanted to send the brother to the man who acted as their agent, and he did not say to him, “Go,” but said to him, “Do you want to go?” Likewise the brother did not say, “I will go,” but said to him, “I will do as you wish.” For he was afraid, both because of the occasions of stumbling and of disobeying his Father. Then, when they were in even greater straits, the elder said to him, “Get up and go”; and he did not say to him, “I hope in my God that he will protect you,” but said, “I hope in the prayers of my Father that they will protect you [?].” Likewise the brother, when he was tempted, did not say, “My God,

deliver me,” but, “God, through the prayers of my Father, deliver me.” And each of them put his hope in the prayers of his Father. See how they yoked obedience to humility. For just as a chariot is yoked together and one horse cannot get ahead of the other without its breaking, so obedience needs to have humility yoked together with it. And how can anyone be counted worthy of this grace unless, as I said, he forces himself to cut off his own wills and hands himself over, after God, to his own Father, doubting in nothing but doing everything with him with full assurance, as one who is obeying God? Who is worthy to receive mercy, who is worthy to be saved?
17. A story is told that once Saint Basil, passing through his monasteries, said to one of the superiors, “Do you have anyone who is being saved?” The abba said to him, “Through your prayers, master, we all want to be saved.” Saint Basil said to him again, “Do you have any of those who are being saved?” Then he understood, for he too was a spiritual man, and said, “Yes.” When the brother came, the saint said to him, “Give me water to wash.” He went and brought him water to wash. After Saint Basil had washed, the saint himself took the washing water and said to the brother, “Take it, and you wash too.” The brother took the water from the saint without questioning. Having tested him in this, the saint said to him again, “When I go into the sanctuary, come and remind me, so that I may ordain you.” Again he obeyed without questioning. And when he saw Saint Basil inside the sanctuary, he went and reminded him, and Basil ordained him and took him with him. For with whom was it fitting for such a blessed brother to be, if not with that holy God-bearer? You have no experience of unquestioning obedience, nor do you know the rest it brings. I once asked the elder Abba John, the disciple of Abba Barsanuphius: “Master, since Scripture says that we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many afflictions, and I see that I have not a single affliction, what should I do, lest I lose my soul?” For I had not a single affliction or care. If ever I happened to have a troubling thought, I would take my tablet and write to the elder, for I used to put my questions to him in writing too, before I became his attendant, and before I had finished writing I felt benefit and relief. Such was the freedom from care and the rest I had. But not knowing the power of the virtue, and hearing that we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many afflictions, I was afraid because I had no affliction. So when I told the elder, he answered me thus: “Do not be distressed; you have nothing to worry about. Everyone who places himself under obedience to the Fathers has this freedom from care and this rest.”

INSTRUCTION 2. On Humility. 1. One of the elders said: “Above all we need humility, being ready to say ‘Forgive me’ at every word we hear. For through humility all the works of the enemy and adversary are destroyed.” Let us examine the meaning of

the elder's saying. Why does he say, “Above all we need humility,” and not rather, “Above all we need self-control”? For the Apostle says, “Everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things.” Or why does he not say, “Above all we need the fear of God”? For Scripture says, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” And again, “By the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil.” Why does he not say, “Above all we need almsgiving,” or “faith”? For it says, “By almsgiving and faith sins are purged away.” And the Apostle says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” If, then, it is impossible to please God without faith, and sins are purged away by almsgiving and faith, and by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil, and the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things, how is it that he says, “Above all we need humility,” passing over all these things that are so necessary? The elder wants to show us that neither the fear of God itself, nor almsgiving, nor faith, nor self-control, nor any other of the virtues can be achieved without humility. That is why he says, “Above all we need humility, being ready to say ‘Forgive me’ at every word we hear; for through humility all the works of the enemy and adversary are destroyed.”
2. See, brothers, how great the power of humility is. See what efficacy there is in saying, “Forgive me.” And why is the devil called not only the enemy but also the adversary? He is called the enemy because he hates mankind, hates what is good, and lays snares; and he is called the adversary because he tries to obstruct every good thing. Does someone want to pray? He opposes him, hindering him through evil thoughts, through distraction, through listlessness. Does someone want to give alms? He hinders him through love of money, through sloth. Does someone want to keep vigil? He hinders him through sloth, through negligence. In every good thing we undertake he sets himself against us. That is why he is called not only the enemy but also the adversary. So through humility all the works of the enemy and adversary are destroyed. For humility is truly a great thing, and every one of the saints traveled the road by this very humility, and by toil shortened the journey, as it says, “Look upon my humility and my toil, and forgive all my sins”; and, “I was humbled, and the Lord saved me.” Humility alone can bring one in, as the elder Abba John used to say, but more slowly. So let us too humble ourselves a little, and we shall be saved. Even if, being weak, we cannot toil, let us strive to humble ourselves. And I trust in the mercy of God that, through even this little done with humility, we too shall find ourselves in the place of the saints there, those who toiled much and served God. Yes, we are weak and cannot

[?] not to be humbled [?]? Blessed, brothers, is the one who has humility. Humility is a great thing. That saint described well the one who has true humility, and that is why he said: "Humility does not grow angry, nor does it make anyone else angry." This may seem strange, since humility is opposed to vainglory alone and of course guards a person against it. But people also grow angry over money and over food. [?] he says that humility does not grow angry nor make anyone else angry? Humility is great, as we said, and it is powerful enough to draw the grace of God into the soul. Then this grace of God [?] shields the soul from these two other grievous passions. For what is more grievous than to grow angry and to provoke one's neighbor to anger, as someone said? Anger is utterly foreign to monks. Truly, if such a person is not quickly shielded by humility, he gradually comes into the state of a demon, troubling others and troubled himself. 3. That is why he says that humility does not grow angry nor make anyone else angry. But why do I speak of [?] two passions [?]? Humility shields the soul from every passion and from every temptation. When Saint Antony saw all the snares of the devil spread out, he groaned and asked God, "Who, then, gets past these?" And what did God answer him? "Humility gets past them." And what further marvel did he add? "And they do not even touch it." Do you see the power, sir? Do you see the grace of this virtue? Truly nothing is stronger than humility. Whatever painful thing happens to the humble person, he at once turns against himself and at once condemns himself as deserving it. He cannot bring himself to blame anyone or to lay the fault on others, and so he passes through it untroubled and unafflicted, in complete peace. That is why he neither grows angry nor makes anyone else angry. That is why the saint rightly said: "Before all things we need humility." 4. There are two kinds of humility, just as there are two kinds of pride. The first pride is when someone despises his brother and belittles him as if he were nothing, while counting himself superior to him. If such a person does not quickly come to his senses and make an effort, he gradually comes into the second pride, so that he becomes proud even against God and ascribes his good deeds to himself and not to God. Truly, my brothers, I once knew someone who came into this pitiable state. At first, if any of the brothers spoke to him, he would sneer at each one and say, "Who is that fellow? There is no one except Zosimas and those like him." Then he began to belittle these too and to say, "There is no one except Macarius." A little later he began to say, "Who

is Macarius? There is no one except Basil and Gregory." Then a little later he began to belittle these too, saying, "Who is Basil, and who is Gregory? There is no one except Paul and Peter." I said to him, "Truly, brother, you will come to despise these as well." Believe me, a short time later he began to say, "Who is Peter, and who is Paul? There is no one except the Holy Trinity." So in the end he grew proud even against God himself, and in this way he lost his mind. That is why, my brothers, we must struggle against the first pride, so that we do not gradually fall into complete pride as well. 5. There is also a worldly pride and a monastic pride. Worldly pride is when someone is proud toward his brother because he is richer or better-looking than he, or better dressed, or of nobler birth. So when we see ourselves taking vainglory in these things, or in our monastery being larger or wealthier, or in having many brothers, we must recognize that we are still in worldly pride. Sometimes a person also takes vainglory in natural gifts. For example, someone takes vainglory in having a fine voice and singing well, or in being capable and serving neatly. These are more respectable than the first, yet they too belong to worldly pride. Monastic pride is when someone takes vainglory in keeping vigil, in fasting, in being devout, in his way of life, or in his zeal. Sometimes a person even humbles himself for the sake of glory. These things belong to monastic pride. It is possible for us not to be proud at all; but if we are, let it at least be over monastic things and not worldly ones. So we have said what the first pride is and what the second is, and likewise what worldly pride is and what monastic pride is. Let us now learn what the two kinds of humility are. 6. The first humility is to consider one's brother wiser than oneself and superior in everything, and simply, as that saint said, to place oneself below everyone. The second humility is to ascribe one's good deeds to God. This is the perfect humility of the saints. It arises naturally in the soul from the practice of the commandments. Consider trees: when they bear much fruit, the fruit itself bends the branches and pulls them down, while a branch that bears no fruit rises up and grows straight. There are even some trees whose branches bear no fruit as long as they point upward; but if someone takes a stone, hangs it on the branch and pulls it down, then it produces fruit. So it is with the soul as well: when it is humbled, then it bears fruit, and the more fruit it bears, the more it is humbled. For the closer the saints draw to God, the more they see themselves as sinners. I remember that we were once talking about humility, and one of the notables of Gaza heard us say that the closer a person draws to God, the more he sees himself as

a sinner. He was astonished and said, "How can this be?" He did not understand and wanted to learn what the saying meant. I said to him, "Sir, you are a leading citizen. Tell me, what do you consider yourself in your city?" He said, "I consider myself a great man, the first in the city." I said to him, "And if you go to Caesarea, what do you consider yourself there?" He said, "I consider myself lower than the great men there." I said to him, "And if you go to Antioch, what do you consider yourself?" He said to me, "I consider myself a commoner." I said to him, "And if you go to Constantinople, close to the emperor, what do you consider yourself there?" He said to me, "I consider myself a pauper." Then I said to him, "You see, that is how the saints are: the closer they draw to God, the more they see themselves as sinners. For Abraham, when he saw the Lord, called himself earth and ashes, and Isaiah said, 'Woe is me, wretched and unclean as I am!' Likewise Daniel, when he was in the den with the lions, and Habakkuk came bringing the bread and said to him, 'Take the meal that God has sent you,' answered, 'Has God then remembered me?'" What humility his heart had! He was in the den with the lions, and they did not harm him, and not just once but a second time; and after all this he was amazed and said, "Has God then remembered me?" 7. Do you see the humility of the saints, how their hearts are disposed? Even when God sent them to help people, they would not consent, out of humility, fleeing from being glorified. A person dressed in pure silk who has a filthy rag thrown at him shrinks from it so that his precious garment is not soiled. In the same way the saints, clothed in the virtues, flee from human glory so that they are not soiled by it. But those who desire glory are like a naked man who is always trying to find a scrap of rag or anything at all to cover his shame. In the same way, the person who is naked of virtues seeks the glory of men. So when the saints were sent by God to help people, they would not consent, out of humility. Moses said, "I beg you, appoint someone else who is able, for I am weak of voice and slow of tongue." Jeremiah said, "I am too young." In short, each of the saints acquired this humility, as we said, by practicing the commandments. No one can put into words what this humility is or how it comes to be in the soul, unless a person learns it by experience; no one can learn it from words. Once Abba Zosimas was speaking about humility, and a sophist who happened to be there heard what he said. Wanting to understand it exactly, he said to him, "Tell me, how do you consider yourself a sinner? Do you not know that you are holy? Do you not know that you have virtues? Look, you see how you practice the commandments. How, when you do such things, can you consider yourself a sinner?" The old man could not find a way to give him an answer, but said to him, "I do not know how to tell you, but that is how I consider myself." But the sophist kept arguing with him, wanting to learn how this could be. The [?] [?] [?] 57. [?] Exodus.

old man could not find a way to explain the matter to him, and he began to say with his holy simplicity, "Do not twist me around; for my part, that is how I consider myself." When I saw that the old man was at a loss for an answer, I said to the sophist, "Is it not like sophistry and medicine? When someone has learned the art well and practices it, little by little, through practicing it, a kind of habit forms in the physician or the sophist. He cannot say, and does not know how to explain, how he came to have the skill. Little by little, as I said, the soul acquired it imperceptibly through practicing the art. It is the same with humility: from the practice of the commandments a habit of humility forms, and it cannot be put into words." When Abba Zosimas heard this, he rejoiced, and at once he embraced me and said, "You have found the answer; it is just as you said." The sophist too was satisfied when he heard it, and he also accepted the explanation. 8. The elders have said certain things that help us understand humility, but no one has managed to say what the disposition itself is as it forms in the soul. For when Abba Agathon was about to die, the brothers said to him, "Are you afraid too, Father?" He said, "I have done all I could to keep the commandments, but I am a man. How do I know whether my work has pleased God? For the judgment of God is one thing, and the judgment of men is another." See, he opened our eyes to understand humility and gave us a way to grasp it. But how it comes about in the soul, as I have often said, no one has managed to say, nor has anyone been able to grasp it in words, unless the soul has been found worthy to learn it from deeds. But the Fathers have told us what brings it about. For it says in the Book of the Elders that a brother asked an old man, "What is humility?" and the old man said, "Humility is a great and divine work. The way of humility is bodily labors undertaken with knowledge, and placing yourself below everyone; this is the way of humility. But humility itself is divine and beyond understanding." Why, then, does he say that bodily labors bring the soul to humility? In what sense are bodily labors virtues of the soul? As for placing oneself below everyone, we said above that it is opposed to the first pride. For how can someone who places himself below everyone consider himself greater than his brother, or be puffed up about anything, or blame or despise anyone? Likewise, praying continually is clearly opposed to the second pride. For it is obvious that the humble and devout person, knowing that no good can be accomplished in the soul without God's help and protection, never stops begging God to have mercy on him. Indeed, whoever prays to God constantly knows where his success came from, if he is found worthy to accomplish anything. He cannot become puffed up or ascribe it to his own strength; instead he ascribes all his good deeds to God, and

always gives thanks to him and always entreats him, trembling lest he lose such help and his weakness and helplessness be exposed. So through humility he prays, and through prayer he is humbled. The more he succeeds, the more he is humbled, and the more he is humbled, the more he is helped and makes progress through his humility. 9. Why, then, does he say that bodily labors bring humility? What does bodily labor have to do with the disposition of the soul? I will tell you. When the soul fell from the commandment into transgression, it was handed over, as Saint Gregory says, to the love of pleasure and to the self-will of error. It came to love bodily things and in a sense became one with the body, and became wholly flesh, as it says: "My spirit shall not remain with these men, because they are flesh." So this wretched soul suffers along with the body and is affected by whatever happens to it. That is why the old man said that bodily labor too leads to humility. For the soul of a healthy person is disposed one way and that of a sick person another; the soul of a hungry person one way and that of a well-fed person another. Likewise, the soul of a man sitting on a horse is disposed one way, that of a man sitting on a throne another, and that of a man sitting on the ground another; the soul of a man wearing fine clothes one way, and that of a man wearing shabby clothes another. Labor, then, humbles the body, and when the body is humbled, the soul is humbled along with it. So he rightly said that bodily labor too leads to humility. That is why, when Evagrius was assailed by blasphemous thoughts, he spent forty days without going under a roof. He was a man of knowledge and knew that blasphemy comes from pride, and that when the body is humbled the soul is humbled along with it. As a result, as the writer says, his body bred ticks like a wild animal's. So his labor was not undertaken because of the blasphemy itself, but for the sake of humility. The old man was right, then, to say that bodily labors lead to humility. May the good God grant us humility, for it rescues a person from many evils and shields him from great temptations.

DISCOURSE 3. On Conscience. 1. When God made man, he sowed in him something divine, like a thought warmer and brighter than the rest, with the nature of a spark. It enlightens the mind and shows it the difference between good and evil. This is called conscience, and it is the natural law. Conscience is the wells that Jacob dug, as the Fathers have said, and that the Philistines filled in. That is, it was by conscience

that all the patriarchs and all the saints before the written law pleased God. But when people buried it and trampled it underfoot through the onset of sin, we needed the written law, we needed the holy [?] prophets, we needed the very coming of our Master Jesus Christ, to uncover conscience and raise it up again, and to rekindle that buried spark through the keeping of his holy commandments. Now it is up to us either to bury it again or to let it shine out and enlighten us, if we obey it. For when our conscience tells us to do something and we ignore it, and it speaks again and we still do not do it but keep trampling on it, then we bury it, and it can no longer speak clearly to us because of the weight lying on it. Like a lamp seen through a screen [?], it begins to show us things more faintly, more darkly as it were. And so, gradually, just as no one can make out his own face in water that has been muddied with a great deal of earth, we find ourselves no longer perceiving what our conscience tells us, so that we think we hardly have one at all. Yet there is no one who does not have a conscience. For it is something divine, as we have already said, and it is never destroyed but always reminds us of our duty. We, however, do not perceive it, because, as I said, we ignore it and trample it down. That is why the prophet mourns over Ephraim and says, "Ephraim overpowered his adversary and trampled on judgment." By "adversary" he means conscience. Hence the Gospel also says, "Make friends with your adversary while you are still on the way with him, or he may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officers, and you will be thrown into prison. Truly I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny." Why does it call conscience an adversary? It is called an adversary because it always opposes our evil will. It tells us when we fail to do what we ought to do, and again when we do what we ought not to do, and it accuses us. That is why it calls conscience an adversary and gives the command [?] about being on the way with it. The way, as Saint Basil says, is this world. 2. So, brothers, let us take care to keep our conscience while we are in this world. Let us not give it cause to reproach us in any matter, and let us not trample on it in anything at all, even the smallest thing. For you should know that it is from these small and naturally trivial things that we come to disregard the great ones. When someone begins to say, "What does it matter if I say this word? What does it matter if I eat this little bit? What does it matter if I busy myself with this thing?", then from this "What does this matter?" and "What does that matter?" he contracts a bad and bitter spreading sore, and he begins to disregard and

trample on his own conscience in great and weightier things as well. And so, advancing little by little, he is in danger of falling into complete insensibility. Therefore take care that we do not neglect the small things; take care that we do not disregard

[?] is; it is a bad habit. Let us be watchful and take care of light matters while they are still light, so that they do not become heavy. Both doing right and sinning begin from small things and lead to great ones, whether good or evil. That is why the Lord commands us to keep our conscience, as if he were solemnly warning each person individually and saying to him, "Look at what you are doing, wretch; be watchful! Make friends with your adversary while you are still on the way with him." He also adds the fear and danger of the matter, saying, "or he may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officers, and you will be thrown into prison." And what next? "Truly I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny." For conscience, as I said, reproves us concerning good and evil, and shows us what to do and what not to do. And it will also accuse us in the age to come; that is why he says, "or he may hand you over to the judge," and the rest. 3. Keeping conscience involves many distinctions. A person must keep his conscience toward God, toward his neighbor and toward material things. Toward God, so that he does not disregard God's commandments. Even in matters where no one sees him and where nothing is required of him by anyone, he keeps his conscience toward God in secret. For example: someone neglected prayer; an impassioned thought arose in his heart, and he was not watchful and did not restrain himself, but went along with it [?] [?] as seemed likely, he suspected someone and condemned him. In short, everything that happens in secret, which no one knows except God and our conscience, we need to guard. This is conscience toward God. Conscience toward one's neighbor means doing absolutely nothing that one knows distresses or wounds one's neighbor, whether by deed, by word, by gesture or by look. For there is a gesture, as I am always telling you, that wounds one's neighbor, and there is a look that can wound. In short, whatever a person knows he is doing deliberately in order to give his neighbor a troubling thought, by it his own conscience is defiled, since it knows that he is acting deliberately to harm or distress. And this is keeping conscience toward the

[?] someone makes bad use of a thing. One should not let a thing be spoiled [?] or thrown away. Even if something has already been thrown down, one should not overlook it, however worthless it may be, but should pick it up and put it in its proper place. One should not misuse one's own clothes. For it may happen, suppose, that someone could wear his garment for another week or two, but he goes off and washes it needlessly [?] before its time and beats it. So instead of its serving him another five months or more, he wears it out with washing and makes it useless; and this is against conscience. Likewise with bedding: often a person could meet his needs with a single small blanket [?], and seeks [?] [?]

…a large mattress. Sometimes he has one made of hair, and wants to change it and get another, either new or handsome, out of vanity or out of carelessness. A man can make do with one patchwork blanket, and he looks for a linen [?] one, and perhaps even quarrels if he does not get it. And if he also begins to look at his brother and say, "Why does he have this, and I do not?", such a man is not making progress. Again, he spreads his garment or his covering out in the sun, and neglects to take it in, and lets it spoil; this too is against conscience. Likewise with food: a man can meet his need with a few greens or pulse, or a few olives, and he will not put up with doing so, but looks for some other food, more pleasant or more costly. All these things are against conscience. The Fathers say that a monk ought never to let his conscience reproach him, in anything whatsoever. So we need, brothers, to be watchful always and to guard ourselves from all these things, so that we do not fall into danger. For the Lord himself forewarned us, as we said above. May God grant us to hear and keep these things, so that the words of our Fathers may not turn into judgment against us.

DISCOURSE 1. On the Fear of God. 1. Saint John says in the Catholic Epistles, "Perfect love casts out fear." What, then, does the saint want to show us by this? What love is he speaking of, and what fear? For the Prophet says in the psalm, "Fear the Lord, all you his saints," and we find countless other sayings like this in the holy Scriptures. If, then, even the saints, who love the Lord so much, fear him, how can he say, "Love casts out fear"? The saint wants to show us that there are two fears, one introductory and one perfect; and that the one belongs to beginners, so to speak, in godliness, while the other belongs to the saints who have been made perfect, who have reached the measure of love. For example: someone does the will of God out of fear of punishment. This man, as we said, is still a beginner; he does not yet do good for its own sake, but out of fear of the lash. Another does the will of God because he loves God, loves him for the very purpose of pleasing God. This man knows what the good itself is; he has come to know what it is to be with God. See, this is the man who has the true love which the saint calls perfect, and this love brings him to the perfect fear. For such a man fears and keeps the will of God no longer because of the lash, no longer to avoid being punished, but because, as we said, he has tasted the very sweetness of being with God, and he fears that he may fall away from it, he fears that he may be deprived of it. This, then, is the

perfect fear, born of this love, that casts out the introductory fear. And that is why he says that perfect love casts out fear. Yet it is impossible to arrive at the perfect fear except by way of the introductory. 2. For there are three dispositions, as Saint Gregory says, by which we can please God. Either we please him because we fear punishment, and we are in the state of the slave; or we pursue the gains of the reward and fulfil what is commanded for our own benefit, and in this we resemble hirelings; or we do it for the sake of the good itself, and we are in the state of the son. For the son, when he comes to understanding, does his father's will not because he is afraid of being beaten, nor in order to receive a wage from him, but because he loves him, and keeps toward him the love and honour that belong to a father, and he is convinced that everything his father has is his. Such a one is counted worthy to hear, "You are no longer a slave, but a son and an heir of God through Christ." Such a one no longer fears God, as we said — that is, clearly, with that introductory fear — but loves him, as Saint Antony says: [?] "I no longer fear God." And when the Lord said to Abraham, after he had offered up his son, "Now I know that you fear God," he meant that perfect fear which arises from love. For how could he say, "Now I know"? Abraham had shown mercy, he had done so much, he had obeyed God and left everything that was his own, and had lived as a stranger in a foreign land among an idolatrous people, where there was not even a trace of godliness; and on top of all this he endured that terrible trial of the sacrifice of his son. And after all this God said to him, "Now I know that you fear God" — clearly he meant the perfect fear, the fear of the saints. For they no longer do the will of God out of fear of punishment, or to receive a reward, but because they love, as we have often said, and they are afraid of doing anything against the will of the one they love. And that is why he says, "Love casts out fear": for they no longer act out of fear, but out of love.

3. This is the perfect fear. But it is not possible to arrive at the perfect fear, as we said before, unless one first has the introductory fear. For it says, "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord"; and again it says, "The beginning and the end is the fear of God." By "beginning" he means the introductory fear, after which comes the perfect fear, that of the saints. The introductory fear, then, belongs to the state

we are in. It guards the soul from all evil, as tempering [?] does. For it says, "By the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil." If, then, someone turns away from evil out of fear of punishment, like the slave who fears his master, he gradually comes to doing good as well, and little by little he begins to hope for some reward for doing good, like the hireling. Then, when he perseveres in fleeing evil out of fear, as we said, like a slave, and again in doing good out of hope, like a hireling, he continues in the good with God's help and is united to God in proportion. Then at last he tastes, and comes to some perception of, the true good itself, and no longer wants to be separated from it. For who can separate him any longer, as the Apostle said, from the love of Christ? Then he reaches the measure of the son, and loves the good for its own sake, and fears because he loves. And this is the great and perfect fear. That is why the Prophet too, teaching us the difference, spoke of this fear: "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord." Pay attention to each word of the Prophet, and see how every expression he uses has force. First he says, "Come to me," calling us to virtue. He adds "children": the saints call "children" those who are transformed through their word from vice to virtue, as the Apostle says: "My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you." Then, after first calling us and urging us toward such a transformation, he says, "I will teach you the fear of the Lord." See the boldness of the saint! When we want to say something good, we always say, "Would you like us to talk a little and exercise ourselves on the fear of God, or on some other virtue?" But the saint did not speak like that; he said with boldness, "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, who loves to see good days?" Then, as though someone had answered, "I do! Teach me how to live and to see good days," he teaches him and says, "Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit." See, first he cuts off the activity of evil through the fear of God. "Keep your tongue from evil" means not to wound your neighbour's conscience in any way, not to slander, not to provoke; and "your lips from speaking deceit" means not to deceive your neighbour. Then he adds, "Turn away from evil." First he spoke of certain particular sins, slander and deceit, and then he added, to cover all wickedness, "Turn away from evil" — that is, simply flee every evil, turn away from everything that leads to sin. Again, he did not say only this

and then fall silent, but he added, "and do good." For there are times when a man does no evil, and yet does no good either; again, there are times when a man does no wrong, and yet shows no mercy either; there are times when a man does not hate, and yet does not love either. So the prophet spoke well when he said, "Turn away from evil and do good." See, he shows that sequence of the three states of which we spoke before: how through the fear of God he has led us by the hand to turning away from evil, and so we are urged on to go further, to the good as well. For if a man is counted worthy to cease from evil and to flee from it, he then naturally does good, guided by the saints. Having said this, he goes on very well and fittingly to say, "Seek peace and pursue it." And he did not say only "seek it," but "run after it," so that you may overtake it. 4. Pay close attention to this saying, and see the precision of the saint. When someone is counted worthy to turn away from evil, and strives with God's help to do good as well, at once the attacks of the enemy come upon him. Then he struggles, he labours [?], he is worn down, not only because he fears to turn back again to evil, as we said about the slave, but also because he hopes, as we said before, for the reward of the good, like the hireling. So while he is being attacked, and fighting and wrestling with the enemy, he does the good, but with much affliction, with much contrition. But when help comes to him from God, and he begins to acquire a certain settled habit of the good, then he sees rest, then he gradually comes to peace, then he perceives what the affliction of war is and what the joy and gladness of peace are. Then he seeks it, then he strives and runs in pursuit of it, to overtake it, to possess it perfectly, to make it dwell within himself. And what is more blessed than the soul that has been counted worthy of this [?]? Such a man, as we have often said, is at the measure of the son. For truly, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." Who can make that soul do good any longer for any other reason than for the enjoyment of the good itself? Who knows that joy, except the one who has experience of it? [?] the perfect [?] to know, as we have often said. See, we have heard what the perfect fear of the saints is, and what the introductory fear of our state is, and what one flees from and what one comes to through the fear of God. Now we also want to learn how the fear of God comes; we want to say what the things are that cut us off from the fear of God. 5. The Fathers said that a man acquires the fear of God by keeping in mind the remembrance of death and the remembrance of punishments, and by examining himself each evening on how he has spent the day, and again each morning on how he has spent the night, and by not being too familiar with others, and by [?] a man who fears God. For it is said that a brother asked one of the elders, "What shall I do, Father, so that I may fear God?" And the elder said to him, "Go, attach yourself to a man who fears God, and from his fearing God [?]." [?]

of God from the soul as familiarity does? When Abba Agathon was asked about familiarity, he said that it is like a great scorching wind: when it comes, everyone flees before it, and it destroys the fruit of the trees. Do you see, brothers, the power of this passion? Do you see its fury? And when he was asked again, "Is familiarity really so harsh?", he said, "There is no passion harsher than familiarity. For it is the mother of all the passions, because it drives out the

6. Familiarity takes many forms. A man can be too familiar by word, by touch and by look. Familiarity leads a man into idle talk, into talking about worldly matters, into playing the fool and stirring up unseemly laughter. It is familiarity, too, to touch someone without need, to raise a hand at someone in jest, to push someone or snatch something from him, to stare at someone shamelessly. All these things come from there being no fear of God in the soul, and from them a man comes little by little to complete contempt. That is why, when God gave the commandments of the Law, he said, "Make the sons of Israel reverent." For without reverence a man does not honour even God himself, nor pay attention even once to any commandment whatever. That is why nothing is more dreadful than familiarity; that is why it is the mother of all the passions: because it casts out reverence, because it drives away the fear of God, because it breeds contempt. It is because we are familiar with one another and shameless toward one another that you speak ill of one another and wound one another. And if one of you sees something that is of no benefit, he goes off and chatters about it, and puts it into the heart of another brother; and not only is he harmed himself, but he harms his brother too, putting the poison of evil into his heart. And often the other had his mind on prayer or on some other good thing, and that man comes and gives him something to gossip about, and not only hinders his progress but brings temptation upon him as well. And nothing is heavier or more ruinous than for someone to harm not only himself but his neighbour too. So it is good, brothers, for us to have reverence, to be afraid of harming ourselves and one another, to honour one another, and to strive

[?] not to look up, not even into one another's faces; for this too [?] is a form of familiarity. And if it happens that someone sees his brother sinning, let him neither [?] him, nor keep silent and leave him to perish, nor again revile him or slander him; but with compassion and the fear of God let him tell someone who is able to correct him, or let him speak to him himself with love and humility, saying, "Forgive me, my brother; inexperienced as I am, I see that perhaps we are not doing this thing well." And if he does not accept it, tell someone else in whom you see that he has confidence, or tell his superior or the abbot, according to the measure of the fault, and be at peace. But do this, as we said, with the aim of having your brother corrected, and not out of chatter, not slandering him, not belittling him, not wanting, as it were, to [?] him, not condemning him, not pretending to correct him while inwardly holding something against him, as I said. For truly, if someone tells even his own abbot, and does not speak for his brother's correction or to keep himself from harm, it is a sin, for it is slander. Rather, let him search his own heart, and if he finds some passionate impulse, let him not speak. And if he examines himself carefully and finds that he wants to speak out of compassion and for the other's benefit, but some passionate thought troubles him inwardly, let him report to the abbot with humility, telling about both himself and his neighbour, and saying, "My conscience bears me witness that I want to speak for his correction, but I sense that there is a mixed thought within me. Whether it is because I once had something against the brother, I do not know; or whether it is a temptation [?] meant to stop me from speaking and to keep the correction from happening, I do not know." And then the abbot tells him whether he ought to speak or not. Sometimes, though, someone speaks neither for his brother's benefit, nor because of harm to himself, nor out of some grudge, but simply telling it, as a piece of idle talk. And what need is there for this chatter? Often the brother also learns that he has spoken about him and is deeply upset, and affliction arises from this, and further harm is added. For when someone speaks solely for the sake of benefit, as we said, God does not allow trouble to arise; he does not let affliction follow, [?]

8. Strive also, as we said, to guard your tongue, so that none of you speaks ill of his neighbour, or wounds anyone by word or deed or gesture or in any way whatever. And do not be touchy, so that when one of you hears a word from his brother he is immediately stung, and either answers him back or stays aggrieved against him. These are not the ways of those who want to be saved; these are not the ways of those who struggle. Acquire the fear of God; meet one another rather with reverence [?], each bowing his head before his brother, as we said, each humbling himself before God and before his brother, and cutting off his own will for his brother's sake. Truly it is a good thing if someone, when doing something, [?]

gives way to his brother and prefers him; the one who gave way benefits more than the other. I do not know of myself ever having done anything good. But if I was protected at all, I know that I was protected by this: that I never preferred myself to my brother, but always put my brother ahead of

myself. Once, when I was still in Abba Seridos's monastery, the attendant of the elder Abba John, the disciple of Abba Barsanuphius, fell ill, and the abba entrusted me with serving the elder. I used to kiss the door of his cell from outside, as one venerates the precious cross; how much more, then, did I value serving him! For who would not want to be counted worthy of serving such a saint? He also spoke wonderfully. Each time, when I had finished my service to him, I would always make a prostration to him so as to receive his leave to withdraw, and he would always say something to me. For the elder had four sayings, and, as I said, every evening as I was about to withdraw he would always tell me one of the four. He spoke like this: "Once," he says — for it was the elder's habit to say this with every saying — "Once, he says, brother: may God preserve love. The Fathers said: To guard your neighbour's conscience begets humility." Again, the next evening he told me: "Once, he says, brother: may God preserve love. The Fathers said: I never put my own will before my brother's." Another time he said again: "Once, he says, brother: may God preserve love. The Fathers said: Flee human things and be saved." And again he said: "Once, he says, brother: may God preserve love. The Fathers said: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." The elder always had one of these four instructions to give me as I withdrew each evening, like someone giving provisions for a journey. And so I kept them as a safeguard for my whole life. And yet, though I had such confidence in the saint and was so devoted to serving him, if I merely sensed that one of the brothers was aggrieved because he wanted to serve the elder himself, I would go to the abba and beg him, saying, "It is more fitting for the brother to do this, if you agree, sir." And neither the abba nor the elder himself allowed it. Still, I did all I could to have the brother preferred. And in the nine years I spent there, I do not know of ever having spoken an unkind word to anyone — even though I had an office, lest anyone say I had none. 7. And believe me, I know that once a brother walked behind me all the way from the infirmary to the church, insulting me, and I walked on ahead of him without saying a single word to him. And even when the abba learned of it — I do not know who told him — and wanted to rebuke him, I stayed there clinging to his feet, saying, "No, for the Lord's sake, it is I who was at fau[lt]

[?]…, the brother has nothing to do with it.
