And again another brother, whether from temptation or from simplicity (God knows which), spent a year urinating by my head at night, so that even my bedding was soaked. Likewise some other brothers came every day and shook out their [?] in front of my cell, and I saw so many bedbugs coming into my cell that I could not keep up with killing them, for there were countless numbers of them because of the heat. So when I went to lie down, they all gathered on me. Sleep came because of my great fatigue, but when I woke up I found my whole body bitten all over. And I never said to any of them, “Don't do this,” or “Why are you doing this?” Nor, as I said, do I know of ever having spoken a word that wounded or grieved anyone. You too must learn to bear one another's burdens; learn to respect one another. If any of you hears a word from someone that displeases him, or if he suffers something against his will, let him not lose heart at once, nor be irritated at once. Let him not be found, at a time of struggle and of profit, with a heart that is slack, untrained and feeble, unable to withstand any assault at all. It is like a melon: if a little twig touches it, at once it makes a wound and the melon rots. Rather, have a firm heart, have patience, so that your love for one another conquers everything that happens. And if anyone has a duty to perform, or if any of you is found to have some business to settle, whether with the gardener, the cellarer or the cook, or simply with anyone at all who serves alongside you, then both the one who seeks the help and the server who provides it should strive, before all else, to keep their own peaceful state. Let him never allow himself to turn aside from God's commandment, whether through agitation, antipathy, attachment or any self-will at all. But whatever the matter turns out to be, whether small or great, let him not despise and neglect it, for indifference is a bad thing. Nor again let him prefer the matter to his own peaceful state, so that he even harms his soul, if it should happen, in order to get the matter done. For whatever matter you find yourselves in, even if it is very urgent and important, I do not want you ever to do anything with contention or agitation. Rather, be fully convinced that every task you do, whether it is great, as we said, or small, is one eighth of what is being sought, while keeping your own peaceful state, even if this means failing in the task, is four and a half eighths. See how great the difference is. 11. So when you do something, if you want to do it perfectly and completely, strive to do the thing itself, which is like the

one eighth, and to keep your own peaceful state [unharmed?], which is the four and a half eighths. But if it turns out to be necessary to transgress [?], to depart from the commandment and to harm [one another?] in order to fulfil the needs of the task, it is not good to lose the four and a half eighths in order to keep the one eighth. For if you know that someone does this, such a person is not carrying out his own task with understanding. Either from vainglory or from a wish to please people he persists in contention, punishing both himself and his neighbour, so that afterwards he may hear that no one could get the better of him. Bah, what heroism! This is not victory, brothers; this is loss, this is ruin. Look, I tell you: if I send any of you on some errand or other, and he sees agitation arising, or any other harm, let him give way. Never harm yourselves or one another. Rather, let the need go unmet and the thing not be done; only do not trouble one another. For, as I said, you lose the four and a half eighths, and that is plain folly. I say this to you not so that you at once become faint-hearted and [?] the tasks, or [despise?] them and throw [?] the materials aside and trample on your conscience because you want to be free of care. Nor again do I say it so that you disobey, and each of you says, “I cannot do this; I am being harmed; it doesn't suit me.” For on that reasoning you will never do any task at all, nor ever be able to fulfil a commandment of God. Rather, put all your strength into doing each of your tasks with love, submitting to one another with humility, honouring one another, encouraging one another. Nothing is stronger than humility. If, however, someone sees that his neighbour is distressed at that moment, or that he himself is, then give way, yield to one another; do not persist until harm follows. For it is better (look, I have said it ten thousand times) that the need not be met as you wish, but as circumstances allow [?], than that you trouble yourselves or distress one another through obstinacy or self-justification, however reasonable it may seem, and so lose the four and a half eighths. For the difference in loss is great. It often happens, too, that a person [loses?] even the one eighth itself and accomplishes nothing at all. For such is the way of contentions. [?] From the very beginning, we do all the works we do in order to benefit from them. [And what benefit is there if we do not humble ourselves before one another?] Instead we do the opposite: we trouble and distress one another. And you know what is said in the Sayings of the Elders: that life and death come from our neighbour. Meditate on these things always among yourselves, brothers. Exercise yourselves in the words of the holy elders. Strive with love and the fear of God to seek what benefits yourselves and one another. In this way you can benefit from everything that happens and make progress with God's help. May our God himself, as the lover of mankind, grant us his
fear. For it says: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is what is required [?]

1. In Proverbs it says: Those who have no guidance fall like leaves, but safety lies in much counsel. See the force of the saying, brothers. See what Holy Scripture teaches us. It makes us secure so that we do not follow our own lead, so that we do not regard ourselves as wise, so that we do not believe that we can direct ourselves. We need help; we need people to guide us after God. [?] Nothing is more wretched, nothing more easily taken captive, than those who have no one to guide them on the way of God. What does it say? Those who have no guidance fall like leaves. At first a leaf is always green, flourishing and pleasing. Then little by little it dries up and falls, and after that it is disregarded and trampled underfoot. So it is with the man who is not guided by anyone. At first he always has fervour for fasting, for vigils, for stillness, for obedience and for other good things. Then after a little while that fervour is quenched, and since he has no one to guide him, to feed and kindle his fervour, he dries up without noticing it and falls. After that he becomes subject to his enemies, who do with him whatever they please. But of those who disclose their affairs and do everything with counsel it says: Safety lies in much counsel. When it says “much counsel,” it does not mean that a man should take counsel with everyone. Clearly it means with the one in whom he ought to have full confidence. Nor does it mean that he should keep silent about some things and speak about others. He should disclose everything and take counsel about everything. For such a man there truly is safety in much counsel. For if a man does not lay open all his affairs, especially if he comes from a bad habit or a bad upbringing, the devil finds in him a single self-will or a single self-justification, and through it he brings him down. When the devil sees that someone does not want to sin, he is not so clumsy at doing harm as to suggest obvious sins to him. He does not say to him, “Go and fornicate,” or “Go and steal.” For he knows that we do not want these things, and he does not bother to tell us what we do not want. Instead he finds us holding on, as I said, to a single self-will or a single self-justification, and through that he harms us under a plausible pretext. That is why it says again: The wicked one does evil when he joins himself to self-justification. The devil is wicked, but he does evil precisely when he joins himself to self-justification, that is, to our self-justification. For then he is stronger, then he does more harm, then he works more effectively. When we hold on to our own way and follow our self-justifications, then, while we think we are doing something good, we are plotting against ourselves, and we do not even know how we are perishing. For how [?]

2. That is why Abba Poemen used to say that self-will is a bronze wall between man and God. See the force of the saying. And he added further: “It is a rock that strikes back,” that is, it opposes and strikes against the will of God. So if a man abandons it, he too can say: In my God I will leap over a wall. My God, his way is blameless. That is wonderfully said. For a man sees that God's way is blameless when he abandons his own will. But when he indulges his own will, he does not see God's way as blameless. Whatever he hears about [it?], he at once finds fault, spits on it, [rejects it?], strikes back. For how can a man who clings to his own will bear with anyone, or be persuaded by any counsel at all? Then the elder also says about self-justification: “If self-justification also comes to the aid of self-will, the man is hard to turn back.” Ah, how well the words of the Fathers fit together! When self-justification is found together with self-will, that is death in particular, great danger, great cause for fear. Then the wretched man falls completely. For who will persuade such a man to believe that someone else sees better than he does what is good for him? Then he gives himself up completely to following his own will and his own [self-justification?], and from then on the enemy brings him down as he pleases. That is why it says: The wicked one does evil when he joins himself to self-justification. And he hates the sound of safety. It says this because the wicked one not only hates safety, but cannot even bear to hear its voice. He hates even the very sound of safety, that is, the mere mention of anything to do with safety. What I mean is this. Before the one who asks about what will benefit him has put anything into practice, before the enemy knows whether he will keep what he hears or not, he hates the very act of asking someone and hearing anything beneficial. The very voice, the very sound of such words, he hates and turns away from. And I will tell you why. He knows that his malice is at once discovered when someone asks and discusses what will benefit him, and there is nothing he hates and fears so much as being found out, because then he can no longer find a way to plot as he pleases. For when the soul makes itself secure by disclosing everything and hearing from someone who knows, “Do this; don't do that; this is good, that is not good; this is self-justification, that is self-will,” and again hears at one time, “This is not the right time for this,” and at another time, “Now is the time,” then the devil cannot find any pretext for harming him or any way of casting him down. For he is always, as I said, being guided, he is made secure on every side, and in him the saying is fulfilled: Safety lies in much counsel. But the wicked one does not want this; he hates it. For he wants to do evil, and he rejoices rather in those who have no guidance. Why? Because they fall like leaves.

3. Look at that brother whom the wicked one loved, about whom he said to Abba Macarius: “I have one friend, and when he sees me he spins round like a weathervane.” Such people he loves, in such people he always rejoices: those without guidance, who do not entrust themselves to someone who is able, after God, to help them and give them a hand. Did that demon not go to all the brothers, when the saint saw him carrying all those tastes of food in [little flasks?]? Did he not attack them all? But each of them, perceiving his plot, ran and disclosed his own thoughts, and found help in the time of temptation, and so the wicked one had no power over them. That wretched brother, however, he found following his own lead and receiving help from no one, and he had him as his plaything. So he went away thanking him and cursing the others. Indeed, when he told Abba Macarius what had happened and the brother's name, and the saint ran to him, he found that this was the cause of his ruin. He found him unwilling to confess; he found him without the habit of disclosing his thoughts. That is why the enemy could turn him wherever he wished. For when the saint asked him, “How are you, brother?” he said, “Well, thanks to your prayers.” And when he asked again, “Don't your thoughts make war on you?” he answered, “So far I am well.” And he would not confess, until the saint skilfully persuaded him to disclose his affairs, spoke the word of God to him, made him secure, and went back. So the enemy came again as usual, wanting to cast him down, and was put to shame. For he found him steadfast; he found him [no longer?] open to mockery. So he went away having achieved nothing, put to shame even by that brother. That is why, when the saint asked him again, “How is that brother, your friend?” he no longer called him a friend but an enemy, and he cursed him, saying, “He too has been perverted; he no longer obeys me either, but has become wilder than all of them.” 4. See why the enemy hates the sound of safety: because he always wants our ruin. See why he loves those who follow their own lead: because they work together with the devil, plotting against themselves. I know of no other fall for a monk than trusting his own heart. Some say that a man falls through this or through that. But I, as I said, know of no fall that happens to anyone except from this. Have you seen someone who has fallen? Know that he followed his own lead. Nothing is more grievous than following one's own lead, nothing more destructive. God sheltered me, and I always feared this danger. When [I was]

in the community, I referred everything to the elder, Abba John. For never, as I said, could I bring myself to do anything without his counsel. Sometimes my thought would say to me, “Won't the elder tell you exactly this? Why do you want to bother him?” And I would say to the thought, “Anathema to you, and to your discernment, your understanding, your prudence and your knowledge, because what you know, you know from the demons.” So I would go and ask the elder, and sometimes it happened that he gave me the very answer I had thought of. Then the thought would say to me, “Well then? Look, it is just what I said. Didn't you bother the elder for nothing?” And I would say to the thought, “But now it is good; now it is from the Holy Spirit. Yours is evil; it is from the demons; it comes from a state of passion.” And so I never allowed my thought to have its way with me without asking. And believe me, brothers, I was in great rest, in great freedom from care, so much so that it even troubled me, as I have told you on another occasion. For I heard that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God, and I saw that I had no tribulation at all. I was afraid and at a loss, not knowing the reason for such rest, until the elder explained it to me: “Do not be [distressed?], for everyone who gives himself up to obedience to the Fathers has this rest and freedom from care.”

So you too, brothers, strive to ask, and not to follow your own lead. Learn what freedom from care this brings, what joy, what rest. But since I said that I was never afflicted, hear also what happened to me at that time in this regard. While I was still there in the community, a great and unbearable grief once came upon me, and I was in such distress and anguish that I was close to giving up my very soul. That affliction came from a plot of the demons. Such a temptation, brought on by the envy of the demons, is very heavy but short-lived: heavy, dark, [comfortless?], allowing no rest at all, but anguish on every side, suffocation on every side. But [grace?] comes [quickly?] … [?] … able to bear it. I was, as I said, in such a state for [some?] days. While I was [?] … of the monastery, losing heart and calling on God about it, I suddenly looked inside the church and saw someone in the habit of a bishop, wearing [?], as if [?] going into the sanctuary. I never used to approach a stranger without need or permission, but something drew me then, and I went in after him. He remained standing for a long time, with his

[?] hands stretched out towards heaven, and I stood behind him, praying with great fear, for the sight of him filled me with great dread. When he had finished praying, he turned and came towards me, and the nearer he came, the more I felt the grief and the dread withdrawing. When he stood in front of me, he stretched out his hand, touched my chest, and tapped on my chest with his fingers, saying: I waited and waited for the Lord, and he paid heed to me and heard my prayer; he brought me up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay. He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps, and he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God. He said all the verses three times, tapping on my chest, as I said, and then he went out. At once there was light in my heart, joy, consolation, sweetness, and I found myself a different man. So I went out running after him, wanting to find him, and I did not find him; he had vanished. From that hour, by the mercies of God, I do not know of ever having been troubled again by either grief or dread. The Lord has sheltered me until now, through the prayers of those holy elders. 5. I have told you this so that you may know how much rest and freedom from care, together with complete safety, a person gains by not following his own lead, but casting his cares upon God and upon those who are able, after God, to guide him. So you too must learn to ask; learn not to follow your own lead. It is good; it is humility, it is rest, it is joy. Why should anyone wear himself out for nothing? No one can be saved in any other way than this. But someone may think, “If a person has no one to ask, what is he to do?” Truly, if anyone sincerely wants the will of God with his whole heart, God never abandons him, but by all means guides him according to his will. Truly, if anyone directs his heart towards the will of God, God will enlighten even a little child to tell him his will. But if someone does not sincerely want the will of God, even if he goes to a prophet, God puts it into the prophet's heart to answer him in accordance with his crooked heart, as Scripture says: If the prophet is deceived and speaks, I the Lord have deceived that prophet. That is why we ought to direct ourselves with all our strength towards the will of God, and not trust our own heart. Even if something is good, and we hear from some holy man that it is good, we should hold that it is good, but not trust ourselves that we are already doing it well, as it rightly ought to be done. Instead we should do it as far as our strength allows, and then refer back how we are doing it and learn whether we have done it well. And even after that we should not feel so free of care, but should await the judgment of God as well, as [?]

…as that holy Agathon said when he was asked, "Are you afraid too, Father?" He answered, "So far I have done what I could, but I do not know whether my work has pleased God. For God's judgment is one thing, and the judgment of men is another." May God shelter us from the danger that comes from those who follow their own lead, and make us worthy to keep the way of our fathers, who were pleasing to his name.

DISCOURSE 6. On not judging one's neighbour. 1. Brothers, if we remembered the words of the holy elders, and if we meditated on them constantly, we would find it hard to neglect ourselves. For if, as they said, we did not despise small things that seem to us insignificant, we would not fall into great and grievous ones. I am always telling you that these little things, saying "What does this matter? What does that matter?", form a bad habit in the soul, and it begins to despise even great things. Do you know how grievous a sin it is to judge your neighbour? What is graver than this? What does God hate and turn away from so much? As the Fathers said, nothing is worse than judging. And yet a person comes to so great an evil, they say, from these things that seem trivial. It starts when one accepts a slight suspicion against one's neighbour, when one says, "What does it matter if I too say this one word? What does it matter if I watch what this brother is saying or what that guest is doing?" Then the mind begins to let go of its own sins and to chatter about its neighbour's. And from this come judging, slandering and despising, and from this one falls into the very things one condemns. Because a person does not care about his own faults, and does not weep, as the Fathers said, for his own dead, he cannot correct himself in anything, but is always busy with his neighbour. And nothing so provokes God, nothing so strips a person bare and brings him to abandonment, as slandering, judging or despising one's neighbour. 2. Slandering is one thing, judging is another, and despising is another again. Slandering is saying something against someone: that So-and-so [?], or that he got angry, or that he committed fornication, or something of that kind. He has already slandered him, that is, he has spoken against his sin with passion. Judging is saying, "So-and-so is a liar, he is an angry man, he is a fornicator." See, he has judged the very disposition of the man's soul and passed sentence on his whole life, saying that he is like this, and he has condemned him as such. And that is a grave thing. For it is one thing to say "He got angry," and another to say "He is an angry man" and so, as I said, to pass sentence on his whole life. Judging is so much graver than any other sin that Christ himself says, "Hypocrite, first take the

beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye." He likened the neighbour's sin to a speck and judging to a beam, so grievous is judging, almost worse than any other sin. That Pharisee, too, praying and thanking God for his good deeds, did not lie but spoke the truth, and he was not condemned for that. For we ought to thank God when we are found worthy to do some good, since he has worked with us and helped us. So, as I said, he was not condemned for saying, "I am not like the rest of men." But when he turned to the tax collector and said, "nor even like this tax collector," then he was condemned. For he condemned the man's very person, the very disposition of his soul, and, in a word, his whole life. That is why the tax collector went down justified rather than he. 3. Nothing is graver or harsher, as I often say, than judging or despising one's neighbour. Why do we not rather judge ourselves and our own faults, which we know exactly and for which we must give an account to God? Why do we snatch God's judgment for ourselves? What do we want with his creature? Should we not tremble when we hear what happened to that great elder who heard that a brother had fallen into fornication and said, "Oh, he has done wrong"? Do you not know what a dreadful thing the Book of the Elders tells about him? A holy angel brought the soul of the man who had sinned to him and said, "See, the man you judged has died. Where do you order me to put him, in the kingdom or in punishment?" Is there anything more fearful than this burden? What else does the angel's word to the elder mean but this: "Since you are the judge of the righteous and of sinners, tell me what you command concerning this lowly soul. Do you have mercy on it? Do you punish it?" The holy elder was so utterly shaken that he spent the whole rest of his life in groans, in tears and in countless labours, begging God to forgive him that sin. And this was after he had fallen on his face at the angel's feet and received pardon. For when the angel said, "See, God has shown you how grave a thing it is to judge; do not do it again," that meant he had been forgiven. And yet the elder's soul would not be consoled at all for that grief until he died. 4. What then do we want with our neighbour? What do we want with someone else's burden? We have something to be anxious about, brothers. Let each one attend to himself and to his own faults. Only God can justify and condemn, for he knows the condition of each person, his strength, his way of life, his gifts, his temperament and his aptitudes, and he judges each of these as he

alone knows. For God judges a bishop's affairs one way and a ruler's another, an abbot's one way and a disciple's another, an old man's one way and a young man's another, a sick man's one way and a healthy man's another. And who can know these judgments except the one who made all things, formed all things and knows all things? I remember hearing that something like this once happened. A slave ship put in at a certain city. In that city there lived a holy virgin who kept close watch over herself. When she learned that the ship had put in, she was glad, for she wanted to buy herself a very small girl. She reasoned, "I will take her and bring her up as I wish, so that she knows nothing of the wickedness of this world." She sent for the master of the ship and found that he had two very small girls, just the kind the virgin especially wanted. At once she gladly paid the price and took one of the girls home. Now when the shipmaster had left the holy woman's house and gone only a little way, a thoroughly depraved actress met him. She saw the other girl with him and wanted to take her; she struck a bargain, paid the price and went away with her. See the mystery of God! See his judgment! Who can give an account of this? The holy virgin took that little one and brought her up in the fear of God, training her in every good work, teaching her the whole monastic way of life and, in a word, all the fragrance of God's holy commandments. The actress took the wretched girl and made her an instrument of the devil. For what else could that pestilent woman teach her except the destruction of her soul? What then can we say about this fearful judgment? Both were small; both were sold without knowing where they were going. One was found in the hands of God, and the other fell into the hands of the devil. Can we really say that God requires of the one what he requires of the other? How could that be? If both fall into fornication or some other transgression, can we say that both have the same judgment, even if they both commit the same fault? How is that possible? The one learned about the judgment, learned about the kingdom, and [?] day and night in the words of God. The other, poor wretch, never knew or heard anything good, but the opposite: everything shameful, everything devilish. How then is it possible to require the same strictness of both? 5. So a human being can know nothing of God's judgments. He alone [?] all things and is able to [?] judge, as he alone understands. It truly happens that a brother does certain things in simplicity, and has [?]
[?] his soul? And even if he happened to [?] be overcome, how do you know how much he struggled, and how much blood he shed before he acted? Perhaps his fault is found almost as righteousness

before God. For God sees his toil and the anguish he went through, as I said, before he acted, and has mercy on him. And do you know that? God has mercy on him, and you condemn him and destroy your own soul? And how do you know how many tears he shed before God over this? You know the sin, but you do not know the repentance. Sometimes we not only judge but also despise. For, as I said, judging is one thing and despising another. Despising means that a person not only judges but also holds the other in contempt: he loathes his neighbour, as it were, and is disgusted by him as by something repulsive. This is worse than judging and far more ruinous. 6. Those who want to be saved do not even look at their neighbour's failings, but always at their own, and they make progress. Such was the man who saw his brother sinning, groaned and said, "Woe is me! As he today, so I tomorrow." Do you see his safety? Do you see the readiness of his soul? How quickly he found a way to escape judging his brother! By saying "surely I too tomorrow," he gave himself fear and concern about the sins he was likely to commit, and so he escaped judging his neighbour. And he was not content with that, but even put himself below him, saying, "He repents of his sin, but I certainly do not repent; I certainly do not get there in time; I certainly do not have the strength to repent." Do you see the enlightenment of a godly soul? He was able not only to escape judging his neighbour but even to put himself below him. And we wretches judge indiscriminately; we are disgusted and we despise, whatever we see or hear or suspect. And what is worse, we do not stop at harming ourselves, but we meet another brother and tell him at once, "Such and such has happened," and we harm him too, putting sin into his heart. And we do not fear the one who said, "Woe to him who gives his neighbour a muddy drink of ruin." We do the work of demons, and we do not care. For what else can a demon do but trouble and harm? And we find ourselves working with the demons for our own destruction and our neighbour's. For whoever harms a soul works with the demons and helps them, just as whoever does a soul good works with the holy angels. 7. Why do we suffer this, except that we do not have love? For if we had love, with compassion and toil, we would not bother to look at our neighbour's failings, as it says, "Love covers a multitude of sins," and again, "Love keeps no account of evil; it bears all things," and so on. So if we had love, as I said, that very love would cover over everything, as the saints do when they see people's failings. [?]

Are the saints blind, then, that they do not see sins? Who hates sin as much as a saint does? And yet they do not hate the sinner or judge him or turn away from him. They suffer with him, admonish him, comfort him and care for him like a sick limb; they do everything to save him. When fishermen cast a hook into the sea and catch a big fish, and feel it thrashing and struggling, they do not pull it in at once and roughly, for the line would snap and the fish would be lost altogether. Instead they skilfully give it line and let it go, as they say, wherever it wants. And when they see that it is worn out and has calmed down from its rush, then they begin to draw it in again, little by little. In the same way the saints draw their brother with patience and love. They do not kick him away or feel disgust at him. A mother with a misshapen son does not feel disgust at him or turn away from him, but gladly dresses him up and does whatever she can to make him look attractive. So the saints always shelter, adorn and support the one who stumbles, so that in time they may correct him, and not let anyone else be harmed by him, and themselves make greater progress in the love of Christ. What did holy Ammonas do when those brothers came to him in a state of agitation and said, "Come and see, abba [?], there is a woman in brother So-and-so's cell"? What tenderness he showed! What love that holy soul had! Knowing that the brother had hidden the woman under the large jar, he went in, sat on it, and told them to search the whole cell. When they found nothing, he said to them, "May God forgive you." And so, the story says, he put them to shame and also did them good, so that they would not readily believe things against their neighbour. And he brought the other brother to his senses, not only sheltering him, after God, but also correcting him when he found the right moment. For as soon as he had put everyone out, he took his hand and said to him, "Look to yourself, brother." At once the brother was ashamed and pierced with compunction; at once the elder's kindness and compassion did their work in his soul. 8. So let us too acquire love; let us acquire tenderness towards our neighbour, so that we may be guarded from terrible slander and from judging or despising anyone. Let us help one another as our own limbs. Who, having a wound on his hand or

his foot or any other limb, feels disgust at himself or cuts off his own limb, even if it festers? Does he not rather clean it, wash it, put plasters on it, bind it up, apply holy water, pray, and ask the saints to pray for him, as Abba Zosimas used to say? In short, he does not give up on his own limb or turn away from it or from its stench, but does everything to make it well. So we too should suffer with one another and help one another, both by ourselves and through others more capable, and devise and do everything to help both ourselves and others. For we are members of one another, as

the Apostle says: "For we, though many, are one body, and each of us members of one another," and "if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it." What do you think communities are? Do they not seem to you to be one body, members of one another? Those who govern are the head. Those who watch over and correct are the eyes. Those who do good by their words are the mouth. The ears are those who obey. The hands are those who labour. The feet are the messengers and those who carry out the services. Are you the head? Govern. Are you an eye? Pay attention and watch. Are you a mouth? Speak and do good. An ear? Obey. A hand? Work. A foot? Serve. Let each one serve the body according to his ability, and always be eager to help one another, whether by teaching and putting the word of God into your brother's heart, or by [?] comforting him in a time of affliction, or by lending a hand in [?]… according to his ability. Be eager to be united with one another, for the more a person is united with his neighbour, the more he is united with God. 9. I will give you an illustration from the Fathers, so that you may understand the force of this saying. Imagine a circle on the ground, that is, a round line drawn with a compass from a centre. The very middle of the circle is what is properly called its centre. Pay attention to what I am saying. Imagine that this circle is the world, that the very middle of the circle is God, and that the straight lines running from the circle to the middle are the paths, that is, the ways of life, of human beings. As far as the saints move inward, longing to draw near to God, they come near to God and to one another in proportion to their advance. The closer they come to God, the closer they come to one another, and the closer they come to one another, the closer they come to God. Understand separation in the same way. When they withdraw from God and turn outward, it is clear that the further they go out and distance themselves from God, the further they are distanced from one another, and the further they are from one another, the further they are from God. See, such is the nature of love. As far as we are outside and do not love God, so far is each of us distant from his neighbour. But if we love God, then the closer we draw to God through our love for him, the more we are united in love with our neighbour, and the more we are united with our neighbour, the more we are united with God. May God make us worthy to hear what is good for us and to do it. For the more we take care and strive to put into practice what we hear, the more [?]… and teaches his will.

DISCOURSE 7. On blaming oneself. 1. Brothers, let us ask why it is that sometimes a person hears a hurtful word and lets it pass without being troubled, as if he had hardly heard it, while at other times he hears one and is immediately troubled. What is the cause of this difference? And does it have only one cause, or

many? I see that it has many causes, but there is one that gives rise, so to speak, to all the others. I will tell you how. First, it happens that a person has just come from prayer or from a good spell of stillness in his cell, and finds himself, so to speak, in a good state; so he bears with his brother and lets the word pass without being troubled. Again, it happens that a person has an attachment to someone, and for that reason bears [?] easily whatever that person inflicts on him. Again, there are times when a person despises the one who wants to hurt him, and makes light of whatever comes from him, not regarding him as a human being and taking no account of anything he says. I will tell you something of this kind that will astonish you. Before I left the monastery, there was a brother there whom I never saw troubled or upset with anyone, though I saw many of the brothers insult and offend him in various ways. Yet that young man bore what came from each of them as though no one were bothering him at all. I was always amazed at how extraordinarily forbearing he was, and I wanted to learn how he had acquired this virtue. So I took him aside privately, made a prostration to him, and begged him to tell me what thought he always kept in his heart when he was insulted or suffered any annoyance from someone, that he showed such patience. He answered, quite arrogantly, "Well, [?] am I to pay attention to these imperfect creatures, or take what comes from them as if it came from human beings? They are [?] dogs." When I heard this, I hung my head and said to myself, "This brother has found the way!" And making the sign of the cross over myself, I went away praying that God would protect both me and him. 2. So, as I said, it also happens that a person is not troubled out of contempt. But that is plain perdition. Being troubled with a brother who distresses you happens either because you were not in a good state at that hour, or because you have some aversion to him. There are many other causes of this too, which have been described in various ways. But if we search carefully, the cause of all our trouble is that we do not [?] blame ourselves. That is why we have all this turmoil; that is why we never find rest. And no wonder, for we hear from all the saints that there is no other way than this. We see that no one has ever travelled any other way and found rest, and yet we expect to have rest, or to keep to a straight path at all, while never bearing to blame ourselves. Truly, if a person practises countless virtues but does not [?] keep to this way, he will never stop distressing others and being distressed, and he will lose all his labours. But what [?]

…[?] — what rest does such a man not have, wherever he goes! As Abba Poemen also said: the one who blames himself, whatever happens to him, whether loss, or dishonour, or any affliction at all, has already judged himself deserving of it, and is never troubled. Is there anything more free of care than this? 3. But someone says: “And if my brother afflicts me, and I search myself and find that I gave him no pretext whatever, how can I blame myself?” Truly, if someone searches himself with the fear of God, he finds that he has certainly given cause, whether by deed, or by word, or by manner. And even if he sees in himself, as he says, that on the present occasion he gave no cause at all in any of these ways, it is likely that he afflicted that brother at another time, either in the same matter or in another; or likely that he afflicted another brother, and ought to suffer for that, or often for some other sin. So if, as I said, someone searches himself with the fear of God and examines his own conscience carefully, he finds that he himself is certainly to blame. Again, sometimes a person sees himself sitting, as it were, in peace and quiet, and when a brother says a word to him that grieves him, he is troubled, and from this he thinks he has good reason to be aggrieved, and speaks against him, saying: “If he had not come and spoken to me and troubled me, I would not have sinned.” This is a mockery, this is false reasoning. Did the one who spoke the word to him put the passion into him? He showed him the passion that was in him, so that, if he wishes, he may repent of it. For this man is like a loaf of pure fine wheat, beautiful on the outside but inside something rotten [?]; and when someone breaks it, then its filth appears. So he too sat in peace, as he thought, but he had the passion within him and did not know it. His brother said one word to him and brought out the filth hidden inside. If, then, he wishes to receive mercy, let him repent and be cleansed and make progress, and he will see that he ought rather to thank his brother, as the one who became the cause of such benefit to him. For temptations no longer weigh on him in the same way; rather, the more he progresses, the lighter he finds them. For the more the soul progresses, the stronger it becomes, and has the power to bear what comes upon it. Just as, if there is a strong animal and someone loads a burden on it, it carries it with ease; and if it happens to stumble, it gets up at once, and people hardly even notice that it stumbled; but if it is a wretched animal, anything at all weighs it down, and if it falls, it needs a great deal of help to get up. So it is with the soul: the more it commits sin, the more wretched it becomes from it. For if sin makes wretched and rots the one who has it, then whatever happens weighs him down; but if a person makes progress, the things that once weighed him down gradually become lighter for him. So it greatly benefits us, and brings much rest and progress, to blame

ourselves and no one else in what happens to us, especially since nothing can happen to us apart from the providence of God. 4. So, if someone says: “How can I not be aggrieved if I need something and do not receive it? For look, I really do need it,” even he has no reason to blame anyone or to be aggrieved with anyone. Rather, if he truly needs something, as he says, and does not receive it, he ought to say: “Christ knows better than I whether I ought to be refreshed, and he himself becomes for me what this thing, or this food, would have been.” The children of Israel ate the manna in the desert for forty years. The manna was of one kind, but it became for each person whatever he needed: for one who needed something salty, it became salty; for one who needed something sweet, it became sweet; in short, for each it became suited to his constitution. So if someone needs an egg and receives nothing but vegetables, let him say to his thought: “If it were good for me, God would certainly have sent it to me; but he can also make these vegetables like an egg for me,” and let him trust God, and it will be counted to him as a martyrdom. For if someone truly deserves to be refreshed, God moves even the hearts of the Saracens [?] to show him mercy according to his need; but if he does not deserve to be refreshed, or it is not good for him, even if he makes a new heaven and a new earth, he does not find rest. [?] Sometimes a person finds refreshment even beyond his need, and sometimes not even what he needs. There are times when God provides even beyond someone's need, since God in his mercy grants each person what he needs. And there are times when he provides for someone even beyond his need, showing him the abundance of his love for mankind and teaching him thankfulness. But when he does not grant him what he needs, he produces by his word the effect of the thing he needs, and teaches him patience. So in everything we ought to look upward: whether we suffer good or ill from anyone, we ought to look upward and give thanks for whatever happens, always taking the blame upon ourselves and saying, as the Fathers said, that if anything good happens, it is God's dispensation, and if anything bad, it is because of our sins. For in truth, whatever we suffer, we suffer because of our sins. The all-holy, even when they suffer, suffer for the name of God, or so that their virtue may be made known for the benefit of many, or so that their reward from God may be multiplied. But how can we wretches say this of ourselves? Sinning in this way every day and gratifying our passions, we have abandoned the straight road the Fathers spoke of, that of blaming ourselves, and we travel the crooked road of blaming our neighbour, and each of us is eager in every matter to put the blame on his brother and throw the burden on him. Each of us is negligent and keeps nothing, and we demand the commandments of our neighbour.

5. Two brothers once came to me, aggrieved with each other. The elder said of the younger: “I give him an order, and he is aggrieved, and I am aggrieved too, because I think that if he had faith and love toward me, he would accept what I say with full assurance.” And the younger said: “Forgive me, sir, but he doesn't speak to me with the fear of God, but as someone who wants to give me orders, and I think that is why my heart is not at peace, as the Fathers say.” Notice how the two blamed each other, and neither of them blamed himself. And again, the two were aggrieved with each other, and though they made prostrations to each other, they remained without peace of heart. One said: “He did not make the prostration to me from the heart, and that is why I was not at peace; for so the Fathers said.” And the other said: “Since he was not disposed in love toward me before I apologized to him, that is why I was not at peace either.” Do you see the mockery, brothers? Do you see the perversity of thought? God knows, I am astonished that we take even the sayings of the Fathers to serve our evil wills and the destruction of our souls. Each of them ought to have put the blame on himself: the one ought to have said, “I did not make the prostration to my brother from the heart, and that is why God did not give him peace”; and the other, “I was not disposed in love toward my brother before he apologized to me, and that is why God did not give him peace.” In the same way they ought to have acted in the earlier matter too. For the first ought to have said, “I speak with arrogance, and that is why God does not give my brother peace.” And the other ought to have reasoned, “My brother gives me orders with humility and love, but I am disobedient and have no fear of God.” Neither of them found the way and blamed himself; each laid the burden on his neighbour. 6. See, this is why we do not manage to make progress, why we do not manage to gain any benefit at all, but spend our whole time against one another, wearing ourselves out. Each of us justifies himself; each lets himself off, as I said before, keeping nothing, and we demand the commandments of our neighbour. That is why we do not even become accustomed to the good: because if we receive even a little light, we immediately demand it of our neighbour, blaming him and saying, “He ought to have done this,” and “Why didn't he do it this way?” Why do we not rather demand the commandments of ourselves, and blame ourselves for not keeping them? Where is that elder who was asked, “What more have you found on this way, Father?” and answered, “To blame oneself in everything”? And the one who asked him praised this and said to him, “There is no other way but this.” Likewise Abba Poemen said with a groan that all the

virtues have come into this house except one virtue, and without it a man stands only with toil. And they asked him which one this was, and he said: “That a man should blame himself.” And St Anthony said that this is the great work of a man: to lay his fault upon himself before God, and to expect temptation until his last breath. Everywhere we find that the Fathers, keeping this and referring everything to God, even the smallest things, found rest. Such was that holy elder who, when he was ill, had a brother put into his food, instead of honey, linseed oil, which is very harmful. Yet the elder said nothing, but ate his first dish in silence, without blaming the brother inwardly or saying that he had been careless. And not only did he not say this, he did not grieve him by so much as a word. When the brother learned what he had done and began to be distressed, saying, “I have killed you, Abba, and you have laid the sin on me by keeping silent,” how gently he answered him, saying: “Don't be distressed, child. If God had wanted me to eat honey, you would have put in honey.” And at once he referred the matter to God. What has God got to do with it, good old man? The brother made a mistake, and you say, “If God had wanted”? What has that to do with the matter? And he says: “Yes. If God had wanted me to eat honey, the brother would have had honey.” And this when the elder was so ill that for many days he could not take food; and yet he was not aggrieved with the brother, but referred the matter to God. And the elder spoke rightly: if God had wanted him to eat honey, he would have turned even the stinking oil into honey. But we, in every matter, come at our neighbour with accusations, blaming him as careless and as acting against his conscience; and if we hear a word, we immediately twist it, saying, “If he hadn't wanted to wound me, he wouldn't have said it.” Where is that saint who said of Shimei, “Let him curse, for the Lord told him to curse David”? Did God tell a murderer to curse the prophet? How then did God tell him? But the prophet, having knowledge, and knowing that nothing draws the mercy of God upon the soul as much as temptations, especially those brought and heaped upon it in a time of affliction and distress, said: “Let him curse David, for the Lord told him.” Why? “So that God may look upon my humiliation and repay me with good in place of his cursing.” Do you see how the prophet acted with knowledge? That is why he was indignant with those who wanted to take vengeance on the man cursing him, saying: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse; the Lord told him.” But we cannot bear to say of our brother, “The Lord told him”; rather, if we hear a word,

we immediately behave like a dog. Someone throws a stone at it, and it leaves the one who threw it, and goes off and bites [?] the stone. That is what we do too: we leave God, who permits trials to come upon us for the cleansing of our sins, and go after our neighbour, saying, “Why did he say this to me? And what has he done to me?” And though we could gain great benefit from such things, we plot the opposite against ourselves, not knowing that everything happens by the providence of God for the good of each. May God give us understanding, through the prayers of the saints. Amen.

DISCOURSE 8. On remembrance of wrongs. 1. The Fathers said that it is foreign to monks to be angry, and likewise to grieve anyone. And again: if anyone has mastered anger, he has mastered the demons; but if anyone is overcome by this passion, he is a complete stranger to the monastic life, and so on. What, then, ought we to say of ourselves, who do not stop at anger and wrath, but sometimes drive ourselves even to remembrance of wrongs? What else but mourn this pitiable and inhuman condition of ours? Let us be watchful, then, brothers, and help ourselves with God's help, so that we may be delivered from the bitterness of this destructive passion. For sometimes someone makes a prostration to his brother, when, as may happen, some disturbance or affliction has arisen between them, and even after the prostration he remains grieved and has thoughts against him. Such a man must not disregard them, but cut them off quickly. For this is remembrance of wrongs, and there is need of great watchfulness, as I said, so that he does not linger in such thoughts and fall into danger. For in making the prostration, he made it because of the commandment, and he healed the wrath for the present, but he did not yet struggle against remembrance of wrongs; and so he remained grieved with his brother. For remembrance of wrongs is one thing, wrath another, anger another, and

for remembrance of wrongs is one thing, wrath another, anger another, disturbance another. 2. I will give you an example, so that you may understand. The person lighting a fire first has a small ember: this is the word of a brother who has hurt him. See, it is still only a small ember. For what is your brother's word? If you bear it, you have put out the ember. But if you keep thinking, “Why did he say that to me? I have something to say to him too. If he hadn't wanted to hurt me, he wouldn't have said it; and believe me, I can hurt him too,” see, you have thrown on little sticks, or something of the sort, like the person lighting a fire, and you have made smoke, which is disturbance. Disturbance is this movement and clash of thoughts which rouses and emboldens the heart. And boldness is the retaliatory rising up against the one who has caused grief, which also becomes audacity, as the blessed Abba Mark said: “Malice meditated in the thoughts emboldens the heart, but when it is destroyed by prayer and hope, it breaks the heart.” For if you had borne your brother's small word, you could have put out, as I said, even that small ember

before the disturbance arose. Yet even this, if you wish, you can easily put out while it is still fresh, by silence, by prayer, by a single prostration from the heart. But if you go on making smoke, that is, emboldening and rousing your heart by thinking, “Why did he say that to me? I have something to say to him too,” then from this very clash, so to speak, and grinding together of the thoughts, the heart is as it were rubbed and heated, and anger flares up. For anger is the boiling of the blood around the heart, as St Basil says. See, anger has arisen; this is what they call quick temper. If you wish, you can put this out too before it becomes wrath; but if you go on troubling others and being troubled, you are like one who throws wood on the fire and makes it burn more, and so at last coals are formed, which is wrath. 3. And this is what Abba Zosimas said when he was asked what the saying means: “Where there is no anger, strife is at rest.” For if, at the beginning of the disturbance, when it begins, as we said, to smoke and give off some sparks, someone gets in first by blaming himself and making a prostration before it flares up and becomes anger, he is at peace. Again, once anger has arisen, if he does not grow quiet, but remains troubled and emboldened, he is like, as we said, someone feeding wood to the fire, and it goes on burning until it makes great coals. And just as coals become charcoal and are stored away and last for many years without spoiling, and do not rot even if someone pours water on them, so too wrath, if it lasts long, becomes remembrance of wrongs, and then, unless a man sheds his blood, he is not rid of it. See, I have told you the difference; understand it. See, you have heard what the first disturbance is, and what anger is, and what wrath is, and what remembrance of wrongs is. Do you see how from a single word it came to so great an evil? For if from the beginning he had laid the blame on himself, and borne his brother's word, and not wanted to avenge himself and say two or even five words in return for one, and repay evil for evil, he would have escaped all these evils. That is why I always tell you: while the passions are fresh, cut them out before they become firmly fixed against you, or you will suffer misery. For pulling up a small weed is one thing, and uprooting a great tree another. Nothing astonishes me so much as that we do not even know what we sing. Every day we sing, and curse ourselves, and do not understand. Ought we not to know what we sing? For we are always saying, “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, then let me fall empty before my enemies.” What does “let me fall” mean? As long as someone stands, he has the strength to resist his enemy: he strikes and is struck, he wins and is beaten, for he is still standing. But if he once falls, how can he still wrestle with his enemy while lying on the ground? And we pray against ourselves

not only that we may fall before our enemies, but that we may even fall empty. 4. Let us say what it means for someone to fall empty before his enemies. To fall means no longer to have the strength to get up, but to lie on the ground. And empty means to have nothing good at all, by which a person might at least be able to rise. For one who gets up can take care of himself again, and at some point come back into the fight. Then we say: “Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it”: not only pursue but also overtake, so that we are in his hands, so that we are defeated in everything, in every matter, and he throws us down, if we repay evil to those who repay us with evil. And we pray not only for this, but also that he may trample our life into the ground. What is our life? Our life is the virtues; and we pray that our life may be trampled into the ground, so that a person may become wholly earthly, with his whole mind down on the earth. “And may he make my glory dwell in the dust.” What is our glory, if not the knowledge that arises in the soul through keeping the holy commandments? So this is what we are saying: that he may turn our glory, as the Apostle says, into our shame, that he may make it dwell in the dust, and make our life and our glory earthly, so that we may think nothing according to God, but everything bodily, everything fleshly, like those of whom God said, “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” See, in singing all these things we curse ourselves if we repay evil for evil; and how many evils we repay for evils, and yet we do not care, but remain indifferent. 5. Repaying evil for evil happens not only in deed, but also in word and in manner. Someone thinks he does not repay evil in deed, but is found, as I said, repaying it in word and in manner. For sometimes a person makes a single gesture, or movement, or glance, and troubles his brother. One can wound one's brother even by a glance or a movement, and this too is repaying evil for evil. Another strives not to repay evil for evil in deed, or word, or manner, or movement, but has grief in his heart toward his brother and is aggrieved with him. See how great a difference of state there is. Another has no grief at all toward his brother; but if he hears that someone has grieved that brother, or that anyone has grumbled against him or reviled him, he is always delighted to hear it, and so he too is found repaying evil for evil in his heart. Another neither holds on to malice nor rejoices to hear reviling against the one who grieved him, but is even grieved if that brother is grieved; yet he is not glad for him to fare well too; and if he sees him honoured or at rest,

[?] …is distressed; this too is a kind of remembering wrongs, though a lighter one. But one ought rather to rejoice in his brother's comfort, to do everything to look after him, and to attend to every matter that serves his care and comfort. We said at the beginning of this discourse that there is someone who makes a prostration asking forgiveness and still keeps a grievance against the other. We say that by making the prostration he has healed his anger, but he has not yet fought against remembering wrongs. There is another who, if someone happens to hurt him, makes prostrations with the other, and they are reconciled, is then at peace with him and keeps no bad memory of him in his heart. But if, some days later, the other happens to say something that hurts him, he begins to recall the earlier things as well, and is disturbed not only about the second offence but also about the first. This man is like someone who has a wound and puts a plaster on it. For the time being the plaster has healed the wound and it has scarred over, but the place is still weaker. Whenever someone throws a stone at him, that place is struck more easily than all the rest of the body and at once begins to bleed. That is what happened to this man too. He had a wound and put on a plaster, which is the prostration asking forgiveness, and for the time being he healed the wound, that is, the anger, just as the first man did. He also began to tend to his remembrance of wrongs by striving to keep no bad memory in his heart, for that is the wound's scarring over. But he has not yet wiped it out completely. He still has a remnant of remembering wrongs, which is the scar, and from it the whole wound easily breaks open again when it receives a small blow. So he must struggle to wipe out the scar completely, so that hair grows over the place, no disfigurement is left, and no one can tell at all that there was ever a wound there. How can he achieve this? By praying with his whole heart for the one who hurt him and saying, 'O God, help my brother, and help me through his prayers.' In this way he is found praying for his brother, which is a sign of compassion and love, and he is humbled by asking for help through his brother's prayers. Where there is compassion and love and humility, what power can anger or any other passion have? As Abba Zosimas said, 'If the devil sets in motion all the engines of his malice together with all his demons, all his schemes come to nothing and are crushed by the humility of Christ's commandment.' And another elder says, 'He who prays for his enemies will bear no grudge.' Put into practice what you hear, and understand it well. For truly, unless you put these things into practice, [?] you cannot acquire them by word alone. What man who wants to learn a craft acquires it by word alone? First he keeps at it, making things and spoiling them, making them and undoing them. In this way, labouring and persevering little by little, he learns the craft, while God sees his labour and his intention and works with him. But we want to acquire the craft of crafts by word,

without setting our hand to the work. How is that possible? Let us take heed to ourselves, then, brothers, and work with diligence while we still have time. May God grant us to remember and keep what we hear, so that it does not become a judgment against us on the day of judgment.

DISCOURSE 9. On Lying. 1. I want to remind you, brothers, of a few things about lying. For I see that you are not very careful to guard your tongues, and because of this we are easily dragged into many things. You see, my brothers, that in everything there is habit, as I always tell you, both for good and for evil. So there is need of great watchfulness, so that we are not carried off by lying. For no one who lies is united with God; lying is foreign to God. It is written that lying is from the evil one, and again that he is a liar and the father of it. See, it calls the devil the father of lying. But the truth is God, for he himself says, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life.' You see from whom we cut ourselves off through lying, and to whom we attach ourselves: clearly, to the evil one. So if we truly want to be saved, we must love the truth with all diligence and guard ourselves against every lie, so that it does not separate us from the truth and from the life. There are three different kinds of lying. There is the one who lies in his thought, there is the one who lies in word, and there is the one who lies with his very life. The one who lies in thought is the one who entertains suspicions. If he sees someone talking with his brother, he becomes suspicious and says, 'They are talking about me.' If they break off their conversation, again he suspects that they broke it off because of him. If someone says a word, he suspects that it was said to hurt him. In short, in every matter he speaks this way about his neighbour, saying, 'He did this because of me; he said that because of me; he did this for that reason.' This is the one who lies in thought. He says nothing true; everything is suspicion. From this come prying, slander, eavesdropping, quarrelling and condemning. Sometimes he suspects something and it turns out, as it happens, to be true. So, he says, wanting to correct himself, he goes prying, reasoning, 'If someone is talking against me, I look to see what my fault is that makes him malign me, and I correct myself.' But first of all, this very beginning is from the evil one, because it started with a lie: not knowing, he suspected what he did not know. How then can a bad tree bear good fruit? If he really wants to correct himself, then when a brother says to him, 'Don't do this,' or 'Why did you do that?', he should not be disturbed. Instead he should make a prostration and thank him, and then he will be corrected. If God sees that this is his intention, he will never let him go astray, but will surely send someone to correct him. But to say, 'I trust my suspicions in order to be corrected,'

and then to eavesdrop and pry, is a pretext of the devil, who wants to lay a trap. [?] While I was still in the community, I was tempted to judge a person's inner state from his outward movements. Something like this happened to me. Once, as I was standing there, a woman passed by carrying a jar of water. I do not know how I was carried away, but I looked at her eyes, and at once the thought suggested to me that she was a prostitute. When the thought suggested this, I was very distressed, and I disclosed it to the elder, Abba John, in these words: 'Master, if without wanting to I see someone's movement and the thought suggests to me what his state is, what should I do?' The elder answered me like this: 'What of it? Is it not possible for someone to have a natural defect and, by struggle, to overcome it? [?] You cannot learn anyone's state from this. So never trust your suspicions, for a crooked rule makes even straight things crooked. Suspicions are false, and they do harm.' From then on, if the thought told me about the sun that it was the sun, or about darkness that it was darkness, I did not believe it. Nothing is more grievous than suspicions. They are so harmful that, when they linger in us, they begin to persuade us, and we actually think we see things that neither exist nor are happening. Let me tell you an astonishing thing about this that I witnessed while I was still in the community. We had a brother there who was greatly troubled by this passion. He trusted his own suspicions, so that he was fully convinced about each one that it was certainly just as his thought pictured it and could not be otherwise. As time went on and the evil grew, the demons led him so far astray that once he went into the garden to spy. He kept watch and listened in secret, and he thought he saw one of the brothers stealing figs and eating them. It was a Friday, and not yet even the second hour. Since he was convinced that he had truly seen the thing with his own eyes, he hid himself, it is said, and went out silently. At the time of the synaxis he watched again to see what the brother who had supposedly stolen and eaten the figs would do at communion. When he saw him washing his hands to go in and receive communion, he ran and said to the abbot, 'Look, Brother So-and-so is going in to partake of holy communion with the brothers. Order that it not be given to him, for I know he has been stealing figs from the garden since morning and eating them.' Meanwhile that brother came in to the holy offering with great compunction, for he was one of the devout. When the abbot saw him, he called him before he could approach the priest who was giving communion, took him aside, and said to him, 'Tell me, brother, what did you do today?' The brother was taken aback and said, 'Where, master?' The abbot said to him,

'This morning when you went into the garden, what were you doing there?' Again the brother, as if astonished, said, 'Master, I have not even seen the garden today, and I was not here in the community this morning. I have only just come back from a journey. Right after the vigil ended, the steward sent me on such-and-such an errand.' The errand he spoke of was many miles away, and the brother had arrived just at the time of the synaxis. The abbot sent for the steward and said to him, 'Where did you send this brother?' The steward answered just as the brother had said: 'I sent him to such-and-such a village.' He made a prostration and said, 'Forgive me, lord. You were resting after the vigil, and so I did not bring him to receive your leave.' When the abbot was fully satisfied, he let them go and receive communion. Then he called the brother who had the suspicions, rebuked him and excluded him from holy communion. Not only that, but after the synaxis he called all the monks together, told them with tears what had happened, and exposed the brother publicly before them all. He aimed at three things by this: that the devil should be put to shame and the sower of suspicions made an example; that the brother's sin should be forgiven through that disgrace and he should receive help from God for the future; and that the brothers should be made more cautious, so that we would never allow ourselves to be persuaded by our own suspicions. After admonishing us and the brother at length about this, he said that nothing is more harmful than suspicions, and he showed it by the example of what had happened. 3. The Fathers said many other things of this kind, in various ways, to safeguard us against the harm of suspicions. So let us strive with all our strength never to trust our own suspicions. Nothing so separates a man from God and from attending to his own sins, and makes him always busy himself with what does not concern him. From this comes nothing good; from this come countless afflictions; and because of this a man never has leisure to acquire the fear of God. Even if evil suspicions are sown in us because of our wickedness, let us immediately turn them into good thoughts, and they will not harm us. For suspicions are evil and never let the soul be at peace. That, then, is lying in thought. The one who lies in word is like this. Suppose someone is too lazy to get up for the vigil. He does not say, 'Forgive me, I was too lazy to get up,' but says, 'I had a fever, I was dizzy, I couldn't get up, I had no strength.' He says ten lying words so as not to make one prostration and be humbled. If someone reproaches him about something, he keeps changing his words and dressing them up so as not to bear the reproach. Likewise, if he happens to have a dispute with his brother, he does not stop justifying himself, saying, 'But you said, but you did, but I didn't say it, but he said it, but this, but that,' anything so as not to be humbled. Again, if he desires something, he cannot bear to say, 'I want this,' but keeps twisting his words, saying, 'I am suffering from this and I need that,' or '[?] I was ordered to,' and he tells lie after lie until he fulfils

his desire. For every sin comes about through love of pleasure, love of money, or love of glory. Likewise lying arises from these three: a man lies either so as not to be reproached and humbled, or to get his own way, or for gain. He does not stop twisting this way and that, contriving everything he can say until he achieves his aim. Such a man is never believed. Even if he speaks a true word, no one can believe him, and even his truth turns out to be doubtful. Sometimes, however, a necessity arises, and if one does not conceal a small matter, it leads to greater trouble and affliction. When such a situation arises and a man sees himself forced to alter his words for this reason, so that there will not be greater trouble and affliction or danger, as I said—as Abba Alonius said to Abba Agathon: 'Suppose two men committed a murder in your presence and one fled into your cell, and the magistrate is looking for him and asks you, "Was a murder committed in your presence?" Unless you use discretion, you will hand the man over to death'—when, then, some great necessity arises, one ought not even then to be unconcerned. He should repent and weep before God and regard such a thing as a time of temptation. And he should not do it continually, but only once in a long while. Theriac and purgatives harm a person if he takes them continually, but if he takes one once in a while out of great necessity, it benefits him. In the same way one should make use of this thing: even if out of necessity he decides to alter his words, it should not be continually, but perhaps once in a long while, when he sees great necessity, as I said. And even this occasional use he should make with fear and trembling, showing God his intention and the necessity, and so he is protected; for even in this he is harmed. 4. So we have said who it is that lies in thought, and who lies in word. Now we want to say also who lies with his very life. The one who lies with his life is someone who, being dissolute, pretends to self-control; or who is greedy, talks about almsgiving and praises compassion; or who is proud and admires humility. He does not admire virtue because he wants to praise it. If he spoke with that aim, he would first humbly confess his own weakness, saying, 'Woe is me, wretch that I am, for I have become empty of every good!' After confessing his own weakness, he could then admire and praise virtue. Nor does he extol virtue with the aim of not scandalizing anyone. For one ought to reason this way as well: 'Yes, I am wretched and given to the passions, but why should I scandalize someone else too? Why should I harm another soul as well and take another's burden on myself?' Then, even if he sinned against himself, he would still have laid hold of the good. For to count oneself wretched is a mark of humility, and

to spare one's neighbour is a mark of compassion. But such a man does not admire virtue, as I said, for any of the reasons mentioned. Either he takes on the name of virtue to cover his own shame, and talks about it as though he himself were virtuous, or, often, he does it to harm and entice someone. For no vice, no heresy, not even the devil himself can deceive anyone except by disguising itself as virtue. As the Apostle says, the devil himself disguises himself as an angel of light, so it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. So too the liar, either because he fears shame and does not want to be humbled, or, as we said, because he wants to entice and deceive someone, talks about the virtues and praises and admires them, as though he had made them his own and had experience of them. This is the one who lies with his very life. Such a man is not simple but double: he is one thing inside and another outside. His life is double and wholly a mockery. So we have said about lying that it is from the evil one, and we have also said about the truth that the truth is God. So let us flee from lying, brothers, so that we may be delivered from the portion of the enemy, and let us strive to acquire the truth, so that we may be united to him who said, 'I am the truth.' May God make us worthy of his truth.

DISCOURSE 10. On Travelling the Way of God with Purpose and Watchfulness. 1. Let us take care of ourselves, brothers; let us be watchful. Who will give this time back to us if we lose it? Truly, we shall look for these days and not find them. Abba Arsenius always used to say to himself, 'Arsenius, why did you leave the world?' But we are so lost and so negligent that we do not know why we left, nor do we know what it was we wanted. That is why we not only make no progress but are always afflicted. This happens to us because we do not keep watch over our hearts. Truly, if we were willing to struggle a little, we would not be afflicted or toil for long. Even if at the start a man has to force himself, by struggling he makes progress little by little and afterwards acts with ease, because God sees him forcing himself and gives him help. So let us too force ourselves; let us make a good beginning; let us at least desire the good for now. We are not yet perfect, but the very desire is the beginning of salvation for us. From desiring, with God's help, we come to struggling, and through struggling a man is helped to acquire the virtues. That is why one of the Fathers says, 'Give blood and receive the Spirit,' that is, struggle, and you will come to have virtue as a settled habit.

2. When I was studying secular learning, at first I found it very hard going. When I came to take up a book, I was like someone about to touch a wild beast. But as I kept forcing myself, God helped me, and I came to have such a habit of it that, in my ardour for reading, I did not know what I ate or drank or how I slept. I never let myself be drawn into having a meal with any of my friends, nor would I even go to talk with one during my reading time, although I was sociable and loved my companions. When the sophist dismissed us, I would wash (for I needed to moisten myself every day, since I became dried out from too much reading) and go back to where I was staying, not even knowing whether I had anything to eat. I could not spare the time even to arrange for my food. But I had a trustworthy man, and he prepared whatever I wanted. So I took whatever I found he had made, keeping my book beside me on the bed, and from time to time I would bend over it. When I slept, I likewise kept it near me on my [?]. As soon as I had dozed a little, I would jump up at once to my reading. Again, in the evening, when I came back after vespers, I lit the lamp and read until midnight. I was in such a state that I felt no pleasure of any kind except from my reading. So when I came to the monastery, I said to myself, 'If secular learning produced such passion and such ardour, because a man devoted himself to reading until it became a habit, how much more should virtue?' And I drew great strength from this. So if someone wants to acquire virtue, he must not be indifferent or distracted. Someone who wants to learn carpentry does not give his attention to another craft. It is the same with those who want to acquire spiritual work: they must not give their attention to anything else, but must meditate on it night and day, on how they can acquire it. Those who do not approach the matter this way not only make no progress but are worn down, carried about aimlessly as they are. For unless someone is watchful and struggles, he easily falls into deviations from the virtues. 3. For the virtues lie in the middle. That is the royal road, of which that holy elder said, 'Walk on the royal road, and count the miles.' The virtues, then, as I said, lie midway between excesses and deficiencies. That is why it is written, 'Do not turn aside to the right or to the left, but walk on the royal road.' And Saint Basil says, 'Upright in heart is the one whose thought does not lean towards excess or deficiency, but is directed towards the mean of virtue.' For instance, I mean this: vice in itself, [?]

[?] is nothing. For it is not any kind of substance, nor does it have any subsistence. Far from it! Rather, when the soul turns aside from virtue it becomes subject to passion, and so brings evil about. That is why it is also punished by it, finding no natural rest in it. It is like wood [and the worm?]: wood does not have a worm inside it, but it develops a little rot, and out of that rot the worm comes into being, and then that very worm eats away the wood. In the same way bronze itself produces rust, and is in turn consumed by the rust. Clothes too produce the moth, and the moth that comes from them destroys them. So it is with the soul. It produces evil itself, though evil did not exist before this and, as I said, has no subsistence, and then the soul itself is punished by that evil.
