Saint Gregory put it well: "For fire is the offspring of matter and consumes matter, just as evil consumes the wicked." We can see the same thing with sick bodies. When someone lives without discipline and does not take care of himself while he is healthy, an excess or a deficiency arises, and from then on he is out of balance. Before this the sickness existed nowhere and was nothing at all. And once the body is healthy again, the sickness is no longer found anywhere, and it was never anything. Likewise evil is a sickness of the soul, which has lost its own natural health, and that health is virtue. 4. That is why we said that the virtues are means. Courage, for example, is the mean between cowardice and rashness. Humility is the mean between pride and the desire to please people. Likewise reverence is the mean between bashfulness and shamelessness, and the other virtues follow the same pattern. So if a man is found worthy of these virtues, he is found honourable before God. To all appearances he is always eating and drinking and sleeping just like other people, yet he is honourable because of the virtues he has. But if someone is not watchful and does not guard himself, he easily turns aside from the road, either to the right or to the left, that is, towards excess or deficiency, and so brings on the sickness that is evil. This is the royal road on which all the saints have walked. The milestones are the various states, which a person ought always to measure, so that he sees where he is, which milestone he has reached, and what state he is in. Here is the kind of thing I mean. We are all like people who have set out from a city with the aim of travelling to the holy city. Some walked five miles and stopped there. Others walked ten. Others got as far as halfway. Others did not travel at all: they left the city, but stayed outside its gates in its stench. Of those who are on the road, some at times walk two miles, lose their way, and go back over those same two; or they walk two and go back five. Others walked as far as the city itself but stayed outside and never went into the city. That is just how we are. There are some of us who left the world and came to the monastery with the aim of acquiring the virtues. Some have made

a little progress and stopped there. Others made a bit more progress. Others got as far as halfway and came to a halt. Others made no progress at all. They seemed to have left the world, but they stayed in the passions of the world and in its stench. Others achieve a little good and then undo it again. Some even undo more than they have achieved. Others did achieve the virtues, but became proud and looked down on their neighbours, and so they stayed outside the city and did not go in. So even they did not reach their goal: though they got as far as the city gate, they stayed outside, and so they too fell short of their own [?]

5. So let each of us learn where he is. Has he left his own city but stayed outside the gate, in the city's stench? Has he gone forward a little, or a long way? Has he reached the halfway point of the road? Does he walk two miles and then undo those two? Does he walk two and undo five? Has he travelled as far as the city and entered Jerusalem? Or did he reach the city but find himself unable to get inside? Let each of us learn his own state and where he is. There are three states in a person. There is the one who acts on the passion, the one who checks it, and the one who uproots it. The one who acts on the passion is the one who carries it out and champions it. The one who checks the passion neither acts on it nor cuts it off. He reasons with it and holds it down, but he still has the passion within him. The one who uproots the passion is the one who struggles against it and does the opposite of what it urges. These three states cover a great range. Take an example. Shall we take a passion and lay it bare? Shall we talk about pride? About fornication? Or would you rather we talked about vainglory? Suppose someone cannot bear to hear a word from his brother. Sometimes a person hears one word and is upset. He answers with five words, or even ten, in return for that one. He quarrels and is upset, and after the quarrel has stopped he keeps brooding against the one who said that word to him. He bears a grudge against him and is sorry he did not say more than he did. He prepares even nastier words to say to him, and keeps telling himself, "Why didn't I say this to him? I could say that to him!" and he goes on raging. That is one state, the one that has evil as a settled habit. May God deliver us from such a state! Such a state is entirely liable to punishment, for every sin that is carried out in action is under hell. Even if such a person wants to repent, he cannot overcome the passion on his own unless he also gets help from some of the saints, as the Fathers said. That is why I always tell you: hurry to cut off the passions before they become habits in you. Then there is another person who hears a word and is upset. He too answers with five words, or ten, in return for one, and he is distressed that he did not say other things three times worse. He is grieved and bears a grudge. But he keeps it up for

a few days and then changes. Another keeps it up for a week and then changes. Another keeps it up for one day and then changes. Another insults, quarrels, is upset and upsets others, and then changes at once. See how many different states there are! And yet all these people are under hell so long as they act on the passion. 6. Let us also talk about those who check the passion. Sometimes a person hears a word and is distressed inside himself, but he is grieved not because he was insulted but because he did not bear it. He belongs to the state of those who struggle, those who check the passion. Another struggles and toils, but in the end is defeated, because the passion weighs him down. Another does not want to answer badly, but is carried away by habit. Another struggles not to say anything bad at all, but is grieved that he was insulted. Still, he condemns himself for being grieved and repents of it. Another is not grieved that he was insulted, but he does not rejoice either. All of these are people who check the passion. But two of them differ from the rest: the one who is defeated while struggling, and the one who is carried away by habit, as well as the one who condemns himself because he did not bear the insult with thanksgiving. The rest are in fear of the danger that threatens those who act on the passion. I said that they belong among those who check the passion because in their disposition they have stopped it. They do not want to act on it; on the contrary, they are grieved as they struggle. The Fathers said that anything the soul does not want lasts only a short time. Still, they ought to examine themselves, in case they are championing, if not the passion itself, then one of its causes, and that is why they are defeated or carried away. There are also some, he says, who struggle to check the passion, but do it by means of a passion. One keeps silent out of vainglory, another out of a desire to please people, or out of some other passion of whatever kind. These people are curing evil with evil. Abba Poemen said that wickedness never does away with wickedness. These people belong with those who act on the passion, even if they are mocked. 7. Next we want to talk about those who uproot the passion. Sometimes a person rejoices when he is insulted, but because he will receive a reward. He is one of those who uproot the passion, but not with understanding. Another rejoices when he is insulted, and holds that he deserves to be insulted because he himself gave the cause. He uproots the passion with understanding. For to be insulted, to take the blame on oneself, and to accept what comes upon one as one's own doing, belongs to understanding. Anyone who prays to God, "Lord, give me humility," ought to know that this is what he is asking for: that God send him someone to insult him. And when someone insults him, he ought also to insult himself and despise himself in his own

thoughts, so that the other person humbles him from outside and he humbles himself from inside. There is yet another who not only rejoices when he is insulted and blames himself, but is also grieved at the agitation of the one who insulted him. May God bring us to such a state! See how wide a range there is within the three states. So, as I said, let each of us learn which state he is in. Does he still act on the passion willingly and champion it? Or does he not do it willingly, but act on it because he is overcome or carried away by habit, and then after acting on it feel distressed and repent of what he did? Does he struggle to check the passion with understanding? Or does he struggle by means of another passion, as we said? Sometimes a person keeps silent out of vainglory or a desire to please people, or, to put it simply, from some merely human reasoning. Has he begun to uproot the passion? And does he uproot it with understanding, doing the opposite of what the passion urges? Let each of us learn where he is and which milestone he is at. We ought to search ourselves not only every day but also every season, every month and every week, and say, "Last week this passion weighed on me in such and such a way. How am I now?" Likewise every season we should say, "Last year this passion overcame me in such and such a way. How am I now?" In this way we should train ourselves each day, checking whether we have advanced a little, or are where we were, or have grown worse. May God give us strength so that for the time being, even if we do not uproot the passion, at least we do not act on it but check it. For it is truly a grievous thing to act on the passion instead of checking it. Let me give you an illustration. The one who acts on the passion and champions it is like a man whose enemy shoots arrows at him, and who takes the arrows in his hands and drives them into his own heart. The one who checks the passion is like a man whose enemy shoots at him, but who wears a breastplate and so does not take the arrow. The one who uproots the passion is like a man who is shot at, takes the arrows and breaks them, or turns them back into his enemy's heart, as it says in the psalm: "Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bows be broken." So let us strive too, brothers. Even if we cannot yet turn their sword back into their own hearts, let us at least not take the arrows and drive them into our own hearts. Let us put on breastplates, so that they do not wound us. May the good God shelter us from them, give us watchfulness, and guide us on the way [?]

[?] and be careful not to neglect yourselves, because even a small negligence brings us into great dangers. Just now I visited a certain brother and found him [recovering?] from an illness. As we talked, I learned that he had a fever for only seven days, and now he has had another forty days and still cannot get his strength back. See, brothers, how miserable it is to fall into an unbalanced condition. People always make light of a small lapse in discipline. They do not know that if the body happens to suffer even a little harm, especially if the person is rather weak, a great deal of effort and time is needed before it is set right. This poor man had a fever for seven days, and look how many days have passed since, and he finds no relief and cannot get his strength back. It is the same with the soul. A person sins a little, and then spends who knows how long dripping blood before he sets himself right. With bodily illness we find various causes. Either the medicines are old and no longer work; or the doctor is inexperienced and gives one medicine in place of another; or the patient is undisciplined and does not keep to what the doctor orders. But with the soul it is not so. We cannot say that the doctor was inexperienced and did not give suitable medicines. For Christ is the physician of souls. He knows everything, and he has provided the fitting medicine for each passion. For example, for vainglory he gave the commandments about humility; for love of pleasure, those about self-control; for love of money, those about almsgiving. In short, each passion has as its medicine the commandment suited to it. So the doctor is not inexperienced. Nor do the medicines fail to work because they are old. For the commandments of Christ never grow old; the more they are put into practice, the more they are renewed. So nothing stands in the way of the soul's health except [?] 2. So let us pay attention to ourselves, brothers. Let us be watchful while there is time. Why do we neglect ourselves? Let us do some good, so that we may find help in the time of temptation. Why are we wasting our life? We hear so much, and we do not care; we make light of it. We see our brothers snatched from our midst, and we are not watchful, though we know that little by little we too are drawing near to death. Look, from the time we sat down to talk until now we have spent two or three hours of our time and come nearer to death. We see that we are losing time, and we are not afraid. Why do we not remember the saying of that elder: "If someone loses gold or silver, he can find more to replace it. But if we lose time by living idly and carelessly, we cannot find more"? Truly, we shall look for one hour of this time and not find it. [?] long to hear the word of God and cannot find it, while we hear so much and make light of it and are not roused! God knows, I am astonished at the

insensibility of our souls. We can be saved, and we do not want to be. While our passions are young we can cut them off, and we do not bother. Instead we let them harden against us, so that we make our final state worse [?]. As I have often told you, it is one thing to uproot a small plant, which comes away at once, and another to uproot a great tree. A great elder once happened to be with his disciples in a place where there were various cypresses, small and large. The elder said to one of his disciples, "Pull up this cypress." It was very small, and the brother pulled it up at once with one hand. Then the elder showed him another, bigger than the first, and said to him, "Pull this one up too." The brother rocked it with both hands and pulled that one up as well. Again the elder showed him another, still bigger, and he pulled that one up too, with more effort. Then he showed him another, bigger still. The brother rocked it hard, toiling and sweating, and with even more effort he got that one out as well. Then the elder showed him one bigger yet. The brother toiled and sweated hard, but could not get it out. When the elder saw that he could not do it, he told another brother to get up and help him, and in this way the two of them together managed to pull it up. Then the elder said to those brothers, "See, brothers, the passions are like this. While they are small, we can cut them off with ease if we want to. But if we neglect them because they are small, they harden, and the harder they get, the more effort they need. And if they grow even stronger against us, then even with effort we can no longer cut them off by ourselves, unless we also have the help of some of the saints, who come to our aid after God." See how much power the sayings of the holy elders have. The Prophet teaches us the same thing in the psalm where he says: "Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you the recompense you repaid us. Blessed is he who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock." 4. Let us examine what is said, in order. By Babylon he means confusion, for that is how the name is interpreted, from "Babel," which is Shechem [?]. By the daughter of Babylon he means enmity. For first the soul is thrown into confusion, and then it brings sin about. He calls her wretched because, as I have told you before, evil has no substance and no subsistence. It comes into being out of nothing through our negligence, and through our right conduct it perishes again and passes into nothing. So the saint says, as though addressing her: "Blessed is he who will repay you the recompense you repaid us." Let us learn what we gave, what we received in return, and what we want to repay. We gave our will, and in return

we received sin. So the word calls blessed those who repay her with this, and to repay her means no longer to commit it. Then he adds: "Blessed is he who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock." That is, blessed is he who takes what comes from you, namely the evil thoughts, and does not give them room even at the start to grow in him, so that evil is not carried out. Instead, quickly, while they are still infants, before they are fed and grow strong against him, he seizes them and dashes them against the rock, which is Christ, and destroys them by taking refuge in [?]

5. See how the elders and holy Scripture all agree. They call blessed those who struggle to cut off the passions while they are young, before experiencing their pain and bitterness. So let us strive, brothers, that we may obtain mercy. Let us toil a little, and we shall find much rest. The Fathers told us how a person ought to purify himself little by little. Each evening he should examine how he spent the day, and again each morning how he spent the night, and repent before God for the sins he has probably committed. But since we truly sin a great deal, and since we are forgetful, we need to search ourselves every six hours, to see how we have spent the time and how we have sinned. Each of us should say to himself: "Did I perhaps say something that hurt my brother? Did I see him doing something and judge him, or despise him, or speak against him? Did I ask the cellarer for something, and when he did not give it to me, did I grumble against him? Did [?] not cook the food well, and did I say something that shamed the cook and upset him? Or, being fussy, did I grumble to myself?" For even if someone grumbles to himself, it is a sin. He should also say: "Did the precentor or another of the brothers say something to me, and instead of bearing it, did I contradict him?" In this way we ought to examine ourselves every day, to see how we have spent the day. Likewise a person ought to search himself to see how he spent the night. Did he get up eagerly for the vigil? Was he short with the one who woke him, or did he grumble against him? For he ought to know that the one who wakes him for the vigil does him a great kindness and becomes the means of great blessings for him. He wakes him to pray to God for his sins, so that he may be enlightened. How could anyone fail to thank such a person? In truth he ought to regard his salvation as coming almost entirely through him.

6. On this subject I will tell you something wonderful that I heard about a great elder who had the gift of second sight. He was standing in church as the brothers began the psalmody, and he saw someone in shining garments come out of the sanctuary. He was holding something like a small bowl containing holy water, and a sponge [?]. He dipped it into the bowl and went round all the brothers, marking each of them with the sign of the cross. As for the places of those who were not there, some of these he marked and others he passed over. Again, when they were about to be dismissed, the elder saw him come out of the sanctuary and do the same thing. So on one occasion the elder stopped him, threw himself at his feet and begged to learn what he was doing and who he was. The one in shining garments said to him, "I am an angel of God. At the synaxis I have been charged to give this seal to those who are in church at the beginning of the psalmody and to those who remain until the dismissal, because of their eagerness and zeal and their good intention." The elder said to him, "And how is it that you seal the places of some who are not there?" The holy angel answered him, "Some of the brothers are zealous and have a good intention, but are absent with the blessing of the Fathers because of an illness that cannot be helped, or else are busy with some task given them under obedience, and for that reason are not there. These receive their seal even though they are absent, since in their disposition they are with those who are chanting. But some could be there and stay away out of negligence. To these alone I have been charged not to give the seal, since they have made themselves unworthy of it." See, then, what a gift a man procures for his brother when he wakes him for the rule of the vigil. So be eager, brothers, never to lose the seal of the holy angel. And if it happens that someone's mind wanders and another reminds him, he ought not to be annoyed. He should pay attention to the good, and thank the one who reminds him, whoever he may be. 7. When I was in the monastery, the abbot made me guest-master with the consent of the elders. I was just getting over a serious illness. Guests would arrive and I would spend the evening with them, and then camel drivers, and I would see to their needs. Often, after I had gone off to sleep, some other need would come up and wake me. Meanwhile the hour of the vigil would arrive, and I had barely snatched a little sleep when, look, the canonarch was waking me. And so I found myself so worn out, whether from fatigue or from illness (for slight fevers were still creeping up on me),

that I was hardly in possession of myself. So, overcome by sleep, I would answer him, "Very well, sir. May God remember your charity and give you your reward. You have given the word; I am coming, sir." Then, when he had gone, I would fall asleep again. I was very distressed at being late in rising for church. And since there was no way for him to keep waiting on me, I asked two of the brothers, one to wake me, and the other not to let me doze during the vigil. And believe me, brothers, I revered them as though my salvation came through them, and I almost venerated them. You too ought to feel this way towards those who rouse you for the rule of the church and for every good thing. As we were saying, then, a person ought to examine how he has spent the day and the night: whether he stood soberly at the psalmody, or was taken captive by passionate thoughts during prayer; whether he listened attentively to the divine readings, or left the psalmody and went out of church with a wandering mind. If someone examines himself in this way every day, and strives to repent for the sins he has committed and to correct himself, he begins to lessen the evil. If he used to commit nine, he commits eight. And so, advancing little by little with God's help, he does not let the passions become entrenched against him. For it is a great danger for someone to fall into the habit of a passion, since, as we have said, even if such a person wants to, he cannot overcome the passion on his own unless he also has help from some of the saints. 8. Do you want me to tell you about someone who had a passion as a habit? Listen to something worthy of many tears. When I was in the monastery, somehow or other the brothers simply liked [?] to confide their thoughts to me. The abbot too [?], with the consent of the elders, entrusted me with the care of this side of things. One day one of the brothers came and said to me, "Forgive me and pray for me, for I steal and eat." I said to him, "Why? Are you hungry?" He said to me, "Yes. The brothers' table is not enough for me, and I cannot ask." I said to him, "Why don't you go and tell the abbot?" He said, "I am ashamed." I said to him, "Do you want me to go?" He said to me, "As you wish, sir." So I went and told the abbot, and he said to me, "Be so kind as to look after him as you think best." Then I took him and said to the cellarer in his presence, "Be so kind as to give this brother whatever he wants at whatever hour he comes to you, and do not refuse him anything." When the cellarer heard this, he said to me, "As you command, so I will do." The brother did this for a few days, and then came and said to me, "Forgive me, sir, for I have started stealing again." I said to him, "Why? Doesn't the cellarer give you whatever you want?" "Yes. Forgive me, he gives me whatever I want.

But I am ashamed in front of him." I said to him, "Are you ashamed in front of me?" He said to me, "No." I said to him, "Then whatever you want, come and take it from me, and do not steal." At that time I had charge of the infirmary. So he would come to me and take as much as he wanted. Then, after some days, he began to steal again, and he came to me in distress and said, "Look, I am stealing again." I said to him, "Why, my brother? Don't I give you whatever you want?" He said, "Yes." I said to him, "Then why do you steal?" He said to me, "Forgive me, I don't know why. I just steal." Then I said to him, "Tell me the truth: what do you do with the things you steal?" He said to me, "I give them to the donkey." And it turned out that this brother was stealing loaves, dates, figs, onions, simply whatever he came across, and hiding them, some under his bedding and some elsewhere. In the end, not knowing what to do with them, when he saw them going bad, he would go and throw them away or put them in front of the animals. 9. There, do you see what it is to have a passion as a habit? Do you see what wretchedness, what misery? He knew that it was evil, he knew that he was doing wrong; he was distressed, he wept; and yet the wretched man was dragged along by the bad habit he had made for himself through his earlier negligence. And Abba Nisterus spoke well: if someone is swept away by a passion, he has become a slave of the passion. May the good God deliver us from bad habit, so that he may not say to us too, "What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to corruption?" I have told you in various ways how a person falls into a habit. Someone who gets angry once is not on that account called irascible, nor is someone who commits fornication once called a fornicator, nor is someone who shows mercy once called merciful. But both virtue and vice, by being practised continually, produce a kind of habit in the soul, and from then on this habit either torments the soul or gives it rest. We have explained in various ways how virtue gives the soul rest and how vice torments it: virtue is natural and is within us, for the seeds of virtue cannot be wiped out. So I said that the more we do good things, the more we come into the habit of virtue; that is, we recover our own proper state, we return to our own health, as one returns from an eye disease to one's proper sight, or from any other illness to one's own natural health. With vice it is not so. Rather, by practising evil we take on a foreign and unnatural habit, as though we had come into the state of some pestilential disease, so that we can no longer be healed without many tears, tears able to move the compassion of Christ towards us. We find the same in bodily things.

There are certain foods that produce, let us say, a melancholic humour. For instance, cabbage is melancholic, and lentils, and some other such things. Now it is not from eating cabbage or lentils or something of the kind once or twice that a melancholic humour forms in a person; but if he eats them often, then the humour builds up and stirs up fevers, and these burn the one who has them. It also brings some people into countless other troubles. So it is with the soul too: if someone persists in sinning, an evil habit forms in the soul, and it is this that torments it.

10. But see this too: sometimes a soul is found with an inclination towards a passion, and if it falls into the practice of that passion even once, it is in danger of passing straight into a habit. The same thing happens in bodily matters. Someone is found to have a rather melancholic constitution because of some earlier negligence, and almost a single food of that kind can immediately stir up and inflame the humour in him. So there is need of much watchfulness, zeal and fear, so that one does not fall into a bad habit. Believe me, brothers: if someone has ten good works and one evil one as a habit, that one which comes from bad habit prevails over the ten good ones. Think of an eagle: if it has got completely out of the trap and only its talon is found caught, through that small thing all its strength is brought down. For even if it is entirely outside, and only its talon is caught, is it not still in the trap? Can the hunter not bring it down whenever he wants? So it is with the soul too. If it has even one passion as a habit, the enemy brings it down whenever he pleases, for through that passion he has it in his grip. That is why I always tell you, "Do not let a passion form a habit in you." Rather let us struggle, praying to God night and day that we may not fall into temptation. And if we are overcome, being human, and slip into a fault, let us strive to get up at once; let us repent for it; let us weep before the goodness of God; let us keep watch; let us struggle. And God, seeing our intention, our humility and our contrition, gives us his hand and shows us his mercy. Amen.

DISCOURSE 12. On the fear of the punishment to come, and that one who wishes to be saved must never be careless about his own salvation. 1. When my feet were aching and I was ill because of them, some of the brothers who came up to visit me asked me to tell them the cause of the illness. They had two aims, I think:

to comfort me and take my mind off the pain a little, and to give me an occasion to say something to them for their benefit. But since the pain did not let me say to you then what I wanted, you need to hear about it now; for telling of an affliction after the affliction is over is a pleasant thing. At sea too, when a storm comes up, everyone is always distressed, but after the storm has passed, they always tell one another with joy and delight what happened. And it is good, brothers, as I always tell you, to refer everything to God and to say that nothing happens apart from God. Certainly God knew that this was good and profitable, and so he did it, even if the thing has some outward cause. For instance, I could have said that because I ate with guests and forced myself a little to keep them company and put them at ease, my stomach became heavy, a flux settled in my foot, and from that I got rheumatism. Or I could give various other causes, for they are never lacking to anyone who looks for them. But the more accurate and profitable thing to say is rather this: God knew that it was good for my soul, and so it happened. For there is nothing God does that is not good; on the contrary, all things are very good. So no one should lose heart over what happens, but, as I said, refer everything to the providence of God and be at rest. There are some people who are so weighed down by the afflictions that befall them that they renounce life itself and would gladly die so as to be rid of them that way. A person suffers this from smallness of soul and great ignorance, not knowing the fearful necessity that follows the soul's departure from the body. 2. It is a great act of God's love for mankind, brothers, that we are in this world. But we, not knowing what is there, think that what is here is heavy; and it is not so. Do you not know what it says in the Sayings of the Elders? A very hard-working brother asked an elder, "My soul longs for death." And the elder said to him, "That is because you are running away from affliction, and you do not know that the affliction to come is much worse than the affliction here." And another likewise asked an elder, "Why do I suffer from acedia when I sit in my cell?" And the elder said to him, "Because you have not yet seen either the rest we hope for or the punishment to come. If you saw these clearly, then even if your cell were full of worms, so that you were sunk in them up to your neck, you would endure it without acedia." But we want to be saved even while we sleep, and that is why we lose heart in afflictions. We ought rather to thank God and count ourselves blessed that we are deemed worthy at all to suffer a little affliction here, so that we may find a little rest there. Evagrius also said that someone who is subject to the passions and prays for a speedier [?]

departure is like a man who begs the carpenter to break up the sick man's bed quickly. For through this body the soul is distracted from its passions and finds comfort: it eats, drinks, sleeps, meets people, goes about with those it loves. But when it leaves the body, it is left alone with its passions, and from then on it is constantly tormented by them, brooding on them, burned by their harassment and torn apart by them, so that it cannot even remember God. For the very remembrance of God comforts the soul, as the psalm also says: "I remembered God and was glad." And yet the passions do not allow it even this. Do you want to learn by an example what I mean? Let one of you come and shut himself up in a dark cell, and for just three days not eat, not drink, not sleep, not meet anyone, not chant psalms, not pray, and not remember God at all; and let him find out what the passions do to him. And this while he is still here! How much more after the soul has left the body, been handed over to them and left alone with them. 3. What the wretched soul has to suffer from them then, one can in some measure understand from things here. When someone has a fever, what is it that burns him? What fire, or what wood, produces that burning? And if someone has a melancholic, ill-balanced body, is it not that very imbalance of his that burns him, troubles him constantly and makes his life a misery? So too the wretched passionate soul is constantly tormented by its own bad condition, always having the bitter memory and the painful brooding of the passions, which constantly burn and inflame it. And besides this, brothers, who can describe those fearful places, those bodies made for punishment that serve the souls in such great and terrible pain and are not destroyed, that unspeakable fire, the darkness, those stern avenging powers, and the countless other torments spoken of in various ways in the divine Scriptures, all corresponding to the evil deeds of souls and to their very evil thoughts? Just as

[?] nor fearsome angels standing by; but if, when people were called, some were simply praised and glorified, and others were sent away in disgrace so that they might not see the glory of God, would not the punishment of that shame and dishonour, and the pain of losing such good things, be more bitter than all of Gehenna? For then the very reproof of conscience and the very memory of what has been done, as we said above, is worse than countless unspeakable punishments. For souls remember everything that happened here, as the Fathers say, words and deeds and thoughts, and they cannot forget any of them. As for what the psalm says, "On that day their thoughts shall perish," it is speaking of the thoughts of this age: about building, lands, parents, children, all buying and selling. As soon as the soul leaves the body it loses these, and it neither remembers nor cares about any of them. But what it did according to virtue or according to passion, these things it remembers, and it loses none of them. What is more, if someone helped another, or was himself helped by someone, he always remembers both the one he helped and the one who helped him. Likewise, if he was harmed by someone, or himself harmed someone, he always remembers both the one who harmed him and the one he harmed. And, as I said, the soul loses nothing of what it did in this world, but remembers everything after it has left the body, and even more clearly and distinctly, since it has been freed from this earthly body. 4. Once we were talking about this with a certain great elder, and the elder said that after leaving the body the soul remembers the passion it acted on, and the sin, and the person with whom it committed it. But I said to him, "Perhaps it is not so. Perhaps it will have the habit that was formed in it by committing the sin, and that is what it remembers." And we went on disputing this point for a long time, wanting to learn. The elder was not persuaded, but said that it remembers the very form of the sin, and the very place, and the very person who sinned with it. And truly, if this is so, we are bringing on ourselves an even greater evil, the worst of all. That is why I always tell you: strive to cultivate good thoughts, so that you may find them there. For whatever a person has here goes out with him, and that is what he will have there. Let us take care to be delivered from such a fate, brothers; let us be zealous, and God will show us his mercy. For he is the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far off at sea. Those at the ends of the earth are those in complete wickedness; those far off at sea are those in utter ignorance; and yet Christ is the hope even of such as these. A little labour is needed; let us labour, so that we may find mercy. If someone has a field and neglects it and it goes to waste, does it not fill with thorns and thistles in proportion to his neglect? And when he comes to clear it, do not his hands bleed in proportion to how full of them it is, as he tries to pull up that bad weed,

[?] …which he allowed to spring up during the time of his negligence? For it is impossible for anyone not to reap what he has sown. Whoever wants to clean his field needs, first of all, to root out all the weeds thoroughly. For if he does not properly pull up all their roots, but only cuts them off at the top, they grow again. So one must, as I said, pull up the very roots; and after cleaning the field well of weeds and thorns and the like, he must turn the soil over well and break up the clods, and then plough it; and only then must he sow it with good seed. For if, after giving it all this care, he leaves it idle, the weeds come up and find the soil soft and good from all the care, and they send their roots down deep and grow stronger and multiply in it.

5. So it is with the soul too. First one must cut off every old attachment and the evil habits. Saint Basil says: “This is no small struggle, to get the better of our own habits. For custom confirmed over a long time generally takes on the strength of nature.” So one must struggle, as I said, against evil habits and against the passions, and not only against these but also against their causes, which are their roots. And unless the roots are thrown out, the thorns are bound to grow again. For there are some passions that have no strength once one cuts off their causes. Envy, for instance, is nothing in itself, but it has certain causes from which it comes, among them love of glory. For someone who wants to be glorified envies the one who is glorified or preferred over him. Likewise anger also arises from other causes, and especially from love of pleasure. Evagrius too mentions this, saying of a certain saint that he used to say: “This is why I cut off pleasures: so as to cut away the pretexts for anger.” And all the Fathers say that every passion is born of these three: love of glory, love of money, and love of pleasure, as I have told you in various ways. So one must cut off not only the passions but also their causes, and so put one's ways well in order through repentance and weeping, and then begin to sow the good seed, which is good works. For as we said about the field, that if one does not sow good seed, the weeds come up and find the soil good and soft from all the care and take deeper root in it, so it is with a person: if, after putting his ways in order and repenting of his former deeds, he neglects to do good works and to acquire the virtues, there happens to him what the Gospel says: “When the unclean spirit goes out of a man, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none, it then says: ‘I will return to my

house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it unoccupied”—that is, empty of all virtue—“swept and put in order. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” For it is impossible for the soul to remain in the same state; it is always moving on, either toward the better or toward the worse. Therefore everyone who wants to be saved needs not only to refrain from doing evil but also to do good, as it says in the psalm: “Turn away from evil and do good.” It did not say only, “Turn away from evil,” but also, “Do good.” For example: if someone was in the habit of doing wrong, he must not only stop doing wrong but also act justly. If he was dissolute, he must not only stop living dissolutely but also practise self-control. If he was irascible, he must not only stop being angry but also acquire gentleness. If someone used to be arrogant, he must not only stop being arrogant but also humble himself. And this is what it means to turn away from evil and do good. For each passion has its opposite virtue: pride has humility, avarice has almsgiving, dissoluteness has self-control, faintheartedness has patience, anger has gentleness, hatred has love. In short, as I said, every passion has its opposite virtue.

6. I have told you this many times. So just as we drove out the virtues and brought in the passions opposed to them, so we must labour not only to drive out the passions but also to bring in the virtues and establish them in their proper place. For we possess the virtues by nature, given to us by God. As soon as God made man, he sowed the virtues in him, as it says: “Let us make man in our image and after our likeness.” It says “in our image” because God made the soul immortal and endowed with free will; it says “after our likeness” with reference to virtue. For it says: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful”; and “Be holy, for I am holy.” And again the Apostle says: “Be kind to one another.” And the psalm says: “The Lord is good to those who wait for him,” and other such texts. This is what “after our likeness” means. So God gave us the virtues by nature; but the passions we do not have by nature. For they do not have any substance or real existence; just as darkness does not subsist as a substance but is a condition of the air, as the great Basil says, coming into being through the absence of light, so it is with the passions. The soul, turning aside from the virtues through love of pleasure, produced the passions and fortified them against itself. So, as I said, we need to do just as with the field: after doing all the preparation, to sow the good seed at once, so that it may also yield good fruit. And again, the one who sows his field must, as soon as he casts the seed, cover it and bury it in the earth; otherwise the birds come and snatch it away and

[?]. And after he has covered it, he waits for God's mercy, until he sends the rain and the seed grows. For however much the farmer labours, cleaning and tending the ground and then sowing, if God does not send rain on his seed, all his labour is in vain. So we too, if we do anything good, must cover it with humility and cast our weakness upon God, begging him to look favourably on our labour; otherwise it comes to nothing. Again, sometimes even after it has rained and the seed has sprouted, the rain does not come again in its season, and the shoot dries up and perishes. For the seed needs rain, and so does the shoot, little by little, until it becomes established; and even then one cannot be free of care. For sometimes, even after it has grown and put out ears, locusts come, or hail, or something of the sort, and destroy the crop. So it is with the soul. When it has laboured and cleansed itself of all the passions we have spoken of, and has striven after all the virtues, it must always look to God's mercy and his protection, so that these may not forsake it and it perish. For just as we said about the seed, that even after it has sprouted and grown and borne fruit, if the rain does not come again little by little, it dries up and perishes, so it is with a person. If, after he has done so much, God withdraws his protection a little and forsakes him, he perishes. And forsaking happens to a person when he does something contrary to his state. For example: if someone is devout and falls into indifference, or is humble and falls into arrogance. And God does not forsake the indifferent person so much if he behaves indifferently, nor the arrogant person if he behaves arrogantly, as he forsakes the devout person if he becomes indifferent, and the humble person if he becomes arrogant. This is what it means for someone to sin contrary to his state; and from this comes forsaking.

7. That is why Saint Basil judges the sin of the devout person one way and that of the indifferent person another. And when someone guards himself against this too, he must take care that, if he does some small good, he does not do it out of vainglory or to please people or from some human calculation, and so lose the very little he did, as we said about the locusts and the hail and the like. Again, with the land, even when the crop suffers no harm but is kept safe until the harvest, not even then can the farmer be free of care. For there are times when, even after someone has harvested his field and completed all his labour, a wicked man comes out of hatred and sets fire to that crop, and destroys the whole crop and all that man's labour. Until he sees that he has cleaned it well and put it in the storehouse, he cannot be free of care. Likewise a person, even when he has managed to escape all the things we have mentioned, must not even then be free of care. For it happens

that after all this the devil finds a way to lead him astray, either through self-justification, or through pride, or by putting into him thoughts of unbelief or of evil heresy; and not only does he destroy all his labours, but he also separates him from God. And whatever he could not do to him through action, he does to him through a single thought. For there are times when even a thought can separate someone from God, if he accepts it and consents to it. So whoever wishes to be saved in truth must not be free of care until his last breath. There is need, then, of labour and much attentiveness, and of praying to God continually, that he himself may protect and save us by his goodness, to the glory of his holy name.

Instruction 13. On enduring temptations without being disturbed and with thanksgiving.

1. Abba Poemen rightly said that the mark of a monk is seen in temptations. For the monk who comes in truth to serve the Lord must, as Wisdom says, prepare his soul for temptations, so that he may never be surprised or disturbed by what happens, believing that nothing happens without God's providence. And where there is God's providence, what happens is wholly good and for the benefit of the soul. For everything God does with us, he does for our good, loving us and sparing us. And we ought, as the Apostle said, to give thanks in everything to his goodness, and never to be despondent or fainthearted at what befalls us, but to receive whatever comes without being disturbed, with humility and with hope in God, convinced, as I said, that whatever God does with us he does out of goodness, does out of love for us, and does well. And these things could not have turned out well in any other way than as God in his mercy has arranged them. If someone has a friend and is fully convinced that he loves him, then whatever he suffers at his hands, even if it is painful, he holds that the friend did it out of love, and he never believes of his friend that he wants to harm him. How much more ought we to hold concerning God, who formed us and brought us from nothing into being, and became man for our sake, and died for us, that he does everything with us out of goodness and out of love for us.

2. With a friend, one can reason: “He does this because he loves me and cares for me, but he does not necessarily have the understanding to manage my affairs, and so he may harm me even without meaning to.” But we cannot say this about God. For he is the source of wisdom, and knows everything that is good for us, and manages our affairs accordingly, down to the most trivial. Again, one may say of a friend that he loves me and cares for me and has the understanding to manage my affairs,

but does not have the power to help me in the things he thinks would benefit me. Nor can we say this about God. For all things are possible to him, and nothing is impossible before him. So, since we know of God that he loves and spares his own creature, that he is the source of wisdom and knows how to manage our affairs, and that nothing is impossible to him but everything serves his will, we ought to know that all he does he does for our good, and we ought to receive it with thanksgiving, as we said before, as from a benefactor and a good Master, even if it is painful. For everything happens by just judgment, and God, who is so merciful, does not overlook even our slightest affliction. But often someone is in doubt and says to himself: “If in times of adversity a person sins because of the affliction, how can he hold that these things are for his good?”

3. We do not sin in adversities except because we shrink from toil and do not want to bear a little affliction or to suffer anything against our wishes; for God does not allow anything beyond our strength to come upon us, as the Apostle said: “God is faithful, who will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able.” But it is we who have no patience, who do not want to toil even a little, nor can bear to accept anything with humility; that is why we are crushed, and the more we strive to escape temptations, the more we weigh ourselves down and lose heart, and we cannot even get out of them. There are some who swim in the sea out of necessity, and if they know the art of swimming, when a wave comes against them, they duck under it until it passes, and then they go on swimming unharmed. But if they try to resist the wave, it pushes them back and flings them a long way. Again, as they begin to swim, another wave comes over them; if they resist again, again it pushes them back, and they only wear themselves out and achieve nothing. But if, as I said, they stoop under the wave and humble themselves beneath it, it passes without harming them, and they go on swimming as long as they wish and doing their work. So it is with temptations too: if someone bears the temptation with patience

[?] …and pride, and from not knowing one's own state, and from fleeing toil, as the Fathers said. That is why we make no progress: because we do not know our own measure, and we have no patience in the work we begin, but want to acquire [?virtue] without toil. Why is the passionate man surprised when he is troubled by a passion? Why is he disturbed, when he himself acted on it? You have it, and you are disturbed? You hold its pledges, and you say, “Why does it trouble me?” Rather endure, struggle, call upon God. For it is impossible for someone who has fallen into acting on the passions not to suffer the affliction of the passions. “Their vessels,” as Abba Sisoes said, “are inside you; give them back their pledge, and they go away.” By “vessels” he meant the causes. So inasmuch as we have loved these things and acted on them, it is impossible for us not to be taken captive by passionate thoughts, which force us to act out the passions even against our will, since we willingly delivered ourselves into their hands. This is what the prophet says about Ephraim, who oppressed his adversary—that is, his own conscience—and trampled down judgment, because he sought Egypt and was carried off by force among the Assyrians. By Egypt the Fathers mean the carnal will, which inclines us toward bodily ease and teaches the mind to be more easily won over by pleasure; and by the Assyrians, the [?] of unclean idols, which carry the mind off by force, even against its will, into sin in act.

5. So if someone willingly gives himself up to bodily pleasure, he is compelled, even against his will, to be carried off by force to the Assyrians and to serve Nebuchadnezzar. Knowing this, the prophet was distressed and said to them: “Do not go down into Egypt. What are you doing, wretches? Humble yourselves a little; bend your shoulder and work for the king of Babylon, and stay in the land of your fathers.” Again he rouses them, saying: “Do not be afraid of him, for God is with us to deliver us from his hands.” Then he also foretells the affliction that will come upon them if they disobey God: “For if,” he says, “you go into Egypt, you will become a desolation, and subject to others, and a curse, and a reproach.” And they say to him: “We will not stay in this land, for we will go into Egypt, and there we will not see war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor go hungry for bread.” So they went down and served Pharaoh willingly. Then they were carried off by force to the Assyrians and served them even against their will.

6. Pay attention to what is being said. Before someone acts on a passion, even if the thoughts campaign against him, he is still in his own city, and he has God helping him. If, then, he humbles himself before God and bears the yoke of affliction and temptation with thanksgiving, and struggles a little, God's help delivers him. But if he flees the toil and goes down into bodily pleasure, then he is led by force and necessity into the land of the Assyrians, and serves them even against his will. Then the prophet says to them: “Pray for the life of Nebuchadnezzar, for his life is your salvation.” Nebuchadnezzar means this: not losing heart under the affliction of the temptation that befalls one, nor kicking against it, but bearing it with humility as one who deserves to suffer, and holding that one is not worthy even to be freed from the burden, but rather that the temptation should continue and be fastened on one all the more—whether one is aware of the cause in oneself at present or not—believing that nothing with God is without judgment or unjust. As that brother said, grieving and weeping when God took away his temptation: “Lord, am I not worthy to be afflicted a little?” Again, it is written that a disciple of a great elder was assailed by fornication. Seeing him toiling, the elder said to him: “Do you want me to ask God to lighten this warfare for you?” But he said: “Even though I am toiling, abba, I see fruit coming to me from the toil. Rather, ask God to give me patience.”

7. See, these are truly the ones who want to be saved: this is bearing the yoke with humility and praying for the life of Nebuchadnezzar. That is why the prophet says: “In his life is your salvation.” The brother's saying, “I see fruit coming to me from the toil,” is like saying, “In his life is my salvation.” As the elder also makes clear to him: “Today I know that you are making progress and surpass me.” For when someone struggles against sin in act and begins to fight, and in the face of passionate thoughts in the mind he humbles himself, is crushed, and struggles, then through the affliction of the struggles he is gradually purified and returns to his natural state. So, as we said, it is from ignorance and

[?] of this: "When sinners sprang up like grass, all who work iniquity peered out, so that they might be destroyed for ever and ever." The sinners springing up like grass are the passionate thoughts. Grass is weak and has no strength. So when passionate thoughts spring up in the soul, then all who work iniquity peer out, that is, they come into view. These are the passions. They appear so that they may be destroyed for ever and ever. For when the passions come into view to those [?], then they are destroyed by them.

[?]. Notice the order of the passage. First the passionate thoughts spring up, then the passions peer out, and then they are destroyed. All this belongs to those who are struggling. But we commit sin in action and are always taking the side of the passions. We do not even know when the passionate thoughts spring up, or when the passions peer out, so that we might struggle against them. Instead we are still down in Egypt, at Pharaoh's wretched brickmaking. Who will grant us at least to come to a sense of our bitter slavery, so that we may be humbled and be eager to find mercy? When the children of Israel were in Egypt and served Pharaoh, they made bricks. Brickmakers at work are always bent down [?], scorched, their eyes on the earth. So too the soul: if it is mastered by the devil and commits sin in action, it tramples down its own mind and makes it think nothing spiritual, but always think and do earthly things. Then out of the bricks they had made they built for him three fortified cities, Pithom, Rameses and On, which is Heliopolis. These are love of pleasure, love of glory and love of money, out of which all sin is made up. When God sent Moses to bring them out of Egypt and out of slavery to Pharaoh, Pharaoh made their labours heavier and said to them, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and worship the Lord our God.'" The devil does the same. When God has already consented to have mercy on a soul and to relieve it of the passions through his Word, or through one of his servants, then the devil weighs the passions down on it all the more and wars against it more violently. The Fathers knew this, and so they strengthen a person through their teaching and do not let him be afraid. One says, "Have you fallen? Get up. And if you fall again, get up," and again, and so on. Another says, "The strength of those who want to acquire the virtues is this: that if they fall, they do not lose heart, but take care [?]." Each of them puts it differently [?]. In one way or another [?], each offers a hand to those who are struggling and are hard pressed by the enemy. For they themselves received this from the divine Scripture, which says:

"Does not one who falls rise again? Or does one who turns away not turn back?" And, "Turn to me, children, and I will heal your wounds, says the Lord," and other such sayings. When the hand of God lay heavy on Pharaoh and his servants, and he was willing to let the children of Israel go, he said to Moses, "Go, worship the Lord your God, but leave your sheep and your oxen behind." These signify the thoughts of the mind, which Pharaoh wanted to keep under his control, hoping through them to draw the children of Israel back to himself. And Moses said to him [?], "No, you will even give us sacrifices and burnt offerings to offer to the Lord our God. Our livestock will go with us, and we will not leave behind so much as a hoof." When Moses had brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, he led them across the Red Sea. God wanted to bring them to the seventy palm trees and the twelve springs of water, but first he brought them to Marah. There the people were in distress, finding nothing to drink because the water was bitter. Then by way of Marah he brought them to the place of the seventy palms and the twelve springs of water. So too the soul: when it stops sinning in action and has crossed the spiritual sea, it must first toil, struggling and suffering much affliction, and so through afflictions enter into the holy rest. For "through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of heaven." Afflictions move God's mercy toward the soul, as the winds move the rain. If rain keeps falling for a long time while the shoot is still tender, it rots it, and its fruit is lost; but the winds dry it out little by little and make it firm. It is the same with the soul. Slackness, freedom from care and ease make it soft and scatter it, but temptations draw it together and unite it to God. As the prophet says, "Lord, in affliction we remembered you." So, as we said, we must not be troubled or grow listless in temptations. We must endure, give thanks in afflictions, and always entreat God with humility to show mercy to us in our weakness and to shelter us from every temptation, to his glory. Amen.

1. Scripture says of the midwives who kept alive the male children of the Israelites that, because the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves. Does it mean physical houses? What sense would there be in building such houses because of the fear of God? On the contrary, we

are taught to leave even the houses we have, when the time comes, because of the fear of God. So it is not speaking of a physical house, but of the house of the soul, which a person builds for himself by keeping God's commandments. Through this Scripture teaches us that the fear of God prepares the soul to keep the commandments, and through the commandments the house of the soul is built. Let us too, brothers, pay attention to ourselves. Let us too fear God, and let us build houses for ourselves, so that we may find shelter in time of winter, in time of rain, lightning and thunder. Winter is very hard on someone who has no house. As for how the house of the soul is built, we can learn the details from a physical house. Anyone who wants to build such a house must make it secure on every side and raise the building on all four sides. He must not take care of one part and neglect the others, since that is no use; it makes his purpose, his expense and his labour all in vain. It is the same with the soul. A person must not neglect any part of his building, but raise it evenly and in proportion. This is what Abba John means when he says, "I want a person to take a little from each virtue, and not do as some do, who hold on to one virtue, stay with it and work at it alone, and neglect the rest." Perhaps they even have some advantage in that one virtue, and so they are not weighed down by the passion opposed to it. But meanwhile the other passions steal in on them and weigh them down, and they do not care, but think they have something great. They are like someone who builds a single wall and raises it as high as he can, then gazes at the height of that wall and thinks he has done something great. He does not see that a single wind, if it comes, will throw it down, for it stands alone, without the bond of the other walls. Nor can anyone make a shelter for himself out of one wall, since he is exposed on every other side. That is not how it should be done. Rather, whoever wants to build his house and make a shelter for himself must build it on every side and make it secure all round. 2. Let me say how. First he must lay the foundation, which is faith, for "without faith," as the Apostle says, "it is impossible to please God." Then he must build up the structure on this foundation in due proportion. Does a chance for obedience come his way? He must lay a stone of obedience. Does a brother provoke him? He must lay a stone of patience. Does a chance for self-control come his way? He must lay a stone of self-control. So with every virtue that comes his way he must lay a stone in the building and raise it all round: a stone of compassion, a stone of cutting off his own will, a stone of meekness, and so on. In all of this he must take care

of endurance and courage. These are the corners. Through them the building is bound together and wall is joined to wall, so that the walls do not lean or break away from one another. Without these no one has the strength to bring any virtue to completion. If someone has no courage in his soul, he does not endure, and without endurance no one can achieve anything at all. That is why it says, "By your endurance you will gain your souls." The builder must also set each stone in mortar. If he sets stone on stone without mortar, the stones break loose and the house falls. The mortar is humility, since it comes from the earth and lies under everyone's feet. Every virtue practised without humility is no virtue, as the Gerontikon also says: "As it is impossible to build a ship without nails, so it is impossible to be saved without humility." So whatever good a person does, he must do it with humility, so that what he has done may be preserved by humility. The house must also have what are called tie-beams. These are discernment, which strengthens the house, joins stone to stone and binds the building together, besides giving the house great beauty. The roof is love, which is the perfection of the virtues, as the roof is of the house. After the roof comes the parapet around the roof terrace. What is the parapet of the roof? It is written in the Law: "If you build yourselves a house and make it a roof, make a parapet for the roof, so that your children do not fall from the roof." The parapet is humility, for it is humility that crowns and guards all the virtues. Every virtue must be done with humility, just as we said each stone is set in mortar. In the same way the perfection of virtue needs humility. And the saints, as they advance, naturally come to humility; as I always tell you, the nearer someone comes to God, the more he sees himself a sinner. And what are the children the Law spoke of, so that they do not fall from the roof? The children are the thoughts that arise in the soul. They must be guarded by humility, so that they do not fall from the very roof. The house is finished: it has the tie-beams and the roof of the virtues. There is the house, which we said is perfection; there too is the parapet; in short, the house is complete. 3. Is anything still missing? We have left out one more thing. What is it? The builder must be skilled. If he is not skilled, he builds crooked, and sooner or later the house falls. The skilled builder is the one who acts with knowledge. For it happens that someone toils at virtue, but because he does not act with knowledge, he undoes his work, or keeps going round in circles [?] and never manages to finish the work, laying one stone and then taking it away again. Another lays one and takes away two. For example: here comes

your brother, and he says something that hurts or wounds you. You keep silent and make a prostration to him; there, you have laid one stone. Then you go off and say to another brother, "So-and-so insulted me. He said this and that to me, and I not only kept silent, I even made a prostration to him." There, you have laid one stone and taken away two. Again, someone makes a prostration because he wants to be praised, and it turns out to be humility mixed with vainglory. That is laying one stone and taking it away. But one who makes a prostration with knowledge is truly convinced that he himself was at fault, and fully persuades himself that he is the cause. That is making a prostration with knowledge. Another practises silence, but not with knowledge, for he thinks he is practising a virtue, yet he is doing nothing. But one who is silent with knowledge [considers that] he is unworthy [?]. Again, someone does not measure himself; he thinks he is doing something great and humbling himself, and he does not know that he has nothing, because he does not act with knowledge. To measure oneself with knowledge is to regard oneself as nothing, not even worthy to be counted among human beings, as Abba Moses said to himself: "Ash-skinned, black one, you who are not a man, why do you come among men?" Again, someone serves a sick person, but he serves in order to have a reward, and this too is not with knowledge. Then if anything unpleasant happens to him, it easily cuts him off from his good work, and he never manages to finish it, because he does not act with knowledge. But one who serves with knowledge serves in order to acquire compassion, to acquire a heart of mercy. Since he has this aim, whatever happens to him, whether trouble from outside or neglect from the sick person himself, he bears it calmly, keeping his eye on his aim and knowing that the sick person does him more good than he does the sick person. Believe me, one who serves a sick person with knowledge is relieved even of passions and inner warfare. I know a brother who was assailed by shameful desire and who was freed from that warfare by serving, with knowledge, a sick man suffering from dysentery. Evagrius too tells of a great elder who freed one of the brothers, troubled at night, from such things by ordering him to serve the sick while fasting. When asked his reason for doing this, he said that nothing quenches such passions as well as mercy does. Again, if someone practises asceticism either out of vainglory or with the idea that he is practising a virtue, he is not practising with knowledge. From this he begins to despise his brother, thinking himself to be something. He turns out not only to be laying one stone and taking away two, but even to be in danger of throwing down the whole wall by judging his neighbour. But one who practises self-control with knowledge does not think he is practising a virtue, and does not want to be praised as an ascetic. He considers that through self-control he acquires chastity, and that through chastity he comes to humility,

as the Fathers say that the way to humility is bodily labour done with knowledge, and so on. In short, one must practise each virtue in this way, so as to acquire it and make it a settled habit. And so he turns out, as we said, to be a good builder of his own house. 4. So whoever wants, with God's help, to come to so good a state must not say, "The virtues are great, and I cannot reach them." That is the mark either of someone who does not trust in God's help or of someone too lazy to undertake anything good. Which virtue do you want? Let us examine it, and you will see that achieving it is within our power. See, it says, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." Do not dwell on how far you are from this virtue and begin to lose heart and say, "How can I love my neighbour as myself? How can I care about his troubles as I do my own, especially those hidden in his heart, which I neither see nor know, as I do my own?" Do not occupy yourself with reckoning up such things, and do not think the virtue too lofty and hard to achieve. For now just make a beginning, trusting in God. Show him your will and your zeal, and you will see the help he gives you to achieve it. For example, suppose there are two ladders, one leading up to heaven and the other leading down to Hades, and you are standing on the earth between the two. Do not try to work out and say, "How can I fly up from the earth and find myself all at once at the top of the ladder?" That is not possible, and God does not require it of you. For now, guard against going down. Do not harm your neighbour, do not strike him, do not slander him, do not revile him, do not despise him. Then begin also to do him a little good: care for your brother with a word, sympathize with him, and if he needs something, give it to him. And so, climbing one step at a time, you will reach the top of the ladder with God's help. By helping your neighbour little by little you come to want what benefits him as much as what benefits you, and his good as your own. This is what "You shall love your neighbour as yourself" means. If we seek, we find, and if we ask God, he enlightens us. For he says in the Gospel, "Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you." "Ask," he says, so that we may call on him

in prayer. "Seek" means that we should look into how this virtue comes about, what produces it, and what we must do to acquire it. Looking into each virtue in this way is what "Seek and you will find" means. And to knock is to put the commandments into practice. Everyone who knocks knocks with his hands, and the hands are understood as the practical life. So we must not only ask, but also seek earnestly and act, so that we may be, as the Apostle said, "equipped for every good work." What does "equipped" mean? When someone wants to build a ship, he first gets ready everything the ship needs, down to small nails, a little pitch, a little tow [?]. Likewise when a woman wants to sew [?], she gets everything ready, down to a little thread. Having everything the work needs ready to hand is what is called being equipped. 5. So let us too be equipped for every good work, having everything ready to do the will of God with knowledge, as he wills and as pleases him. What does the Apostle mean by "the will of God, good, acceptable and perfect"? Everything that happens happens either by God's permission or by his good pleasure. As it says in the prophet, "I am the Lord, who makes light and creates darkness," and again, "There is no evil in a city that the Lord has not done." By evil he means everything that brings harm, that is, the hardships that come upon us for our correction [?] because of our wickedness, such as [?] famine, earthquake, drought, diseases and wars. These do not happen by God's good pleasure but by his permission: God permits them to be brought upon us for our benefit. God does not want us to want these things or to cooperate with them. For example, it may be God's will, by permission as we said, that a city be overthrown. Does he then want us, because it is God's will that it be overthrown, to set fire to it ourselves and burn it, or to take axes and tear it down? Again, God may permit someone to be afflicted or to fall ill. Because it is his will that the man be afflicted, does he want us to afflict him? Or to say, "Since it is God's will that he be sick, let us not have mercy on him"? God does not want this; he does not want us to serve that kind of will of his. He wants us to be so good that we do not will what he himself does in that way. What, then, does he want? He wants us to will his good will, the will that is done by his good pleasure, as I said. That is everything done according to the commandments: loving one another, showing compassion, giving alms, and all such things. That is the good will of God. But what is the acceptable will? It is not the case that anyone who does good necessarily does it in a way that is acceptable. Let me say how. It happens that someone finds [Isaiah 45:7; Amos 3:6]

…someone [sees] an orphan girl, poor and beautiful, and is pleased with her because of her beauty, and takes her in and brings her up [?] because she seemed to him an orphan, poor and beautiful. See, this too is God's will and it is good, but it is not well-pleasing. The well-pleasing is when someone gives alms not for some human reason, but for the sake of the good itself, out of compassion; this is well-pleasing to God. And the perfect is when someone gives alms not stingily, nor reluctantly, nor carelessly, but with all his strength and all his will, giving as though he himself were receiving, doing good as though he himself were the one being helped; and then it becomes perfect. And so a person is found doing the will of God, as the Apostle says, the good and well-pleasing and perfect. See, this is what it means to act with knowledge. (6.) For one needs to know the very good of almsgiving and its grace: that it is great, that it can even forgive sins, as the prophet says: "The ransom of a man is his own wealth." And again elsewhere he says: "Redeem your sins by almsgiving." And the Lord himself said: "Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful." He did not say: Fast, as your heavenly Father fasts. Nor did he say: Be without possessions, as your heavenly Father is without possessions. But what does he say? "Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful." For this virtue in particular imitates God; it bears his very likeness. So, as we said, we must always attend to this aim and act with knowledge. For there is a great difference in the aim of almsgiving too. One person gives alms so that his field may be blessed, and God blesses his field; another gives alms for the sake of his ship, and God saves his ship; another gives for his children's sake, and God saves and guards his children; another gives to be glorified, and God glorifies him. God rejects no one. Rather, he grants each what he wants, so long as his soul is not harmed by it. But all these have received their reward; for they laid up nothing for themselves with God, since the aim they set before themselves was not the benefit of their soul. You gave so that your field would be blessed; God blessed your field. You gave for your children's sake; God guarded your children. You gave to be glorified; God glorified you. What then does God owe you? He has paid you the reward for what you did. Then there is another who gives alms in order to be delivered from the punishment to come. See, this one does it for the sake of his soul; he acts according to God, yet not as God wishes. For he is still in the condition of a slave. A slave does not do his master's will because he wants to, but because he is afraid of being beaten. In the same way this man gives so that he may be delivered from punishment, and

God delivers him from it. Another gives alms so that he may receive a reward. This is higher than the first, but even this is not yet as God wishes. For he is not yet in the disposition of a son; rather, just as a hired hand does his master's will in order to receive his wage from the master and make a profit, so this man too acts in order to profit and have a reward. For there are three dispositions in which we may do good, as Saint Gregory says; I have told you this on other occasions too. Either we do good because we fear punishment, and then we are in the condition of a slave; or in order to receive a reward, and then we are in the disposition of a hired hand; or for the sake of the good itself, and then we are in the disposition of a son. For a son does not do his father's will out of fear, nor because he wants to receive a wage from him, but because he wants to serve him, to honour him and give him rest. So we too ought to give alms in this way, for the sake of the good, suffering with one another as with our own members; serving another as though we ourselves were being served through him; giving as though we ourselves were receiving. This is almsgiving with knowledge; in this way we are found in the disposition of a son, as we said. No one can say: "I am poor and have nothing to give alms from." For even if you cannot give like those rich men who put their gifts into the treasury, give two mites like the poor widow, and God accepts them from you above those gifts. You do not have even that? But you have strength, and you can show mercy to the sick by serving them. You cannot do even that? You can encourage your brother with a word. Show him mercy, then, by a word, and listen to the one who says: "A good word is better than gifts." Suppose you cannot help even by a word: if your brother is provoked against you, you can show him mercy and bear with him in the time of his agitation, seeing that he is being harassed by the common enemy; and instead of saying a single word and troubling him further, you can keep silent and have mercy on him and on his soul, drawing him away from the enemy. Again, if your brother sins against you, you can show him mercy and forgive him his sin, so that you too may receive forgiveness from God. For he says: "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." And so you are found showing mercy to your brother's soul by pardoning him for the wrong he did you. For God has given us the power, if we wish, to pardon one another the trespasses committed even against ourselves. And though you have no way of showing mercy to his body, you show mercy to his soul.
