And what mercy is as great as mercy to the soul? For just as the soul is more precious than the body, so the mercy shown to the soul is greater than the mercy

shown to the body. So no one can say: "I cannot show mercy." Each person can show mercy according to his ability and the state of his soul; only let each strive to do with knowledge whatever good he does, as we said about each of the virtues. For we said that the one who acts with knowledge is the approved and skilled craftsman, who builds his own house securely. The Gospel also speaks of this: "The wise man builds his house on the rock," and nothing hostile can shake [?] it. May God, the lover of mankind, grant us to hear and to do what we hear, so that these words may not become a judgment against us on the day of judgment; for to him be glory forever. Amen.

INSTRUCTION 15. On the Holy Fasts. 1. In the Law God commanded the sons of Israel to give a tithe each year of everything they acquired; and by doing so they were blessed in all their works. Knowing this, the holy apostles resolved, for the help and benefit of our souls, to hand this down to us in a greater and loftier form: to tithe the very days of our life and, as it were, to consecrate them to God, so that in this way we too might be blessed in our works and might each year atone for the sins of the whole year. And having made their reckoning, they sanctified for us, out of the three hundred and sixty-five days of the year, these seven weeks of the fasts; for this is how they set apart seven weeks. But in time the Fathers agreed to add another week to them, partly to give preliminary training and, as it were, to smooth the way for those about to enter the labour of the fasts, and partly to honour the fasts with the number of the holy Forty Days which our Lord fasted. For the seven [?] weeks, when the Saturdays and Sundays are taken out, come to forty days, while the fast of Holy Saturday is honoured on its own, because it is the most sacred, and the only fast among all the Saturdays of the year. But the seven weeks without the Saturdays and Sundays come to thirty-five days; then, when Great Saturday is added, and half of the bright and light-giving night, they make thirty-six and a half days, which is precisely the tenth of the three hundred and sixty-five days of the year. For the tenth of three hundred is thirty, the tenth of sixty is six, and the tenth of five is one half. There you have thirty-six and a half days, as we said. This is the tithe, so to speak,

of the whole year, which the holy apostles sanctified for us for repentance, as a cleansing of the sins of the whole year, as I said. So whoever keeps himself well, as he ought, during these holy days is blessed, brothers; for even if he, being human, happened to sin, whether from weakness or from negligence—see, God has given these holy days so that, if someone strives with watchfulness and humility to take care of himself and to repent during them, he may be cleansed of the sins of the whole year. And then his soul is relieved of its burden, and so he comes pure to the holy day of the Resurrection and partakes of the holy mysteries without condemnation, having become a new man through the repentance of these holy fasts; and he continues in spiritual joy and gladness, celebrating with God the whole of holy Pentecost. For Pentecost is the resurrection of the soul, as it says; and this is also why, as a symbol, we do not kneel in the holy church during the whole of Pentecost. 2. Everyone, then, who wishes to be cleansed of the sins of the whole year through these days must first keep himself from carelessness about food. For carelessness about food, as the Fathers say, breeds every evil in a person. Then he must likewise take care not to break the fast without great necessity, not to seek out pleasant foods, and not to weigh himself down with too much food or drink. For there are two kinds of gluttony. Sometimes a person is assailed in the matter of taste: he does not always want to eat a great deal, but he wants what is pleasant. And it happens that such a person eats a food he likes and is so overcome by the pleasure of it that he keeps holding that food in his mouth, chewing it for a long time and not having the heart to swallow it because of the pleasure. This is called laimargia. Another is assailed by the desire to be full: he does not want good foods and does not care about taste, but whether they are good or bad [?], he wants only to eat; whatever they may be, all he cares about is filling his belly. This is called gastrimargia. And I will tell you the reason for these names. Among the pagan writers, margainein means to be mad, and someone who is mad is called margos. So when that disease and madness concerns filling the belly, it is called gastrimargia, from margainein, that is, the belly being mad. When the pleasure concerns only the throat, it is called laimargia, from the throat being mad. These things, then, must be guarded against and fled with all watchfulness by anyone who wishes to be cleansed of his sins. For they do not arise from the body's need but from passion; and if he gives way to them, they become sin for him. It is like living lawfully in marriage and committing fornication: the act is the same, but it is the aim that makes the difference in the

matter. For the one comes together with his wife to have children, the other to satisfy his own love of pleasure. So too with eating, one can find that eating out of need and eating for pleasure are the same act, but the aim is what makes the sin. Eating out of need is when someone determines for himself how much to take each day and observes whether the amount he has set weighs him down, so that he needs to take away a little of it, and he takes it away; or whether it does not weigh him down but his body is not sustained by it, so that he needs to add a little more, and he adds a little. In this way he tests his need well, and from then on he keeps to the fixed amount, taking it not for pleasure but with the aim of sustaining his body's strength. And whatever one takes, one should take it with prayer, and condemn oneself in one's thoughts as unworthy of any comfort whatever; and one should pay no attention if some, as is natural, are given care because of some need or necessity, so as not to seek relief oneself too, or think that relief is a light matter for the soul. 3. Once, when I was in the community, I went to visit one of the elders (for there were many great elders there), and I found the brother who served him eating with him, and I said to him privately: "You know, brother, these elders whom you see eating and receiving a little care are like people who acquired a purse and kept working and putting money into that purse until they had filled it; and after sealing it, they worked again and gathered for themselves another thousand coins, so that in time of need they would have something to spend and could keep what was in the purse. So these men too kept working and storing up treasure for themselves, and after sealing their treasures they worked for a little more, and they keep this for a time of sickness or old age, so as to spend from it while keeping the rest stored up. But we have not even acquired the purse itself; what are we to spend from?" For this reason, as I said, even if we take something out of need, we must condemn ourselves and count ourselves unworthy of every kind of care, and even of the monastic life itself, and take it with [?] fear. And then it does not become a condemnation for us. So much, then, for self-control of the belly. 4. But we need not only to watch over our diet but also to keep away from every other sin, so that just as we fast with the stomach, we may also fast with the tongue, keeping away from slander, from lying, from idle talk, from abuse, from anger, in short, from every sin committed through the tongue. Likewise we must fast with the eyes: not looking at vain things, not letting our eyes be bold, not staring at anyone shamelessly. Likewise we must keep our hands and feet from every evil

deed. And fasting in this way, as Saint Basil says, with an acceptable fast, keeping away from every evil worked through all our senses, let us come to the holy day of the Resurrection, as we have already said, new and pure and worthy to partake of the holy mysteries—having first gone out to meet our Lord and received him with palms and olive branches, as he sits on a colt and enters the holy city. What does his sitting on a colt mean? He sat on a colt so that, as the Word of God, he might turn back the soul that had become irrational and, as the prophet says, like the senseless beasts, and might subject it to his own divinity. And what does it mean to meet him with palms and olive branches? When someone goes out to war against the enemy and comes back victorious, each of his own people meets him with palms as a victor; for the palm is a symbol of victory. Again, when someone is wronged by another and wants to approach the one who is able to avenge him, he carries olive branches, crying out and begging to be shown mercy and to obtain help; for olives are a symbol of mercy. That is why we too meet our Master Christ with palms as a victor, for he conquered the enemy for our sake; and with olive branches, asking mercy from him, so that we too, by asking, may conquer through him and be found carrying his victory trophies, not only for the victory which he won for us, but also for the one which we too have won through him, by the prayers of all the saints. Amen. INSTRUCTION 16. To some cell-dwellers who had asked him about visiting. 1. The Fathers say that sitting in the cell is half, and visiting the elders is half. The saying means that both in the cell and outside the cell there is equal need of watchfulness, and of knowing why one ought to keep stillness by oneself and why one ought to visit Fathers and brothers. For if someone is watchful about this aim, he strives to act as the Fathers said. When he sits in his cell, he prays, meditates, does a little handiwork, and attends to his thoughts as far as he can. And when, again, he goes visiting at some time, he observes and looks at his own state: whether he benefits from meeting the brothers or not, and whether he can return to his cell unharmed. But if he sees that he has been harmed in some way, he learns his weakness; he learns that he has not yet gained anything from stillness, and he returns humbled to his own cell, weeping, repenting, beseeching God about his weakness, and so from then on he sits paying attention to himself. Then he comes back among people again and sees whether he is still overcome

by the same things as before, or by others; and so he returns again to his cell, doing the same things in the same way, weeping, repenting, praying to God about his state. For the cell lifts up, but people test. So the Fathers spoke rightly when they said that sitting in the cell is half, and visiting the elders is half. 2. You too, then, when you visit one another, must know why you are leaving your cell, and never go off at random. For whoever travels without an aim, as the Fathers said, labours in vain. So everyone who does anything must certainly have an aim and know why he is doing it. What, then, is the aim we should have when we go to one another? First, love; for it says: "You have seen your brother; you have seen the Lord your God." Second, to hear the word of God; for surely, when there are many, the word of God is stirred up more: what one person often does not know, another asks about. And then also, as I said before, to learn one's own state. I mean something like this: suppose someone goes to eat with others who have gathered. He should observe himself and see, if a good dish is set out and he likes it, whether he can control himself and not take any of it; or whether he strives not to take advantage of his brother by taking more than he does; or, if something is served in portions, whether he strives not to take the larger portion and leave his brother the smaller. For sometimes a person is not even ashamed to stretch out his hand, put the small portion in front of his brother, and take the large one in front of himself. What, after all, can the difference between the larger portion and the smaller be? How much is there between the two portions, that for such cheap and trivial things he is found taking advantage of his brother and sinning? Again, he pays attention to whether he can restrain himself from many dishes, and not, as is likely to happen when he finds a variety of foods, give himself over to stuffing himself; whether he guards himself against over-familiarity; whether, when he sees his brother preferred, or given more comfort than himself, he is unaffected; whether, when he sees one person being over-familiar with another, or talking a great deal, or behaving in some other undisciplined way, he pays no attention to him and does not judge him, but rather pays attention to the most devout, and strives to do as is said of Abba Anthony: that when he went to visit certain people, whatever good thing he saw that each of them had, he took it and held on to it—from one his [?], from another his humility, from another his stillness—and so he found that he had in himself what each of them had. 3. See, this is how we ought to act, and this is why we ought to visit; and when we return to our cells, we ought to examine ourselves and learn in what we have benefited,

[?] …or in what we were harmed. If we find at once that we were protected, let us thank God, who protected us so that we passed through unharmed. Where we went wrong, let us repent, weep and mourn our own condition. For each of us is harmed or helped [?] by his own condition, since no one harms anyone else. If we are harmed [?], we are harmed, as I said, by our own condition. For, as I always tell you, if we wish, we can be either helped or harmed by anything at all. And I will give you an example, so that you may learn that this is so. Suppose someone is standing in some place at night. I do not mean a monk, but anyone at all in the city. Three men pass by him. One thinks to himself that the man is waiting for someone so that they can go off and commit fornication. The second thinks he is a thief. The third thinks that a friend has called to him from the house next door, and that he is waiting for him to come down so that they can go off together somewhere to pray. Look: all three saw the same man in the same place, and yet the three did not have the same thought about him. One imagined this, another that, and the third something else, each plainly according to his own condition. Think of bodies that are melancholic and full of bad humours. They turn every food they take into bad humour, even if the food is wholesome. The cause is not in the food. As I said, the body itself is badly tempered, and so it necessarily works on the food according to its own temperament and changes it. In the same way, a soul with a bad disposition is harmed by everything, even by what is good for it. Imagine a jar of honey, and someone drops a little wormwood into it. Does not that little bit spoil the whole jar and make all the honey bitter? We do the same. We pour out a little of our own bitterness and spoil our neighbour's good, because we view it through the bad disposition within us. But those who have a good disposition are like someone whose body has good humours. Even if he eats something harmful, his body turns it into good humour according to its own temperament, and that bad food does not hurt him, because, as I said, his body has good humours and works on the food according to its own temperament. We said of the first body that its bad temperament changes even good food into bad humour. In the same way, this well-tempered body changes even bad food into good humour. I will give you an example, so that you may act on it. The pig has a body with very good humours. Its food is carob pods, date stones and mud. Yet because its body has good humours, it changes even such food into good humour. So we too, if we have a good disposition and a good condition, can, as I said before, be helped by everything, even if the thing is not helpful in itself. Proverbs puts it well: He who looks gently will be shown mercy. And elsewhere it says: All things are hostile to a foolish man. 4. I heard of a certain brother that when he visited

one of the brothers and saw that his cell was untidy and neglected, he would say to himself: "Blessed is this brother. He is free from care about many things, or rather about all earthly things, and so he has lifted his whole mind upward. That is why he does not even have time to put his cell in order." And when he went to another brother and saw that his cell was in order, clean and well kept, he would say to himself: "This brother's cell is as clean as his soul. The state of his cell matches the state of his soul." He never said of anyone, "This one is untidy" or "This one is vain". Because his own condition was good, he was helped by every one of them. May the good God grant us a good condition, so that we too may be helped by everyone and never notice our neighbour's wickedness. And if our own wickedness makes us notice or suspect it, let us at once turn our thought to thinking well of him. For not knowing our neighbour's wickedness gives birth, with God's help, to goodness, and goodness pleases God. To him be glory for ever.

INSTRUCTION 17. To those in monasteries who are superiors [?], on how they ought to govern brothers, and how one should submit to those in charge. 1. If you are in charge of brothers, look after them with firmness of heart and with tender compassion. Teach them what they must do by deed and by word, but more by deed, since examples are more effective. If you can, give them a pattern in bodily labours too. If you are weak, give it by the good condition of your soul and by the fruits of the Spirit that the Apostle lists: love, patience, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness, and self-control against all the passions. When faults occur, do not be very indignant. Calmly point out the harm that comes from the fault. If a rebuke is needed, consider the person and choose a suitable time. Do not be exacting about small faults either, as if you yourself were perfectly just. Do not reprove constantly. That is burdensome, and when reproof becomes a habit it leads to insensibility and contempt. Do not give orders in a commanding way, but take counsel with the brother humbly. Words like that encourage him, persuade him better and give your neighbour rest. When a brother is agitated and opposes you, guard your tongue and say nothing at all in anger, and do not let your heart be lifted up against him. Remember that your brother is a member in Christ

and an image of God, assailed by our common enemy. Have compassion on him. Otherwise the devil may take him captive through the wound of anger and kill him with resentment, and a soul for whom Christ died may be lost through our carelessness. Remember that you too are subject to the same judgment on anger. Knowing your own weakness, have compassion on your brother, and give thanks that you have found an occasion to forgive, so that God may forgive you greater and more numerous things. For: Forgive, and you will be forgiven. But do you think your forbearance harms your brother? Yet the Apostle commands us to overcome evil with good, not with evil. The Fathers also say: "If you are moved to anger while rebuking another, you are satisfying your own passion. No sensible person tears down his own house to build his neighbour's." If the agitation persists, force your heart and pray like this: "O God, lover of mankind and lover of souls, in your ineffable goodness you made us from nothing to share in your good things, and when we turned away from your commandments you called us back through the blood of your only-begotten Son, our Saviour. Now too stand by us in our weakness. As you once rebuked the stormy sea, rebuke now the agitation of our hearts. Do not be bereaved in a single hour of us both, put to death by sin. Do not say to us: What profit is there in my blood, if I go down to corruption? Nor: Amen, I say to you, I do not know you, because your lamps have gone out for lack of oil." When this prayer has calmed your heart, you can then, with understanding of heart, reprove and rebuke as the Apostle instructs. With compassion you can heal and correct him as a weak member. For then the brother too accepts the correction with full conviction, condemning himself for his harshness, and through your peace you will bring peace to his heart. So let nothing separate you from the holy teaching of Christ: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart. Our first concern must be a peaceful condition. We should not trouble our hearts even on just grounds, or supposedly for the sake of a commandment, since we are convinced that we practise all the commandments for the sake of love and purity of heart. If you govern your brother in this way, you will hear the voice that says: If you bring forth

what is precious from what is worthless, you will be as my mouth. 3. When you are under obedience, never trust your own heart, for old attachments have blinded it. Do not follow your own judgment in anything, and do not settle anything by yourself without asking and taking advice. Do not consider your own views more reasonable and just than those of the one who governs you, and do not set yourself up to examine his actions, even if you often judge him to be mistaken [?]. This is a deception of the evil one. It aims to hinder obedience in all things with faith, and the secure salvation that obedience brings. Then you submit with rest, and you travel the way of the Fathers without danger and without going astray. Force yourself in everything and cut off your will. By the grace of Christ you will come through habit to the practice of cutting it off, and from then on you will do it without strain or distress. Then it turns out that what you want always happens. It is not that you want things to happen as you wish. You want them as they happen, and you are at peace with everyone. This applies, of course, to matters that involve no transgression of a commandment of God or of the Fathers. Strive to find in everything a way to blame yourself, and hold fast to counting yourself as nothing [?] in your knowledge. Believe that everything that concerns us, down to the smallest things, is under God's providence, and you will bear whatever comes upon you without agitation. Believe that dishonours and insults are healing medicines for the pride of your soul. Pray for those who revile you as for true physicians, convinced that whoever hates dishonour hates humility, and whoever flees those who provoke him flees meekness. Do not wish to know your neighbour's wickedness, and do not entertain suspicions against him. If our own wickedness sows such suspicions, hasten to turn them into good thoughts. Give thanks in everything, and act with goodness and holy love. Above all, let all of us guard our conscience in everything: in matters towards God, towards our neighbour, and with material things. Before saying or doing anything, let us examine whether it is according to God's will. Then, having prayed, let us speak or act, and lay our weakness before God, and his goodness will come with us in

Do you not want to fall into anger and resentment? Then have no attachment at all to material things. Do not lay claim to any object whatever, but do not despise it as worthless either. If anyone wants it from you, give it. And if through carelessness or contempt it is

broken or lost, do not be anxious. You must do this not because you despise the monastery's property. You are bound to look after it with all your strength and all diligence. Do it because you want to keep yourself calm and undisturbed, while always showing God that you have done what you can. You will manage this if you do not handle things as your own, but as dedicated to God, with only their care entrusted to you. The one attitude keeps you from being attached, as I said. The other keeps you from despising them. If you do not have this aim, be sure of this: you will never stop being disturbed and disturbing others.
My mind rejoices in these words and wants things to be so. Why, then, am I not ready when the moment comes to act?

Because you do not meditate on them constantly. If you want to have them when the time comes, meditate on them always and occupy yourself with them, and I trust in God that you will make progress. Join prayer to your meditation. Care for the sick. First, so that you may gain compassion from it, as I have often said. Then, so that whenever you yourself fall ill, God may raise up someone to care for you. For, it says, the measure you give will be the measure you get back. If you are eager to do something conscientiously, as far as you are able, you ought to know and be fully convinced that you do not yet know the true way. You ought to accept it calmly, without distress and with joy, when you hear that you were wrong in what you thought you were doing conscientiously. For through the judgment of your companions, either what is lacking is corrected or what is done well becomes more secure. Strive to make progress, so that if affliction comes upon you, whether in body or in spirit, you may be able to bear it without distress, without feeling its weight, and with patience. If you hear that you have done something you did not do, do not be alarmed at all or flare up. At once make a prostration to the one who told you and say humbly, "Forgive me and pray for me," and then keep silent, as the Fathers said. But if he asks you whether the thing is true or not, then make a prostration with humility and tell him truthfully how the matter stood. After you have spoken, make another prostration with humility and say, "Forgive me and pray for me." 4.
What shall I do, since I do not have the same condition when I meet the brothers?

[?] …of the brothers you cannot have yet. But for now, strive not to be scandalized by anything. Do not condemn anyone or speak against anyone, and pay no attention to any word, deed or gesture of the brothers that does not benefit you. Strive instead to edify yourself in everything, and do not wish to show off in word or deed or to seek vainglory. Acquire freedom in your way of life and in your speech, down to the smallest thing. Know this. If someone is assailed or afflicted by a passionate thought and gives in to it [?], he strengthens the thought against himself. It is as if he gives it power to fight and afflict him all the more. But if he struggles, opposes the thought and does what is contrary to it, as we have often said, the passion weakens and loses its power to fight and afflict him. So, by struggling little by little with God's help, he overcomes the passion itself. May God protect us through the prayers of all the saints. Amen.

INSTRUCTION 19. Various sayings of the same, in brief. Abba Dorotheus used to say that someone who holds to his own understanding or his own thought cannot submit or follow what his neighbour thinks good. He also said that since we are subject to passions, we ought not to trust our own heart at all, for a crooked ruler makes even straight things crooked. He also said that it is no great thing to refrain from judging someone who is in affliction and submits to you, or even to have compassion on him. The great thing [?] is to refrain from judging or trampling on someone who contradicts you out of his own passion, not to side with someone who judges him, and to rejoice with someone who is preferred to you. He also said that someone who does not despise all material things, all glory and bodily comfort, and even his own rights, cannot cut off his

will. He is not freed from anger and grief, and he does not give his neighbour rest. He also said: Do not demand love from your neighbour. For whoever demands it is troubled if it is not returned. Instead, show love to your neighbour yourself and give him rest, and so you will bring your neighbour too to [?]

He also said that if someone does something according to God, temptation is sure to come to him. For every good thing is either preceded or followed by temptation, and what is done according to God is not secure unless temptation has tested it. He also said: Nothing creates unity so much as rejoicing in the same things and thinking the same things. He also said: It is a mark of humility not to make light of a neighbour's kindness. One must accept it with thanksgiving, even if it is small and very slight. He also said: For my part, if some matter comes up, I would rather [?] act on my neighbour's advice and fail with his advice, if it turns out that way, than follow my own judgment and succeed. He also said: In every matter it is good to provide ourselves with a little less than we need, for it does no one good to have comfort in everything. He also said: In whatever matter came my way, I never wanted to get around it by human cleverness. I always do the little that is in my power, whatever it may be, and leave everything to God. He also said: Someone who has no will of his own always does his own will. He has nothing of his own beyond that, so whatever happens satisfies him, and he is always found doing his own will. For he does not want things to happen as he wants. He wants them as they happen. He also said: One should not correct a brother at the very moment he is sinning against one, nor at any other time for the sake of one's own revenge. He also said that love according to God is stronger than natural love. He also said: Do no evil, not even in jest. It happens that someone at first does evil with a laugh, but later, even against his will, he becomes fixed in

He also said that one should not wish to be freed from a passion because one wants to escape the distress it causes. One should truly hate it, as it says: I hated them with perfect hatred; they became my enemies.

He also said that it is impossible for anyone to be angry with his neighbour unless his heart is first lifted up against him, so that he despises him and considers himself superior. He also said: It is a sign that someone acts on a passion willingly when he is troubled at being reproved or corrected for it. But to bear calmly the
reproof for it, that is, the correction, is a sign that he acted on it because he was overcome or did not know better.

INSTRUCTION 20. A letter of the saint to a brother who had asked him about insensibility of soul and the cooling of love. 1. Brother, these things help against insensibility of soul. Continual reading of the divine Scriptures helps, together with the sayings of the God-bearing Fathers that move to compunction. So does remembering the fearful judgments of God, the soul's departure from the body, and the fearful powers that will meet it, the powers with whom it did evil in this short and miserable life. Remember too that you will stand before the dread and impartial judgment seat of Christ, and that you will have to give an account not only of deeds but also of words and thoughts, before God, all his angels and the whole of creation. Keep constantly in mind also the sentence that the fearful and just Judge will pronounce on those at his left: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. It is good also to remember the great afflictions that human beings suffer. Only in this way, and with difficulty, will the hard and insensible soul be softened and come to perceive its own evil condition. Your weakness in love for the brothers comes from accepting suspicious thoughts and trusting your own heart, and also from being unwilling to suffer anything that goes against your wishes. So do you want God to help you? First of all, do not trust your own suspicions at all. Strive with all your strength to humble yourself before the brothers and to cut off your own will for their sake. If one of them insults you or afflicts you in some other way, pray for him, as the Fathers said, as for someone who is doing you great good, a physician for your love of pleasure. This will lessen your anger, for according to the holy Fathers love is the bridle of anger. Above all, beseech God to give you watchfulness and understanding to know his good, acceptable and perfect will, and also strength to be equipped for every good work [?].

QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS OF THE SAME ABBA DOROTHEUS to the great elder, Saint Barsanuphius, and to his disciple Abba John, called the Prophet because of the gift [?] he had from God. QUESTION 1. From Abba Dorotheus to Abba John.
On mourning. Question 2. How can I keep mourning while I go in and out among people and carry out my duties? And [?] without tears.

[?] not mourning through tears, but tears through mourning. A person who lives among people acquires mourning if he cuts off his own will and pays no attention to other people's faults. For his thoughts gather [?], and once gathered they produce godly sorrow in the heart, and sorrow [?]. Question 3. What does enduring dishonour contribute to [?]? Answer. Take a man who is in debt to others. If he has not paid off the debt, he is a debtor wherever he goes, and he has no freedom to sit down anywhere and rest. But if he first suffers people's reproaches, he is ashamed, and then he pays the debt back. Once he is free, he can go out in public with confidence and great boldness, and sit wherever he likes. It is the same with a person: if he does all he can to bear insults, dishonour and losses for the sins he has committed, he learns humility and toil, and through these his sins are forgiven, as it is written: “See my humility and my toil,” and so on. Consider how many insults and reproaches our Master Christ endured before the cross, and only after these did he come to the cross. In the same way, no one can come into perfect, fruitful stillness and into the holy rest of perfection unless he first suffers with Christ and bears all his sufferings, remembering the Apostle who says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.” So do not be deceived, for there is no other way of salvation but this. [?] may he be with you according to his will, so that he may lay the foundation of your building well upon the rock, which is Christ. Question 4. Which way saves more surely, the way of toil or the way of humility? Tell me also, master, about forgetfulness, about attachment to certain people, and about guarding

Toil by itself is in vain and counts for nothing. For Scripture says: “See my humility and my toil, and forgive all my sins.” Whoever has this arrives quickly. Whoever has [?] the humility of being set at nought has the same, for being set at nought takes the place of toil. But whoever has humility on its own does enter, though more slowly. If anyone wants to hold on to true humility, let him not reckon himself as anything at all in any matter. This is true humility. Whoever receives the fire that the Lord came to cast upon the earth does not admit forgetfulness and captivity, because he always feels the fire. Take an example. If a man is at the point of death and fire comes near him, he feels it at once because of the pain. And whatever a man may be held captive by, if a burning coal falls on him [?]. Nor [?] does the fire remain in captivity, brother; it is quenched, since it is no longer fire. If you want to be freed from captivity too, you cannot do it any other way except by acquiring this fatherly [?] fire for yourself, for those things vanish before its heat. One acquires this fire by longing for God. It is good not to have too close a friendship with anyone of your own age, for such familiarity does not let mourning come. Do not be friends with anyone else who takes your mourning away from you either, for that does you no good and rather harms you. No one can acquire anything good except with much toil. So train your eyes not to look at anyone, and they will not fill your heart with that terrible over-familiarity which brings a monk's labours to utter ruin. Brother, unless the heart does all these things, seeking the Lord night and day, a person cannot make progress. If you give yourself to these things, you will attain them, for Scripture says: “Be still,” and so on. May the Lord grant you to understand these things.

What is the difference between being set at nought and humility? And what, again, is contrition of heart? If someone acquires the state of being set at nought by humbling himself in his heart, does he still need the outward reproaches and insults of people, and humbler tasks? Further, ought the humble-minded person to practise lowly deeds, or also to speak humbly?

Being set at nought takes two forms: one comes from the heart, and the other is brought on by people. Being set at nought by people is greater than being set at nought from the heart, because what comes from the heart does not involve nearly as much toil as what comes from people. For the heart labours greatly under what is brought on

from outside. But rushing of one's own accord into humble tasks does not lead anyone to progress; perhaps it leads rather to vainglory. What leads to progress, and to acquiring the state of being set at nought, is to be given an order and not argue back, but to carry it out obediently. Contrition of heart means not letting the heart [?] be taken up with alien thoughts. Humility means not reckoning oneself as anything at all in any matter, and cutting off one's own will in everything, so as to submit to everyone and to bear calmly whatever comes from others. This is true humility, and vainglory finds no room in it. Speaking humbly brings vainglory and does more harm than good. It is enough to say: “Forgive me, and pray for me.” Question 6. Should one cut off one's will in good things, or in indifferent things, or also in things that lead to the breaking of a commandment? And if I am given an order beyond my state, ought I to decline it, so that I do not bring grief and disturbance on myself later? Further, if someone needs the abba, to ask him something [?], and tells me to help him in the matter, should I agree to it, or does it bring me honour, as though I reckoned myself something after all? Further, if someone asks me to say a prayer, should I agree to put my hand to it and help someone? How far should one decline or contend where there is a transgression?

Brother, whoever wants to be [?] ought to have no will at all in any matter. The Lord taught this when he said: “I came into the world not to do my own will,” and so on. For the one who wants to do this or that, and declines for these reasons, either shows himself more discerning than the one who gives him the order, or is being mocked by demons. Both are evil and demonic, so you ought to obey in everything. Your abba, who gives you orders, bears your judgement, since he will be required to give an account for you. If an order seems heavy to you, ask him, and leave the matter to his discernment. But if it is brothers who give you the order, and you see or think that the matter will do harm or is beyond your strength, again ask the abba and do what he tells you. For if you try to judge not only the matters but also the people, you will bring affliction on yourself. Where the matter seems good, show obedience to the brothers. But where your thought hesitates, whether because the thing is beyond your strength or because it will do harm, refer it to your abba and do whatever he judges. For he knows what he is doing and how he cares for your [?]

soul, and be at rest. [?] then [?] to you, according to God [?]. For everything that is according to God is beneficial and brings no grief or disturbance. Nothing bad comes from what is good, since every good thing bears good fruit. [?] if someone asks you [?] to the abba, do it as if fulfilling an order [?] that you heard from the abba. For if he sets you at the gate and says, “Tell me about everyone who comes,” are you reckoning yourself something on your own account, or carrying out an order? Whether the abba [?] or does not say, that is no concern of yours. As for when you go into a cell [?]: if he tells you to pray, say “Forgive me” up to three times; and if he still insists after the third time, then do it with humility. And you, too, ask someone up to three times; if he does not want to, stop in peace and do not distress him. This is the true way of God. Take care to walk in it without hypocrisy and with a pure heart, while God gives you his hand and helps you through his grace. Question 7. Should one make concessions to the body in matters of diet when it has not yet completely broken down? And if someone's constitution does not agree with the usual food? And if someone who is suffering nothing declines a particular food as producing a particular passion, does he do well?

If a person sees that he is not troubled by any passion or under attack, he ought to make a small concession to the body. But if he is under attack, he should not. For it is clear that this apparent weakness too comes from the demons, since in true weakness, which is from God, the warfare also slackens. So where there is warfare, it is beneficial to wear down the body even if it falls ill, for it drives out [?] the soul. But if the cause of the disorder is clear, as when the body is weakened by a journey, perhaps, or by severe injuries, one ought to make concessions, though soberly and no more than necessary, since the demons too polish [?] their own. As for a poor constitution, one can sometimes force the thought a little. But if one cannot, one makes a small concession, for this too is a weakness. If someone learns that a particular food produces a passion, he ought not to eat it, for it proves to be a defeat for him, and he ought to guard [?]. Take care not to let this slip into forgetfulness, and believe that you are being saved along with those whom God helps and saves. Question 8. If I am eating with the brothers and my need is satisfied sooner [?], is it good for me to get up, or to stay until everyone gets up? And if I measure my portion of bread against all the dishes, do I do better?

[If] your need [is satisfied] and you cannot sit there without eating, get up. To sit and not eat is a greater thing than that. But to make your mouthfuls last [?] over all the [?dishes] is better than either. Question 9. What shall I do? I fear the shame of being dishonoured, and if I fall into conversation with certain people I am drawn into it so strongly and taken captive that I almost forget myself, and I am always ashamed to leave them.

If the conversation leads to edification and does not get in the way [?] of something more necessary, stay until the other has finished speaking. But if it is unprofitable, say: “Forgive me, I am still weak.” As for shame, think of the shame that sinners are going to suffer before all in the presence of the Lord, and of the passing [shame] that is for nothing [?]

Discourse 22. By the same holy Dorotheus: an explanation of certain phrases of holy Gregory that are sung with a melody [?] at holy Easter. 1. I should like to say a few words to you about the hymns we sing, so that you are not carried away by the melody, but so that your mind too may be kindled in proportion to the power of the words. What did we just sing? “Day of resurrection: let us offer ourselves as fruit.” In ancient times the children of Israel brought gifts to the Lord at feasts and festivals, as the law required: sacrifices, whole burnt offerings, firstfruits and the like. So holy Gregory exhorts us to keep the feast to the Lord as they did, and he urges us on, saying: “Day of resurrection,” that is, day of the holy feast, day of the divine festival, day of Christ's Pascha. What is Christ's Pascha? The children of Israel kept the Passover when they came out of Egypt. But the Pascha that holy Gregory now urges us to celebrate is kept by the soul when it goes out of the spiritual Egypt, that is, out of sin. For when the soul passes over from sin to virtue, it keeps the Passover to the Lord, as Evagrius said: “The Lord's Pascha is a passing over from evil.” Today, then, is the Lord's Pascha, the day of the bright feast, the day of the resurrection of Christ, who crucified sin and died and rose again for us. So let us also offer gifts to the Lord, sacrifices and whole burnt offerings, but not of irrational animals, which Christ does not want. For he did not desire the sacrifice and offering of irrational beings, and he took no pleasure in whole burnt offerings of calves and sheep. Isaiah also says: “What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord,” and so on. But since the Lamb of God was sacrificed for us, as the Apostle says, “For our Pascha has been sacrificed,

Christ,” to take away the sin of the world, and “became a curse for us,” as it is written, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” in order to redeem us from the curse of the law and so that we might receive adoption as sons, we too ought to offer him some gift of our own that pleases him. 2. What gift, then, or what sacrifice ought we to offer Christ on the day of the resurrection to please him, since he does not want sacrifices of irrational animals? The saint himself teaches us this too. Having said, “Day of resurrection,” he added, “let us offer ourselves as fruit.” And the Apostle says: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and well-pleasing to the Lord, which is your spiritual worship.” How, then, ought we to present our bodies to God as a living and holy sacrifice? By no longer doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, but walking by the Spirit and not gratifying the desire of the flesh. For this is what it means to put to death our earthly members. This is called a living sacrifice because the irrational animal that is led to sacrifice is sacrificed [?once] and dies. But the saints, offering themselves to God as a thank-offering, sacrifice themselves to God every day while still alive, as David says: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.” This is what holy Gregory means by “Let us offer ourselves as fruit”: that is, let us sacrifice ourselves, let us put ourselves to death all day long, as all the saints did for the sake of Christ our God, for the sake of him who died for us. And how did they put themselves to death? By not loving the world or the things in the world, as the Catholic Epistles say, but by renouncing the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes and the pride of life, that is, love of pleasure, love of money and vainglory; and by taking up the cross and following Christ, crucifying the world to themselves and themselves to the world. Of these the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.” See, this is how the saints put themselves to death. 3. And how did they offer themselves as fruit? By not living for themselves, but making themselves slaves to God's commandments and giving up their own wills for the sake of the commandment and of love for God and neighbour. As holy Peter said: “See, we have left everything and followed you.” What did he leave? He had no money, no possessions, no gold or silver. He had a net, and an old one at that, as holy John Chrysostom said. Yet he left, as he said, all his own wills and every attachment to this age, so that it is clear that even if he had had money

or property, he would have despised that too. And taking up the cross he followed Christ, in keeping with the saying, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” See, this is how the saints offered themselves as fruit: by putting themselves to death, as we said, to every attachment and to their own will, and living for Christ alone and for his commandments. So let us too offer ourselves as fruit, as holy Gregory teaches, for God wants us, his most precious possession. Truly, man is more precious than all the visible creatures. The Creator brought those into being by a word, saying, “Let this be,” and it was; and again, “Let the earth bring forth this,” and it was; and, “Let the waters bring forth,” and so on. But man he fashioned and adorned with his own hands. He appointed all those other things for man's service and rest, set him up as king over them all, and gave him the delights of paradise to enjoy. And what is more wonderful still, when man fell from there through his own sin, God called him back again through the blood of his only-begotten Son. So of all visible things man is God's most precious possession, and not only most precious, as the saint said, but also most his own. For “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And again: “God made man; in the image of God he made him,” and “he breathed into his face the breath of life.” And our Lord himself, when he came to dwell among us, took on the form of a man, the flesh of a man, of a new man; in short, he became everything that man is, except sin. 4. Through this he made man his own; he appropriated him, so to speak. So the saint spoke rightly and fittingly when he called man “the most precious possession.” Then he adds something even clearer: “Let us render to the Image what is according to the image.” How are we to do this? Let us learn from the Apostle, who says: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit.” Let us make our image clean, as we received it; let us wipe it clean of the filth of sin, so that its beauty may shine out through the virtues. David prays for this beauty when he says: “Lord, by your will grant strength to my beauty.” So let us cleanse what is according to the image in us, for God wants it back from us as he gave it: without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind. Let us render to the Image what is according to the image. Let us recognise our dignity. Let us learn what great goods we have been granted. Let us learn in whose image we were made. Let us not be ignorant of the great gifts he has given us purely out of his goodness and not because of our own worth.

Let us know that we were made in the image of God who made us. Let us honour the archetype. Let us not outrage the image of God in which we were made. Who, setting out to paint the emperor's image, would dare to put rotten paint on it, dishonour the emperor and be punished? No, he uses only precious, bright colours worthy of the emperor's image. Sometimes gold leaf is even applied to images of emperors, and the painter takes care to put into the image all of the emperor's visible features as far as he can, so that anyone who sees the image, which contains the whole imperial likeness, may think he is almost looking at the emperor himself, the archetype itself. For the image is glorious and splendid. So let us not dishonour our archetype either. We were made in the image of God; let us make our own image pure and honourable and worthy of the archetype. For if someone who dishonours the image of an earthly emperor, who shares his own nature, is punished, what ought we to suffer if we despise the divine image within us and do not render it back pure, as the saint said? 5. So let us honour the archetype. Let us know the power of the mystery, and for whom Christ died. The power of the mystery of Christ's death is this. We had obliterated what is according to the image in us through sin, and so we were dead, as the Apostle says, in trespasses and sins. Then God, who had made us in his own image, took pity on his own creature and his own image, became man for our sake, and accepted death on behalf of all, so that he might bring us, who had been put to death, back to the life from which we had fallen through disobedience. For he ascended his holy cross and crucified sin, the sin through which we had been driven out of paradise, and he led captivity captive, as it is written. What does “he led captivity captive” mean? Since Adam's transgression the enemy had taken us captive and held us in his power. From then on, when people's souls left their bodies, they went to Hades, for paradise had been shut. So Christ ascended to the height of the holy and life-giving cross and by his own blood delivered us from the captivity into which the enemy had taken us through the transgression. That is, he snatched us back out of the enemy's hand and, as it were, took us captive in turn, having conquered and overthrown the one who had made us captive. That is why it is called leading captivity captive. This is the power of the mystery. This is why Christ died for us: so that, as the saint said, he might bring us, who had been put to death, back to life. So we have been delivered from Hades through Christ's love for mankind, and it is now in our power to go to paradise. For the enemy no longer rules over us as a tyrant as he did before, nor does he hold us enslaved. 6. Only let us take care, brothers, and guard

ourselves from sin in act. For I have told you many times before that every sin committed in act brings us under subjection again, because we cast ourselves down and enslave ourselves of our own free will. Is it not a disgrace and a great misery if, after he has redeemed us from Hades by his own blood, and after we have heard all this, we go back and throw ourselves into Hades again? Do we not then deserve an even worse and more pitiable punishment? May God, who loves humankind, have mercy on us and give us watchfulness, so that we may understand and help ourselves, and find a little

DISCOURSE [?]. An explanation of the sayings of St Gregory that are chanted for the holy martyrs. 1. It is good to chant from the words of the holy God-bearing Fathers, because everywhere they are always eager to teach us everything that leads to the enlightenment of our souls. In them we also have the chance to learn from the appropriate words the very meaning of the commemoration being celebrated, whether it is a feast of the Lord, or of the holy martyrs, or simply of the Fathers, or any holy and illustrious day. So we too ought to chant with watchfulness and set our mind on the meaning of the words of the saints, so that not only our mouth, as it says in the Gerontikon, but also our heart chants together with our mouth. From the earlier hymn, then, we learned a little about holy Easter, as far as we were able; let us see now what St Gregory wants to teach us about the holy martyrs. The hymn for them which we sang just now, taken from his words, says: "Living victims, rational whole burnt offerings," and so on. What does "living victims" mean? A victim is anything dedicated as a sacrifice to God, a sheep, say, or an ox, or something of that kind. Why then does he call the holy martyrs "living victims"? Because a sheep brought for sacrifice is first slaughtered and dies, and only then is it divided and cut up for God. But the holy martyrs had their flesh cut while they were still alive, as they were scraped, tortured and dismembered. Sometimes the executioners would cut off their hands, and their feet and tongues, and gouge out their eyes, and on top of this they would scrape their sides until the very structure and arrangement of their internal organs could be seen. All these things, as I said, the saints endured while still alive, while they still had their souls in them, and that is why they are called "living victims." And "rational whole burnt offerings": why? Because a sacrifice is something different. Sometimes they do not offer the whole sheep but only its first portion, as it says in the Law: "the right shoulder, and the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys," and similar parts. Those who offered these were bringing sacrifices; they were offering, as it were, the first portion. And this is call-

ed a sacrifice. A whole burnt offering, on the other hand, is when they burn the whole sheep or ox, or whatever is being offered, entirely, as it says there: "the head with the feet and the entrails"; and sometimes the hide and the dung too. In short, they burn up the whole thing completely. This is called a whole burnt offering. In this way the sons of Israel performed both the sacrifices and the whole burnt offerings according to the Law. 2. Those sacrifices and whole burnt offerings were symbols of the souls that wish to be saved and to offer themselves to God. I will tell you a little about these things too, from what the Fathers have said, so that when you read them you may lift up your thoughts a little and our soul may be nourished. The shoulder, they say, stands for the practical life; for the hands are understood to refer to this, and, as we have said on various occasions, the shoulder is the strength of the hand. So they offered the strength of the right hand, that is, of good works, for the right hand is taken to mean what is good. And the same goes for all the other things we mentioned: the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys and the fat on them, the loins, the fat on the thighs, the heart, the breast, and so on. These too are likewise symbols. For all these things, as the Apostle says, happened to them as types, but they were written down for our instruction. And I tell you how the soul, as St Gregory says, has three parts. For it has the desiring part, the spirited part and the rational part. So they offered the lobe of the liver. The Fathers take the liver to mean desire, and the lobe of the liver is its tip. So in symbol they offered the tip of the desiring part, that is, its first portion, the finest and most precious part of it. This signifies loving nothing before God, and preferring nothing among all the objects of desire to the desire for God. For we said that they offered him the more precious part. The kidneys too, and the fat on them, and the loins, and the fat on the thighs signify the same thing by a kind of analogy, for there [?], they say, is desire. See, these are symbols of the desiring part. The symbol of the spirited part is the heart, for they say that anger resides there, and St Basil indicates this too when he says: "Anger is a boiling of the blood around the heart." The breast is a symbol of the rational part, for they take the chest to mean this. That is why they say that Moses, when he clothed Aaron in the high-priestly vestment, put the oracle on his breast, according to God's command. All these things, then, as we said, are symbols of the soul that through the practical life, with God's help, is purifying itself and returning to its natural state. For Evagrius says that the rational soul acts according to nature when its desiring part longs for virtue, its spirited part fights on virtue's behalf, and its rational part applies itself to the contemplation of created things.

A whole burnt offering, however, is when they offered the victim whole and entire and burned it just as it was, intact, complete, perfect. As we said above, this is a symbol of the perfect; it belongs to those who say, "See, we have left everything and followed you." It was to this measure that the Lord urged the man who said to him, "All these things I have kept from my youth," to come. For he answered him, "You lack one thing." What was it? "Take up your cross and come, follow me." So the holy martyrs offered themselves wholly to God in this way, and not only themselves but also what was theirs and what was around them. For, as St Basil says, what we are is one thing, what is ours is another, and what is around us is another; I have told you this on other occasions too. We are the mind and the soul; what is ours is the body; and what is around us is possessions and the other material things. So the saints offered themselves to God with their whole heart, their whole soul and their whole strength, as it is written: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind." For they despised not only children and wives and glory and money and all the rest of their property, but even their own bodies; and that is why they are called whole burnt offerings. And "rational," because man is a rational living being, and they were perfect sacrifices to God. Then comes the next phrase: "Sheep who know God and are known by God." How do they know God? As the Lord himself showed and taught when he said: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know my own and am known by my own." Why did he say, "My sheep hear my voice"? It means: they obey my word and keep my commandments, and for this reason they know me. For it is by keeping the commandments that the saints draw near to God, and the nearer they draw to him, the more they know him and are known by him, since God knows all things, both hidden things and deep things and things that do not exist. Why then does he say of the saints that they are "known by God"? Because, as I said, drawing near to him through the commandments, they know him and are known by him. For when someone turns away and distances himself from something, to that extent he is said not to know it; likewise, by drawing near, he is said to know and to be known. It is in this sense, then, that God too is said not to know sinners, insofar as they distance themselves from him. That is why the Lord himself says to such people: "Truly I tell you, I do not know you." So the saints, as I have often said, the more they acquire the virtues through the commandments, the more closely they are joined to God; and the more closely they are joined to him, the more they know him and are known by him. "Whose

fold wolves cannot enter." A fold is an enclosed place where the shepherd gathers his sheep and guards them, so that they are not carried off by wolves or stolen by robbers. But if the fold is weak at any point, it is easy to get into, and is readily plotted against by both wolves and robbers. The fold of the saints, however, is secured and guarded on every side; as the Lord said, it is where thieves do not break in, and nothing else harmful can plot against it. Let us pray, then, brothers, that we too may be counted worthy to be pastured with them, and to be found in the place of that blessed delight and rest of theirs. For even if we have not attained the state of the saints, even if we are not worthy to be in their glory, still we can avoid falling out of paradise, if we are watchful and force ourselves a little; as St Clement also says, even if someone is not crowned, let him strive not to be found far from those who are crowned. For in the palace there are great and splendid ranks of service, say the senate, the patricians, the generals, the prefects, the silentiaries, for these are highly honoured ranks. But there are also others serving in the same palace for a few coins; yet they too are said to serve the emperor, and they are inside the palace, even if they do not have the glory of the great; still, for the present they are there. And it happens that, advancing little by little, they too attain great ranks and splendid dignities. So let us also strive to escape sin in act, so that for the present we may get free of Hades; and in this way, through God's love for humankind, we can attain the very entrance to paradise, by the prayers of all the saints. Amen.
